articles.title: Connecting Claude and Other LLMs to a Custom .NET MCP Server – A Production‑Ready Guide
articles.description:
Quick Answer


connecting Claude and other LLMs to a custom .NET MCP server: Learn how to architect, secure, and optimize a custom .NET MCP server for Claude, Azure OpenAI, and other LLMs. Real‑world code, performance tricks, and production pitfalls included.
When you bolt Claude, GPT‑4 or any other LLM straight into a .NET endpoint, the first 200 requests look great. But as soon as you hit a few hundred concurrent users, you start seeing a cascade of symptoms: 200‑plus millisecond latency, sporadic 429s, cache pollution, and a brittle tool‑calling pipeline that breaks on the slightest provider change. The root cause is that most quick‑starts treat the LLM as a black‑box HTTP call and ignore the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the contract that lets you swap providers, reuse KV caches, and enforce tenant isolation without touching business logic.
Consider a SaaS company that offers a knowledge‑base chatbot to its customers. They ship a minimal API that forwards every user query to Claude. Within a week the product is used by 12,000 concurrent sessions. Suddenly the team sees:
Average response latency jumps from 800 ms to 3.2 s.
Rate‑limit errors from Claude surface 12% of the time.
Tenant A receives answers that belong to Tenant B.
Tool calls (e.g., SQL lookup) start timing out because the adapter no longer preserves the tenantId in the cache key.
Under the hood, the API was a simple wrapper around ClaudeClient.ChatAsync and a naive MemoryCache. There was no MCP layer, no unified tool registry, no observability, and no failover strategy. The result: a production system that can’t scale, is insecure, and is hard to debug.
Protocol‑agnostic vs. provider‑specific optimisations  
Pros of MCP: One codebase for all LLMs, centralised caching, consistent observability, easier compliance checks.


Cons: You lose provider‑level tuning knobs (e.g., Claude’s parallel_requests or Azure-ai-foundry-vs-azure-openai-service-observability-in-production-20261007" class="internal-link">Azure’s function_call Semantics) unless you expose them in the MCP schema. Adding a new field means updating every adapter and potentially breaking existing deployments.
Centralised cache vs. distributed cache  
Pros: A single Redis cluster simplifies key design and eviction policies.


Cons: Network latency to Redis can dominate inference time if the cluster is in a different region. A per‑tenant cache shard can mitigate this but increases operational complexity.
Strict tenant isolation vs. performance  
Pros: Prefixing keys with {tenantId}: guarantees no cross‑tenant leakage.


Cons: It reduces cache hit rates for shared system prompts. A shared cache with a deterministic hash of the system prompt and tenant ID can mitigate but requires careful key design.
Use the following matrix to decide whether to adopt a custom MCP Server or stick with provider SDKs.



Criterion
Custom MCP
Provider SDK




Multi‑tenant isolation required
✓
✗


Need to switch providers at runtime
✓
✗


Observability across providers
✓
✗


Latency budget < 1 s
✓ (with careful caching)
✓ (but no cache reuse)


Operational overhead acceptable
✓
✗ (less code but more provider lock‑in)



In most SaaS or enterprise scenarios, the benefits of a MCP Server outweigh the extra operational burden.
Even with a well‑designed MCP Server, you can hit failure modes:
Cache stampede – If many tenants hit a cache miss for the same system prompt, the server will flood the LLM backend. Mitigate with LazyCache or a SemaphoreSlim per key.
Provider drift – When a provider updates its API (e.g., Claude adds a new field), the adapter can silently break. Implement a versioned MCP schema and a health‑check that validates adapter compatibility.
Back‑pressure misconfiguration – A bounded channel that’s too small will drop requests under load; too large will consume memory. Tune the channel size based on observed QPS and average inference latency.
Security mis‑configuration – If tenant isolation is disabled or the API key is leaked to a malicious tenant, the KV cache can be read or corrupted. Use Azure AD scopes that map 1 to tenant IDs and enforce them in every request.
Ignoring the Metadata bag – Developers often forget to propagate tenant IDs into the adapter, leading to cross‑tenant cache pollution.
Hard‑coding system prompts – Embedding the system prompt in code means every provider change requires a redeploy. Store system prompts in a shared KV store and reference them by hash.
Over‑caching the entire conversation – Caching the full chat history can quickly exhaust Redis memory. Cache only the last N tokens or the prompt + first assistant message.
Not handling provider rate limits – A 429 from Claude is treated as a fatal error. Implement back‑off and a fallback policy (e.g., switch to Claude Instant).
Missing observability hooks – Without tracing at the adapter level, you can’t correlate latency spikes to specific providers or tool calls.
In a recent production rollout for a financial services firm, we adopted the following pattern that cut latency by 35% and eliminated cross‑tenant leaks:
Use RedisCache with HashTags to group keys by tenant. The key format is {tenantId}:prompt:{hash} and the hash is a SHA‑256 of the concatenated system prompt + user message.
Implement a RequestQueue that is a bounded Channel<McpChatRequest> with a back‑pressure strategy that returns HTTP 429 when full.
Expose a ProviderRegistry that maps provider names to adapters and includes a HealthCheck endpoint that pings each adapter’s /health route. If a provider is unhealthy, the registry marks it as degraded and routes traffic to a fallback provider.
Instrument the MCP server with OpenTelemetry, exporting traces to Azure Monitor. Use span.SetAttribute("provider") and span.SetAttribute("tenant") to filter dashboards by tenant.
For tool execution, use a ToolExecutorFactory that lazily loads executors from a DI container. This keeps the startup footprint small and allows adding new tools without redeploying the MCP server.
Deploy the MCP server as a stateless container in Azure Container Apps with a scale‑out rule based on CPU% > 70% and QPS > 200. Use a sidecar Redis instance in the same subnet to reduce network hops.
Inference latency – The adapter adds ~5 ms overhead. Cache hits reduce token count by 15–25%, cutting provider cost per request.
Throughput – With a 30 ms per request average, a single container can handle ~3k QPS. Scale horizontally by adding more replicas; use Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler with custom metrics.
Cache hit ratio – A 70% hit ratio on the KV cache keeps token usage low. Monitor CacheHitRate in Redis and adjust TTLs accordingly.
Network hops – Keep the MCP server, Redis, and LLM provider in the same region to avoid 200–300 ms round‑trips. If you must cross regions, use Azure Front Door to route traffic and reduce latency.
When scaling a MCP server, remember:
Statelessness – All state must be external (Redis, blob storage). This allows the autoscaler to spin up new instances without losing context.
Connection pooling – Use HttpClientFactory to pool connections to LLM providers. Disable KeepAlive for providers that don’t support it to avoid socket exhaustion.
Graceful shutdown – Implement IHostedService.StopAsync that drains the request queue before terminating. This prevents orphaned requests that never hit the LLM backend.
Observability – Expose a /metrics endpoint for Prometheus. Include metrics for request_latency_seconds, cache_hit_rate, provider_errors_total, and tenant_requests_total.
Cost control – Use Azure Cost Management to set alerts on token usage. Combine this with a RateLimiter that caps requests per tenant to avoid runaway costs.
Expose a single, unified /chat REST endpoint that accepts a JSON body with model, prompt, temperature, max_tokens and returns a standardized JSON response containing content, usage, provider, and cost_estimate.
Implement a provider‑router that maps the model field to the corresponding provider SDK via a shared interface, and add a fallback path to an alternative provider when the primary returns an error or times out.
Add per‑request cost estimation headers (e.g., X-Estimated-Cost) derived from live provider pricing tables, and emit provider‑specific latency metrics to your observability stack (Prometheus/CloudWatch).
Integrate a circuit‑breaker that trips after three consecutive failures for a provider, temporarily redirecting traffic to a safe fallback or returning a 503 with a Retry-After header.
Store all prompt templates in a versioned, cache‑able repository; load them at startup and expose a /prompts/{name} endpoint that returns the current template and its hash to detect drift.
Deploy a feature‑flag (e.g., LaunchDarkly, Split.io) that toggles between the custom MCP implementation and the provider SDK directly, enabling controlled roll‑outs and instant rollback if issues surface.
Connecting Claude and other LLMs to a custom .NET MCP server is not a novelty; it’s a maturity step that turns a brittle prototype into a production‑grade platform. The trade‑offs are clear: you pay operational overhead for a unified protocol, but you gain tenant isolation, observability, and the flexibility to orchestrate multiple providers. By following the patterns above—centralised adapters, bounded queues, tenant‑aware caching, and a robust observability stack—you can build a system that scales, stays secure, and remains maintainable even as you add new LLMs, tool calls, or vector database integrations.

whaeh: The Zero-Friction Terminal Copilot for Your Pipes
articles.description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle
When you're knee-deep in terminal outputs, scrolling through hundreds of lines of log files, Kubernetes pod descriptions, or sprawling man pages breaks your flow state. Copy-pasting logs into a web browser AI tool or managing bulky CLI chat interfaces slows you down.
whaeh (pronounced like that reaction when your command fails) is a lightweight, zero-dependency Go CLI tool that integrates seamlessly into standard Unix pipes (|). You pipe any stdout or stderr stream into whaeh alongside a natural language prompt, and it acts as an immediate terminal co-processor.
Instant Command Flag Discovery: Instead of searching through long man pages, pipe them straight to whaeh (e.g., man yt-dlp | whaeh "give me the command to download video as mp4").


Live Incident & Log Debugging: Intercept errors and debug live workloads without context switching (e.g., kubectl logs nginx-test | whaeh "what's the issue" or kubectl describe pod nginx-test | whaeh "why is this pod failing").


Terminal Stream Summarization: Distill large text dumps, build outputs, or trace files into quick action items right inside your shell.




  
  
  Demo


  
  



  
  
  Code




  
 / 
        whaeh
      
    

  
    
    
  



whaeh
whaeh is a Unix-style CLI for asking an AI about piped input or files.
Installation
Requirements
Go 1.23 or later
An AI provider:


Ollama running locally (the default)
Google Gemini
OpenAI
Install from source
git clone https://github.com/veenoise/whaeh.git
cd whaeh
go install .
The whaeh executable is installed in Go's binary directory. Make sure that
directory is on your PATH, then verify the installation:
whaeh version
To build a local executable instead:
go build -o whaeh .
Quick start
Ollama is the default provider and uses http://localhost:11434. Make sure
Ollama is running and that the selected model is available:
ollama pull llama3.2
whaeh "find the relevant command"
Ask about piped input or a file:
man tar | whaeh "how do I create a gzipped archive?"
whaeh --file README.md "summarize this"
For a one-off provider or model, use command-line flags:
whaeh --provider ollama
…

View on GitHub
whaeh is written in Go to guarantee instant startup times, zero external runtime dependencies, and cross-platform binary compatibility across Linux, macOS, and Windows.
Open-Source Local Inference: Built with first-class support for Ollama, allowing developers to run open-weight models locally (such as Gemma) for fully offline, air-gapped terminal operations.


Flexible Multi-Provider Backend: Includes native adapter interfaces to toggle dynamically between local Ollama models and cloud APIs like Gemini or OpenAI, depending on performance needs or available resources.


Unix Pipe Architecture: Utilizes standard Go os.Stdin buffer processing to capture piped terminal streams alongside command-line arguments without blocking stdout or corrupting ANSI formatting.




┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Piped Terminal Output   │
│ (logs, man pages, etc.) │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │
             ▼
      [ stdin stream ]
             │
             ├───────────────────┐
             ▼                   ▼
   ┌──────────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐
   │ Prompt Arguments │  │ whaeh CLI     │
   │ ("why is it down")│  │ (Go Binary)   │
   └──────────────────┘  └───────┬───────┘
                                 │
                   ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
                   ▼                           ▼
        [ Local Ollama / Gemma ]      [ Cloud APIs (Gemini/OpenAI) ]

In systems engineering and infrastructure operations, terminal output often contains sensitive operational data: internal IP addresses, database schemas, environment variables, or trace tokens.
Air-Gapped Data Privacy: Sending live system logs or kubectl describe outputs to external third-party endpoints is a major security risk for enterprise infrastructure. Running whaeh backed by local, open-weight models via Ollama guarantees that sensitive telemetry never leaves the machine.


Zero Latency & Cost Controls: Pipe operations happen thousands of times a day. Open models eliminate pay-per-token pricing models and network round-trips, turning whaeh into a instantaneous, cost-free utility.


Custom Model Fine-Tuning: Open-source architectures enable engineering teams to fine-tune local models on internal company documentation, runbooks, and proprietary CLI flags.

articles.title: How to run Kimi K3 in the Vercel AI SDK — one npm package, two lines of code
Detecta deepfakes políticos en 2026 con herramientas gratuitas
articles.description:
Deepfakes de líderes mundiales en 2026: cómo detectarlos en tiempo real con herramientas open‑source Introducción En los últimos meses Google Trends ha mostrado picos “Breakout” en búsquedas como “deepfake presidente” o “video falso elecciones”. Cada vez son más los clips falsos que aparecen en redes sociales y que ponen en riesgo la credibilidad de la información política. En este artículo verás, en menos de 5 min, cómo funciona la tecnología que genera esos vídeos, cuáles son los casos más virales de 2026 y, lo más importante, cómo montar un detector en tiempo real usando solo software libre. Tipo de modelo Ventajas Desventajas Herramientas open‑source más usadas (2026) GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks) Rápidos de entrenar, buen nivel de detalle estático Artefactos visibles en bordes, poca coherencia temporal DeepFaceLab, Faceswap Difusión (Stable Diffusion Video, DDIM) Vídeos suaves, menos ruido, sincronía labial avanzada Necesitan GPU potente y más tiempo de inferencia Stable‑Video‑Diffusion, AnimateDiff Hybrid (GAN + Difusión + Audio‑Lip‑Sync) Calidad casi fotográfica, audio perfectamente alineado Complejidad de pipeline, consumo energético alto Sora‑Pipeline, Audio2Face En 2026 la combinación difusión + audio‑lip‑sync es la que está detrás de la mayoría de los deepfakes políticos virales (por ejemplo, el falso discurso de la presidenta de Brasil en el G20). Fecha Líder Tema del vídeo Plataforma donde se viralizó Comentario de detección 12 mar 2026 Ursula von der Leyen (UE) “Anuncio de nuevo impuesto a la IA” TikTok (8 M visualizaciones) Detectado por DeepDetect por parpadeo irregular 27 abr 2026 Joe Biden (EE. UU) “Mensaje de apoyo a la reforma migratoria” Twitter (12 M retweets) Modelo de difusión con audio‑lip‑sync, sin artefactos visibles 03 may 2026 Xi Jinping (China) “Declaración sobre la crisis climática” Weibo (15 M vistas) Detectado por análisis de compresión JPEG (artefactos en fondo) 19 jun 2026 Narendra Modi (India) “Invitación a elecciones anticipadas” WhatsApp (cadenas de 2 M) Señalado por DeepTrace por inconsistencias en la luz del fondo A continuación tienes un pipeline mínimo que puedes ejecutar en una máquina con GPU (NVIDIA RTX 3080 o superior). Usa únicamente librerías gratuitas y está listo para procesar vídeos en directo desde una URL o archivo local. # Sistema operativo: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (también funciona en WSL2) # Python >= 3.10 # CUDA 12.x + cuDNN Instala los paquetes necesarios: # 1. Crear entorno virtual python3 -m venv venv_deepdetect source venv_deepdetect/bin/activate # 2. Instalar PyTorch con soporte CUDA pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121 # 3. Librerías de detección pip install opencv-python ffmpeg-python tqdm \ transformers==4.41.0 \ diffusers==0.27.0 \ facenet-pytorch==2.5.2 \ numpy==1.26.4 # Modelo de detección de artefactos de compresión (DeepDetect) git clone https://github.com/DeepDetectAI/deepdetect.git cd deepdetect git checkout v2.1 # versión optimizada para vídeo python -m pip install -e . # Modelo de análisis de parpadeo (BlinkCheck) basado en MediaPipe git clone https://github.com/google/mediapipe.git cd mediapipe python -m pip install . import cv2, ffmpeg, numpy as np, torch from deepdetect import DeepDetectModel from mediapipe import solutions as mp_solutions from tqdm import tqdm # Cargar modelos dd_model = DeepDetectModel('weights/compression_artifacts.pt') blink = mp_solutions.face_mesh.FaceMesh( static_image_mode=False, max_num_faces=1, refine_landmarks=True, min_detection_confidence=0.5, min_tracking_confidence=0.5, ) def analizar_video(ruta): """Devuelve un puntaje de autenticidad entre 0 (fake) y 1 (real).""" # 1️⃣ Extraer frames (1 fps para rapidez) probe = ffmpeg.probe(ruta) fps = eval(probe['streams'][0]['r_frame_rate']) total_frames = int(probe['streams'][0]['duration'] * fps) step = int(fps) # 1 frame por segundo scores = [] for i in tqdm(range(0, total_frames, step)): out, _ = ( ffmpeg.input(ruta, ss=i/fps) .filter('scale', 640, -1) .output('pipe:', vframes=1, format='image2', vcodec='png') .run(capture_stdout=True, capture_stderr=True) ) img = cv2.imdecode(np.frombuffer(out, np.uint8), cv2.IMREAD_COLOR) # 2️⃣ Artefactos de compresión comp_score = dd_model.predict(img) # 3️⃣ Parpadeo anómalo results = blink.process(cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR_RGB)) blink_score = 0.0 if results.multi_face_landmarks: # cálculo muy simplificado: distancia entre párpados landmarks = results.multi_face_landmarks[0].landmark eye_dist = np.linalg.norm( np.array([landmarks[159].x, landmarks[159].y]) - np.array([landmarks[145].x, landmarks[145].y]) ) blink_score = 1.0 - np.clip(eye_dist * 30, 0, 1) # 1 = normal # 4️⃣ Combinar final = 0.6 * comp_score + 0.4 * blink_score scores.append(final) return float(np.mean(scores)) if __name__ == '__main__': url = 'https://example.com/video.mp4' # o ruta local puntaje = analizar_video(url) print(f'🔎 Puntaje de autenticidad: {puntaje:.2f}') if puntaje < 0.5: print('⚠️ Probable deepfake') else: print('✅ Parece genuino') Cómo funciona Compresión – El modelo DeepDetect reconoce patrones de cuantización típicos de los algoritmos de exportación de vídeo sintético. Parpadeo – Los deepfakes basados en GAN suelen generar parpadeos irregulares; MediaPipe mide la apertura de los párpados y detecta anomalías. Ponderación – Se combinan ambos indicadores (60 % compresión, 40 % parpadeo) para obtener un puntaje global. 3.4. Integración rápida en una página web Si prefieres un widget HTML/JS que cualquiera pueda usar sin instalar nada, copia este bloque en tu sitio y enlaza el script deepdetect-widget.js (disponible en el repositorio del artículo).
El widget permite arrastrar un archivo o pegar una URL y muestra el puntaje en segundos. Herramienta mencionada: Heroku

articles.description: この記事では、Amazon EC2 インスタンス構成証明、NitroTPM、Attestable AMI を使用して、セルフマネージド型データベースでゼロオペレーターアクセス (ZOA) を実現する方法を説明します。Nix Flakes で再現可能な AMI をビルドして PCR 測定値を算出し、AWS KMS キーポリシーの条件に設定します。これにより、LUKS で暗号化された EBS ボリュームを、正しい AMI で起動したインスタンスでのみ復号できるようにします。PostgreSQL を例に、dm-verity やセキュアブートを組み合わせたブート時の信頼チェーンも詳しく解説します。

サイトを支える静的サイトジェネレーターも、Eleventy から Deno ベースの Lume へ移行するという大きな技術的転換も経験しました。
 -->
 Information
記事執筆中に Deno が1年後に開発を終了するという発表が飛び込んできました。
Deno is joining Cloudflare | Deno
Lume を採用しているので、今後の動向を注視して動きたいと思います。

この5年は、生成AIの進化とともに歩んだ5年でもありました。
2023年、トップページのコラム「豆香の豆知識」を GPT-3 で開始。その後 GPT-4、GPT-4 Turbo、GPT-4o と、豆香は世代交代を重ねてきました（GPT-5 へのアップデートを忘れてたことを記事書いてて思い出しました😅）
2024年には記事サイドバーの挿絵を DALL-E-3 で自動生成する機能を追加。豆香は記事 PR へのコメントやアクセス集計の通知役としても社内で活躍しています
2024年に英訳記事の自動生成を開始(現在は多くの記事が英語で読めます)、2025年には中国語訳も追加し、海外からのアクセスも徐々に伸びています
自社メディアの運営自体に生成AIを積極的に取り込んできたのも、このサイトらしい特徴だと思います。
恒例企画・コミュニティの醸成
#
執筆の裾野を広げるための企画も定着してきました。
アドベントカレンダー: 2022年に初開催(16名、うち7名が初投稿)して以来、毎年末の恒例行事に
夏のリレー連載: 2023年に初開催(14本、新規執筆者11名、営業職や新卒社員もデビュー)
春の新人向け連載: 2024年に初開催し、新人エンジニアやプロジェクトマネージャー向けの記事群が生まれる場に
これらの企画を通じて、普段は筆を執らないメンバーがデビューするきっかけが生まれ、現在の執筆者数の広がりにつながっています。
SNS をはじめとしたメディアとの連動
#
公式 X(旧Twitter) アカウントの開設から始まり、Bluesky、Facebook、note と発信チャネルを広げてきました。執筆者が JJUG CCC などの社外カンファレンスに登壇する機会も生まれ、記事が社外での発表につながる好循環も生まれています。
技術発信 – 豆蔵 MAMEZO
営業、採用への波及効果
#
記事を書き続けてきたことで、デベロッパーサイトはエンジニア個々人のスキルや得意領域をアピールする場としても機能するようになってきました。実際に、記事を読んだお客様から執筆者を名指しで新規の引き合いをいただき、そのまま受注につながったケースも出てきています。
今後の展望
#
5周年の節目を迎え、現在デベロッパーサイトはリニューアルに向けて動き出しています。より読みやすい、モダンなサイトへと生まれ変わる予定です。多くの読者にとって「最もノイズが少なく、技術情報に集中できるUI」を目指し、記事ページの可読性向上や、ダークモードのネイティブ対応も計画しています。実装プロセス自体も最新のAI駆動開発（AI-Driven Development）で進めていきます。サイト自体を「生成AIを実践投入するための社内プロジェクト」として位置づけることで、これまで積み重ねてきた生成AIとの歩みをさらに一歩進めたいと考えています。
内容についても、さらなる充実を目指し、開発系の Tips はもちろんのこと、ロボティクスや生成 AI など我々が取り組み、また読者の皆様も興味を持つであろう内容を充実させて行きたいと考えています。アドベントカレンダーや夏のリレー連載、春の新人向け連載といった恒例企画も継続し、まだ執筆デビューしていないメンバーが筆を執るきっかけを作り続けていきます。また、英訳・中国語訳記事の拡充を通じて、国内にとどまらず海外のエンジニアにも豆蔵の技術発信を届けていきたいです。
次の5年、10年先も「開発に役立つサイト」として、そして豆蔵という会社の技術力・人となりが伝わるメディアとして育てていきたいと考えています。
さいごに
#
以上、豆蔵デベロッパーサイト5周年の振り返りでした。改めて振り返ってみると、立ち上げ当初2名だった執筆陣が83名まで広がり、900本を超える記事が積み上がったことに、感慨深いものがあります。ここまで続けてこられたのは、折にふれて記事を書いてくれた執筆者の皆さん、そして何より読み続けてくださっている読者の皆さんのおかげです。この場を借りて御礼申し上げます。
6年目以降も、変わらず技術と現場のリアルを発信するメディアであり続けたいと思います。引き続き豆蔵デベロッパーサイトをよろしくお願いいたします。
よかったらフィードの購読、X や Bluesky でのフォローもお願いします。Facebook でも本サイトの注目記事をはじめ豆蔵に関するイベントを紹介しています。note にも時々本サイト関連の記事が掲載されています。

articles.title: vLLM起動をAWS Lambda化！最安スポット探索と自動フォールバック機能の実装
articles.description:
はじめに # これは、思いついたアイデアや気になるクラウド技術を、まずは好奇心のままに手を動かして形にしてみる技術検証ログです。 前回の記事（EC2スポット×vLLMをSSMでセキュア化！ポート開放ゼロで繋ぐ）では、AWS Systems Manager（SSM）Session Managerによるポートフォワーディングを導入し、セキュリティグループのインバウンドを完全に閉塞（ポート開放ゼロ）しながら、SSH鍵管理を完全撤廃したセキュアなGPU利用環境を構築しました。 しかし、第3回・第4回と機能を追加していく中で、クライアント側（WSL / Mac等）の起動スクリプト（Bash）に新たな運用課題が生じていました： 探索レイテンシーの遅さ（直列処理の限界）: スポット枯渇（全滅）時の対応: InsufficientInstanceCapacity）することがあります。その際、エラーでスクリプトが止まり、手動でオンデマンドインスタンスを立て直すなどの二度手間が発生していました。 ローカル環境の肥大化と保守性: そこで今回は、「いっそクラウド側で世界中の最安スポットGPUを並列で高速に自動探索・起動してくれるサーバーレスAPIを作ってしまえば面白いのでは？」というアイデアを形にするため、これらの判定・探索ロジックをすべてクライアントから切り離し、AWS Lambdaによる「サーバーレスGPUブローカー」 へと進化させます。 Pythonの concurrent.futures によるマルチリージョン・マルチAZの高速並列スキャン（1秒台で完了）と、スポット枯渇時のスマートな「オンデマンド・フォールバック機能」 を実装した実践的な手法を紹介します。 --> Information 📚 関連する過去の検証記事 第1回（基本構成）: AWS×UserDataでvLLMを自動起動！停止時コストほぼゼロのローカルLLM環境 第2回（Cline連携）: 自前vLLMをOpen WebUI経由でVS Code（Cline）に接続！トークンフリーで開発する 第3回（スポット活用）: EC2スポットインスタンス×vLLMでGPUコストを大幅削減する 第4回（SSMセキュア化）: EC2スポット×vLLMをSSMでセキュア化！ポート開放ゼロで繋ぐ サーバーレスGPUブローカーのアーキテクチャ # 📌 このセクションの要点 flowchart TD subgraph Client ["ローカル開発端末 (Bashスクリプト)"] CLI["./01_start_vllm_ssm.sh
(--on-demand / --strategy)"] Tunnel["SSM ポートフォワーディング
(localhost:8000 -> EC2:8000)"] end subgraph AWS_Mgmt ["AWS 管理基盤 (Lambda)"] Broker["vLLM Broker Lambda
(Python 3.12 / Boto3)"] Advisor["AWS Spot Advisor
(JSON 中断率)"] end subgraph Multi_Region ["マルチリージョン EC2 群"] direction LR R1["東京 (ap-northeast-1)"] R2["オレゴン (us-west-2)"] R3["バージニア (us-east-1)"] R4["オハイオ (us-east-2)"] R5["フランクフルト (eu-central-1)"] end CLI -->|"1. invoke (JSON)"| Broker Broker -.->|"並列価格・AZ取得 (1秒)"| Multi_Region Broker -.->|中断頻度取得| Advisor Broker -->|"2. スポット起動試行 (順次)"| Multi_Region Broker -- "スポット全滅時: エラー案内 or
オンデマンド(cost/latency)起動" --> Multi_Region Broker -->|"3. Instance ID & Region 返却"| CLI CLI -->|4. SSM ポートフォワード接続| Tunnel アーキテクチャの進化ポイント # 項目 第4回までの構成 (クライアントBash) 今回の構成 (Lambda ブローカー) メリット 探索速度 15〜30秒以上（CLIを直列実行） 約1〜2秒（Pythonスレッド並列） 待ち時間を大幅に短縮 クライアントの責務 価格・中断率の取得、探索計算、起動試行 Lambda呼び出しとSSMトンネル接続のみ 複雑な探索ロジックから解放 スポット枯渇時 エラーで中断、手動対応 明確なエラー案内 & オンデマンド切替 開発作業を止めずにリカバリ可能 通常起動戦略 なし 「コスト最安」または「レイテンシー最小」 業務の優先度に応じた柔軟な選択 スポット枯渇時のフォールバック設計 # スポットインスタンスは余剰キャパシティを利用するため、世界中でGPU需要がピークに達した時間帯には、全候補リージョンで InsufficientInstanceCapacity が返ってくる「スポット枯渇」が発生します。 本システムでは、以下の2段構えのフォールバックポリシーを採用しています： デフォルト（スポット起動時）: ALL_SPOT_EXHAUSTED を返却。エラーメッセージには「通常起動オプション（--on-demand）を付与して再実行できる旨」を分かりやすく案内します。勝手にオンデマンド課金に切り替わって意図せぬ出費が発生する事故を未然に防ぎます。 オンデマンド指定時（--on-demand）: --on-demand フラグを指定して再実行します。その際、以下の2つの戦略（--strategy）を選択できます： cost（最安コスト重視・デフォルト）: 海外リージョンを含めた全リージョンのオンデマンド定価（ドル換算）を比較し、最も定価が安いリージョンで起動。 latency（低遅延重視）: 物理的に最も近い東京リージョン（ap-northeast-1）を最優先で起動し、快適なタイピング・レスポンスを確保。 Lambda関数の実装 (handler.py) # Lambda関数のコアロジックです。外部ライブラリを必要とせず、標準ライブラリ（concurrent.futures, urllib.request）と boto3 だけで完結します。 --> Information 💡 工夫ポイント：UserDataのS3外出しと3行ブートストラップ S3（s3://${S3_BUCKET}/scripts/startup.sh）へ外出し しています。 EC2に渡すUserDataは「S3からスクリプトを取得して実行するわずか3行」に留めることで、以下のメリットが得られます： Lambdaコードの大幅なスリム化: 100行を超えるBashヒアドキュメントを排除でき、コード全体の可読性が向上。 高速な試行錯誤: 起動スクリプトを微修正したいとき、Lambda関数を再ビルド・再デプロイすることなく、S3上のスクリプトを更新するだけで即時反映。 UserDataの16KB制限回避: スクリプトがどれだけ肥大化しても、EC2のUserDataサイズ上限（16KB）に抵触しません。 handler.py（クリックで展開） """ vLLM GPU Spot Broker Lambda マルチリージョンのスポット探索、最適リージョン選定、Spot起動、Terminateを統括するサーバーレスブローカー """ import json import logging import urllib.request import concurrent.futures import boto3 from botocore.config import Config import os logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) # 候補リージョンとインスタンスタイプ env_regions = os.environ.get("TARGET_REGIONS") CANDIDATE_REGIONS = [r.strip() for r in env_regions.split(",") if r.strip()] if env_regions else ["ap-northeast-1", "eu-central-1", "us-east-2", "us-east-1", "us-west-2"] INSTANCE_TYPE = os.environ.get("INSTANCE_TYPE", "g6.xlarge") IAM_ROLE_NAME = os.environ.get("INSTANCE_PROFILE_NAME", "vllm-ssm-instance-profile") TAG_SERVER_NAME = os.environ.get("TAG_SERVER_NAME", "vllm-ssm-spot-node") S3_BUCKET_NAME = os.environ.get("S3_BUCKET_NAME", "vllm-models-storage") ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME = os.environ.get("ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME", "vllm-openai") # リージョン別 AMI ID キャッシュ (Ubuntu 22.04 Deep Learning AMI) AMI_MAPPING = { "ap-northeast-1": "ami-0152728adca68ed36", "eu-central-1": "ami-0efde0090dab8cacf", "us-east-2": "ami-032b37e4db407994d", "us-east-1": "ami-012ba162b9cd2729c", "us-west-2": "ami-0ca70308d230e8a6e", } # リージョン別 オンデマンド参考価格 ($/h: g6.xlarge) と東京からの目安RTT (ms) ON_DEMAND_METRICS = { "ap-northeast-1": {"price": 1.3412, "latency_ms": 15, "name": "東京 (最低遅延・国内)"}, "us-west-2": {"price": 0.9840, "latency_ms": 110, "name": "オレゴン (コスト最安・中遅延)"}, "us-east-2": {"price": 0.9840, "latency_ms": 150, "name": "オハイオ (コスト最安)"}, "us-east-1": {"price": 0.9840, "latency_ms": 170, "name": "バージニア (コスト最安)"}, "eu-central-1": {"price": 1.2024, "latency_ms": 230, "name": "フランクフルト"}, } # S3外出しブートストラップ UserData (本体は s3://.../scripts/startup.sh から高速取得) USERDATA_BOOTSTRAP = """#!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail LOG_FILE="/var/log/userdata-bootstrap.log" exec > >(tee -a "${LOG_FILE}" | logger -t user-data -s 2>/dev/console) 2>&1 AWS_REGION="__AWS_REGION__" S3_BUCKET="__S3_BUCKET_NAME__" DOCKER_IMAGE="__DOCKER_IMAGE__" echo "=== S3から起動スクリプト (startup.sh) を取得 ===" aws s3 cp "s3://${S3_BUCKET}/scripts/startup.sh" /tmp/startup.sh --region "${AWS_REGION}" chmod +x /tmp/startup.sh echo "=== startup.sh 実行 ===" /tmp/startup.sh "${AWS_REGION}" "${S3_BUCKET}" "${DOCKER_IMAGE}" """ def get_spot_advisor_data(): """Spot Advisor から中断頻度ランクを取得""" url = "https://spot-bid-advisor.s3.amazonaws.com/spot-advisor-data.json" tiers = {} try: req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "Lambda-Broker"}) with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=3) as res: adv = json.loads(res.read().decode("utf-8")).get("spot_advisor", {}) for r, info in adv.items(): tier = info.get("Linux", {}).get(INSTANCE_TYPE, {}).get("r", 4) tiers[r] = tier except Exception as e: logger.warning(f"Spot Advisor 取得失敗: {e}") return tiers def query_region_metrics(region, advisor_tiers): """単一リージョンのスポット価格・AZ数を取得""" boto_cfg = Config(connect_timeout=2, read_timeout=3, retries={"max_attempts": 1}) ec2 = boto3.client("ec2", region_name=region, config=boto_cfg) try: res = ec2.describe_spot_price_history( InstanceTypes=[INSTANCE_TYPE], ProductDescriptions=["Linux/UNIX"], MaxResults=10, ) prices = res.get("SpotPriceHistory", []) if not prices: return None # 最安値とAZ数 min_price = min(float(p["SpotPrice"]) for p in prices) azs = set(p["AvailabilityZone"] for p in prices) az_count = len(azs) tier = advisor_tiers.get(region, 4) return { "region": region, "min_price": min_price, "az_count": az_count, "tier": tier, } except Exception as e: logger.error(f"Error querying {region}: {e}") return None def select_best_region(): """全候補リージョンを並列評価して最適リージョンを算出""" Lambda 関数 (${FUNCTION_NAME}) の作成/更新 ===" if aws lambda get-function --region "${REGION}" --function-name "${FUNCTION_NAME}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "既存のLambda関数コードを更新中..." aws lambda update-function-code \ --region "${REGION}" \ --function-name "${FUNCTION_NAME}" \ --zip-file "fileb://${TMP_ZIP}" >/dev/null else echo "新しいLambda関数を作成中..." aws lambda create-function \ --region "${REGION}" \ --function-name "${FUNCTION_NAME}" \ --runtime "python3.12" \ --role "${ROLE_ARN}" \ --handler "handler.lambda_handler" \ --zip-file "fileb://${TMP_ZIP}" \ --timeout 60 \ --memory-size 256 \ --description "Multi-region spot instance broker for vLLM" >/dev/null fi rm -f "${TMP_ZIP}" echo "=== デプロイ完了！ ===" echo "Lambda 関数名: ${FUNCTION_NAME} (${REGION})" 探索ロジックを手放したクライアント側スクリプト (01_start_vllm_ssm.sh) # ローカルPC側の起動スクリプトは、複雑なマルチリージョン計算や中断率データの取得をすべてクラウド側へ手放し、「Lambdaを呼び出して起動されたインスタンス情報を受け取り、SSMポートフォワーディングを張る」 というローカル環境の接続・トンネル管理に専念する構成へと進化します。 01_start_vllm_ssm.sh（クリックで展開） #!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail # ============================================================================== # 01_start_vllm_ssm.sh # Lambdaブローカーを呼び出して最安スポットを起動し、SSMポートフォワーディングで安全に直結する # ============================================================================== SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)" INSTANCE_STATE_FILE="${SCRIPT_DIR}/.current_instance_id" TUNNEL_PID_FILE="${SCRIPT_DIR}/.current_tunnel_pid" REGION_STATE_FILE="${SCRIPT_DIR}/.current_region" TUNNEL_LOG="${SCRIPT_DIR}/.current_tunnel.log" BROKER_REGION="ap-northeast-1" FUNCTION_NAME="vllm-spot-broker" # オプション解析 USE_ON_DEMAND="false" STRATEGY="cost" while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do case "$1" in --on-demand) USE_ON_DEMAND="true" shift ;; --strategy) STRATEGY="${2:-cost}" shift 2 ;; -h|--help) echo "使用方法: $0 [オプション]" echo "" echo "オプション:" echo " --on-demand 通常起動（オンデマンド）で起動する（デフォルトはスポット起動）" echo " --strategy 通常起動時の優先戦略（デフォルト: cost）" echo " cost : オンデマンド単価が最も安いリージョンを選択（米オレゴン等: 約\$0.98/h）" echo " latency : レイテンシーが最も小さいリージョンを選択（東京: 約\$1.34/h）" echo " -h, --help ヘルプを表示" exit 0 ;; *) echo "不明なオプション: $1" echo "ヘルプ: $0 --help" exit 1 ;; esac done TMP_RES=$(mktemp) if [ "${USE_ON_DEMAND}" = "true" ]; then echo "=== 1. サーバーレスGPUブローカー（Lambda）呼び出し [通常起動 / 戦略: ${STRATEGY}]... ===" PAYLOAD=$(jq -n --arg mode "on-demand" --arg strategy "${STRATEGY}" '{"action":"launch","mode":$mode,"strategy":$strategy}') else echo "=== 1. サーバーレスGPUブローカー（Lambda）呼び出し [スポット探索 & 起動]... ===" PAYLOAD='{"action":"launch","mode":"spot"}' fi aws lambda invoke \ --region "${BROKER_REGION}" \ --function-name "${FUNCTION_NAME}" \ --payload "${PAYLOAD}" \ --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \ "${TMP_RES}" >/dev/null STATUS=$(jq -r '.status // "error"' "${TMP_RES}") if [ "${STATUS}" != "success" ]; then ERROR_CODE=$(jq -r '.error_code // ""' "${TMP_RES}") MESSAGE=$(jq -r '.message // ""' "${TMP_RES}") echo "==========================================================" if [ "${ERROR_CODE}" = "ALL_SPOT_EXHAUSTED" ]; then echo "❌ スポット在庫切れ: 全候補リージョンでスポットインスタンスを調達できませんでした。" echo "----------------------------------------------------------" echo "【試行した候補リージョンと結果】" jq -r '.fallback_attempts[]? | " - \(.region) (\(.score // "-")点 / \(.rank // "-")): \(.reason)"' "${TMP_RES}" echo "" echo "💡 通常起動（オンデマンド）であれば確実に起動可能です。" echo " 以下のコマンドで再実行してください:" echo "" echo " # コスト最安リージョン（米オレゴン等: 約\$0.98/h）で通常起動:" echo " $0 --on-demand --strategy cost" echo "" echo " # レイテンシー最小リージョン（東京: 約\$1.34/h）で通常起動:" echo " $0 --on-demand --strategy latency" else echo "エラー: Lambdaの起動リクエストが失敗しました。" echo "${MESSAGE}" cat "${TMP_RES}" fi echo "==========================================================" rm -f "${TMP_RES}" exit 1 fi MARKET_TYPE=$(jq -r '.market_type // "spot"' "${TMP_RES}") INSTANCE_ID=$(jq -r '.instance_id' "${TMP_RES}") SELECTED_REGION=$(jq -r '.region' "${TMP_RES}") echo "${INSTANCE_ID}" > "${INSTANCE_STATE_FILE}" echo "${SELECTED_REGION}" > "${REGION_STATE_FILE}" echo "==========================================================" if [ "${MARKET_TYPE}" = "on-demand" ]; then STRAT=$(jq -r '.strategy // "cost"' "${TMP_RES}") PRICE=$(jq -r '.on_demand_price // "-"' "${TMP_RES}") LATENCY=$(jq -r '.latency_ms // "-"' "${TMP_RES}") REG_NAME=$(jq -r '.region_name // ""' "${TMP_RES}") echo " ⚡ 通常起動（オンデマンド）完了: 戦略 = ${STRAT}" echo " 選定リージョン : ${SELECTED_REGION} (${REG_NAME})" echo " インスタンスID : ${INSTANCE_ID}" echo " オンデマンド価格: \$${PRICE}/h" echo " 目安レイテンシー: 約 ${LATENCY} ms" else PRICE=$(jq -r '.spot_price // "-"' "${TMP_RES}") SCORE=$(jq -r '.score // "-"' "${TMP_RES}") RANK=$(jq -r '.rank // "-"' "${TMP_RES}") echo " 🏆 最適スポットリージョン選定完了: ${SELECTED_REGION} (${RANK} / ${SCORE}点)" echo " インスタンスID: ${INSTANCE_ID}" echo " スポット価格 : \$${PRICE}/h" FALLBACK_COUNT=$(jq -r '.fallback_attempts | length // 0' "${TMP_RES}") if [ "${FALLBACK_COUNT}" -gt 0 ]; then echo " ⚠️ 上位候補リージョンで一時的なスポット在庫不足が発生したため、自動フォールバックしました:" jq -r '.fallback_attempts[] | " - \(.region) (\(.score)点 / \(.rank)): \(.reason)"' "${TMP_RES}" fi fi echo "==========================================================" rm -f "${TMP_RES}" # インスタンスの実行状態（running）待機 echo "インスタンスが running 状態になるのを待機中..." aws ec2 wait instance-running --region "${SELECTED_REGION}" --instance-ids "${INSTANCE_ID}" # Git Bash環境向けにSessionManagerPluginのパスを追加 if [ -d "/c/Program Files/Amazon/SessionManagerPlugin/bin" ]; then export PATH="${PATH}:/c/Program Files/Amazon/SessionManagerPlugin/bin" fi # --- 2. SSMエージェントのオンライン待機 --- echo "=== 2. SSMエージェントのオンライン待機 ===" echo "EC2インスタンス内部のSSM Agentが接続されるのを待機中..." SSM_OK=false for i in {1..30}; do STATUS=$(aws ssm describe-instance-information \ --region "${SELECTED_REGION}" \ --filters "Key=InstanceIds,Values=${INSTANCE_ID}" \ --query "InstanceInformationList[0].PingStatus" \ --output text 2>/dev/null || true) if [ "${STATUS}" = "Online" ]; then echo " SSM Agent が Online になりました！ (${i}回目の試行)" SSM_OK=true break fi echo -n "." sleep 3 done echo "" if [ "${SSM_OK}" != "true" ]; then echo "エラー: SSM Agent が Online になりませんでした。IAMロールやアウトバウンド通信を確認してください。" exit 1 fi # --- 3. サーバー側での vLLM 起動待機 (S3モデルDL・コンテナ起動) --- echo "=== 3. サーバー側での vLLM 起動待機 (http://127.0.0.1:8000/health) ===" echo "UserDataによるS3モデルダウンロードとvLLM起動を待機しています（通常2〜4分程度）..." SERVER_READY=false for i in {1..90}; do CMD_ID=$(aws ssm send-command \ --region "${SELECTED_REGION}" \ --instance-ids "${INSTANCE_ID}" \ --document-name "AWS-RunShellScript" \ --parameters 'commands=["curl -s -m 2 http://127.0.0.1:8000/health >/dev/null && echo OK || echo WAITING"]' \ --query "Command.CommandId" \ --output text 2>/dev/null || true) if [ -n "${CMD_ID}" ]; then sleep 2 RES=$(aws ssm get-command-invocation \ --region "${SELECTED_REGION}" \ --command-id "${CMD_ID}" \ --instance-id "${INSTANCE_ID}" \ --query "StandardOutputContent" \ --output text 2>/dev/null || true) if [[ "${RES}" =~ "OK" ]]; then echo " サーバー側の vLLM が正常に応答しました！" SERVER_READY=true break fi fi echo -n "." sleep 5 done echo "" if [ "${SERVER_READY}" != "true" ]; then echo "警告: サーバー側のvLLM起動待機がタイムアウトしました。UserDataログを確認してください。" fi # --- 4. 既存トンネルの整理と新規SSMポートフォワーディング確立 --- echo "=== 4. SSMポートフォワーディングの確立 (ポート開放不要トンネル) ===" if [ -f "${TUNNEL_PID_FILE}" ]; then OLD_PID=$(cat "${TUNNEL_PID_FILE}" | tr -d '[:space:]') if [ -n "${OLD_PID}" ] && ps -p "${OLD_PID}" > /dev/null 2>&1; then echo "古いポートフォワードプロセス (PID: ${OLD_PID}) を終了します..." kill -9 "${OLD_PID}" 2>/dev/null || true fi rm -f "${TUNNEL_PID_FILE}" fi pkill -f "AWS-StartPortForwardingSession.*8000" 2>/dev/null || true # バックグラウンドでSSMポートフォワーディングを開始（ログを .current_tunnel.log に出力） nohup aws ssm start-session \ --region "${SELECTED_REGION}" \ --target "${INSTANCE_ID}" \ --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSession \ --parameters '{"portNumber":["8000"],"localPortNumber":["8000"]}' \ > "${TUNNEL_LOG}" 2>&1 & TUNNEL_PID=$! echo "${TUNNEL_PID}" > "${TUNNEL_PID_FILE}" echo "SSMポートフォワーディングを開始しました (PID: ${TUNNEL_PID})" sleep 2 # --- 5. ローカル疎通確認 --- echo "=== 5. ローカル疎通確認 (http://localhost:8000/health) ===" LOCAL_OK=false for i in {1..10}; do if curl -s -m 3 "http://localhost:8000/health" > /dev/null 2>&1; then echo " ローカルからの直結疎通を確認しました！ (HTTP 200 OK)" LOCAL_OK=true break fi echo -n "." sleep 2 done echo "" if [ "${LOCAL_OK}" != "true" ]; then echo "警告: ローカル接続に失敗しました。トンネルログを確認してください:" cat "${TUNNEL_LOG}" 2>/dev/null || true fi echo "==========================================================" echo " サーバーレスGPUブローカーによる直結完了！" echo " EC2 Instance ID : ${INSTANCE_ID} (${MARKET_TYPE}, Region: ${SELECTED_REGION})" echo " セキュリティ : インバウンドルール 0件（完全閉塞）" echo " トンネル接続 : localhost:8000 -> EC2:8000 (SSM暗号化)" echo " Web UI / API : http://localhost:8000/v1" echo "" echo " VS Code の Cline から接続してください (Base URL: http://localhost:8000/v1)" echo " 検証終了時は以下のコマンドでリソースを破棄してください:" echo " ./02_stop_vllm_ssm.sh" echo "==========================================================" 実際の動作パターンと検証 # 1. 通常のスポット起動（1秒台で最適リージョンを選定・起動要求） # 引数なしで実行すると、Lambdaが全リージョンを並列評価し、最安・低中断率のスポットをわずか1秒台で引き当てます。 $ ./01_start_vllm_ssm.sh === 1. サーバーレスGPUブローカー（Lambda）を呼び出し中 [スポット起動]... === ========================================================== 🏆 最適スポットリージョン選定完了: us-west-2 (Rank A / 68点) インスタンスID: i-087654321fedcba09 スポット価格 : $0.4264/h ========================================================== インスタンスが running 状態になるのを待機中... === 2. SSMエージェントのオンライン待機 === EC2インスタンス内部のSSM Agentが接続されるのを待機中... . SSM Agent が Online になりました！ (1回目の試行) === 3. サーバー側での vLLM 起動待機 (http://127.0.0.1:8000/health) === UserDataによるS3モデルダウンロードとvLLM起動を待機しています（通常2〜4分程度）... ................................ サーバー側の vLLM が正常に応答しました！ === 4. SSMポートフォワーディングの確立 (ポート開放不要トンネル) === SSMポートフォワーディングを開始しました (PID: 53120) === 5. ローカル疎通確認 (http://localhost:8000/health) === . ローカルからの直結疎通を確認しました！ (HTTP 200 OK) ========================================================== サーバーレスGPUブローカーによる直結完了！ EC2 Instance ID : i-087654321fedcba09 (spot, Region: us-west-2) セキュリティ : インバウンドルール 0件（完全閉塞） トンネル接続 : localhost:8000 -> EC2:8000 (SSM暗号化) Web UI / API : http://localhost:8000/v1 VS Code の Cline から接続してください (Base URL: http://localhost:8000/v1) 検証終了時は以下のコマンドでリソースを破棄してください: ./02_stop_vllm_ssm.sh ========================================================== 2. スポット枯渇時（フォールバック案内） # 世界的にGPUキャパシティが逼迫している時間帯では、Lambdaがすべての候補リージョンを試みた上でスマートにフォールバック案内を返します： $ ./01_start_vllm_ssm.sh === 1. サーバーレスGPUブローカー（Lambda）を呼び出し中 [スポット起動]... === ========================================================== ❌ スポット在庫切れ: 全候補リージョンでスポットインスタンスを調達できませんでした。 ---------------------------------------------------------- 【試行した候補リージョンと結果】 - us-west-2 (68点 / Rank A): スポット余剰キャパシティ不足 (在庫切れ) - us-east-2 (74点 / Rank A): スポット余剰キャパシティ不足 (在庫切れ) - eu-central-1 (78点 / Rank S): スポット余剰キャパシティ不足 (在庫切れ) - us-east-1 (68点 / Rank A): スポット余剰キャパシティ不足 (在庫切れ) - ap-northeast-1 (43点 / Rank C): スポット余剰キャパシティ不足 (在庫切れ) 💡 通常起動（オンデマンド）であれば確実に起動可能です。 以下のコマンドで再実行してください: # コスト最安リージョン（米オレゴン等: 約$0.98/h）で通常起動: ./01_start_vllm_ssm.sh --on-demand --strategy cost # レイテンシー最小リージョン（東京: 約$1.34/h）で通常起動: ./01_start_vllm_ssm.sh --on-demand --strategy latency ========================================================== 3. オンデマンド起動への切り替え # 今すぐ作業を進めたい場合は、案内通りに --on-demand を付与して再実行します。 最安コスト重視（--strategy cost）: $ ./01_start_vllm_ssm.sh --on-demand --strategy cost === 1. サーバーレスGPUブローカー（Lambda）を呼び出し中 [通常起動 / 戦略: cost]... === ========================================================== ⚡ 通常起動（オンデマンド）完了: 戦略 = cost 選定リージョン : us-west-2 (オレゴン (コスト最安・中遅延)) インスタンスID : i-01122334455667788 オンデマンド価格: $0.9840/h 目安レイテンシー: 約 110 ms ========================================================== ... 低遅延重視（--strategy latency）: $ ./01_start_vllm_ssm.sh --on-demand --strategy latency === 1. サーバーレスGPUブローカー（Lambda）を呼び出し中 [通常起動 / 戦略: latency]... === ========================================================== ⚡ 通常起動（オンデマンド）完了: 戦略 = latency 選定リージョン : ap-northeast-1 (東京 (最低遅延・国内)) インスタンスID : i-09988776655443322 オンデマンド価格: $1.3412/h 目安レイテンシー: 約 15 ms ========================================================== ... 検証終了時のリソース破棄スクリプト (02_stop_vllm_ssm.sh) # 作業が終了したら、破棄スクリプト（02_stop_vllm_ssm.sh）を実行します。ローカルのSSMトンネルプロセスを安全に切断した上で、Lambdaブローカーに終了リクエストを発行し、EC2インスタンスおよびEBSボリュームを確実に破棄します。 02_stop_vllm_ssm.sh（クリックで展開） #!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail # ============================================================================== # 02_stop_vllm_ssm.sh # SSMポートフォワードプロセスを終了し、Lambda経由でGPUインスタンスを破棄する # ============================================================================== SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)" INSTANCE_STATE_FILE="${SCRIPT_DIR}/.current_instance_id" TUNNEL_PID_FILE="${SCRIPT_DIR}/.current_tunnel_pid" REGION_STATE_FILE="${SCRIPT_DIR}/.current_region" TUNNEL_LOG="${SCRIPT_DIR}/.current_tunnel.log" BROKER_REGION="ap-northeast-1" FUNCTION_NAME="vllm-spot-broker" # 1. SSMポートフォワードプロセスの終了 echo "=== 1. SSMポートフォワードプロセスの終了 ===" if [ -f "${TUNNEL_PID_FILE}" ]; then TUNNEL_PID=$(cat "${TUNNEL_PID_FILE}" | tr -d '[:space:]') if [ -n "${TUNNEL_PID}" ] && ps -p "${TUNNEL_PID}" > /dev/null 2>&1; then echo "SSMポートフォワードプロセス (PID: ${TUNNEL_PID}) を終了中..." kill -9 "${TUNNEL_PID}" 2>/dev/null || true fi rm -f "${TUNNEL_PID_FILE}" fi pkill -f "AWS-StartPortForwardingSession.*8000" 2>/dev/null || true # 2. Lambdaブローカーへのインスタンス破棄リクエスト echo "=== 2. サーバーレスGPUブローカー（Lambda）へリソース破棄リクエスト ===" TMP_RES=$(mktemp) aws lambda invoke \ --region "${BROKER_REGION}" \ --function-name "${FUNCTION_NAME}" \ --payload '{"action":"terminate"}' \ --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \ "${TMP_RES}" >/dev/null STATUS=$(jq -r '.status // "error"' "${TMP_RES}" 2>/dev/null || echo "error") if [ "${STATUS}" = "success" ]; then COUNT=$(jq -r '.count // 0' "${TMP_RES}") echo "==========================================================" echo " 🛑 破棄完了！ 稼働中のインスタンス ${COUNT} 台を Terminate しました。" jq -r '.terminated_instances[]? | " - [\(.region)] \(.instance_id)"' "${TMP_RES}" 2>/dev/null || true echo "==========================================================" else echo "警告: Lambda経由の破棄でエラーが返されました。ローカル情報による直接破棄を試みます..." AWS_REGION=$(cat "${REGION_STATE_FILE}" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '[:space:]' || echo "ap-northeast-1") INSTANCE_ID=$(cat "${INSTANCE_STATE_FILE}" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '[:space:]' || echo "") if [ -n "${INSTANCE_ID}" ]; then aws ec2 terminate-instances --region "${AWS_REGION}" --instance-ids "${INSTANCE_ID}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true echo "インスタンス ${INSTANCE_ID} (${AWS_REGION}) を直接Terminateしました。" fi fi rm -f "${TMP_RES}" "${INSTANCE_STATE_FILE}" "${REGION_STATE_FILE}" "${TUNNEL_LOG}" echo "スポットインスタンス、EBSボリューム、SSMトンネルの破棄が完了しました！" まとめ # 今回は、マルチリージョンのGPU調達ロジックを AWS LambdaによるサーバーレスGPUブローカー へと刷新しました。 並列探索による高速化: Pythonのマルチスレッドにより、全リージョン・AZのスポット価格・中断率取得から判定までをわずか1〜2秒で完結。 クライアントの責務スリム化: 複雑なマルチリージョン探索や中断率集計、フォールバックの重厚なロジックをクラウド側へ切り離し、ローカルスクリプトは接続とプロセス管理のみに専念。 耐障害性の向上（スマートなフォールバック）: スポット全滅時も勝手に高額課金せず、明確なエラー通知と再試行オプション（コスト最安 vs 低遅延）を提供。 クラウドの余剰リソースを徹底的に使い倒すための、極めて実用的で回復力の高いGPU基盤が完成しました。

articles.title: 話題の逆解析 MCP「REA」を Claude Code に隔離してつないだ——静的解析の A/B 試験と安全設計
articles.description:
はじめに

articles.title: Stop Waiting for the Backend: A Frontend Developer's Guide to API Prototyping
The Trilemma of Autonomy: Navigating AI, Blockchain, and Regulation in the Digital Frontier
articles.description:
Introduction


The digital landscape is rapidly evolving, driven by the unprecedented convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and blockchain technology. We are witnessing the emergence of autonomous economic agents, powered by AI, engaging directly with decentralized financial infrastructure. Recent data indicating AI agents have executed a staggering 138 million cryptocurrency payments underscores a pivotal shift towards an automated, blockchain-enabled economy, with the United States at the forefront of AI model spending and development. This synergy promises unparalleled efficiency, transparency, and new paradigms for value exchange.
However, this transformative potential is not without its complex challenges. The rapid pace of innovation often outstrips the capacity of existing regulatory frameworks, creating an environment of uncertainty and potential friction. The sentiment expressed by Kalshi's CEO regarding fragmented, state-led oversight pushing U.S. prediction markets offshore serves as a stark warning: overly restrictive or ill-informed regulation risks stifling domestic innovation and ceding leadership in crucial emerging sectors. Compounding these regulatory hurdles are profound ethical and safety concerns surrounding the very autonomy of AI. The call from leading AI figures, including the "Godfather of AI" and hundreds of scientists, to potentially disconnect advanced AI models from the internet, introduces a fundamental tension to the vision of AI seamlessly integrated with decentralized networks. This article will delve into this complex trilemma, exploring the synergistic opportunities between AI and blockchain, the critical regulatory challenges they face, and the existential questions surrounding AI control, particularly within the dynamic U.S. innovation ecosystem.
The foundational promise of blockchain technology lies in its ability to create secure, immutable, and transparent ledgers for transactions, enabling trustless interactions without central intermediaries. This distributed ledger technology (DLT) has given rise to cryptocurrencies, decentralized finance (DeFi), and decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs), fundamentally reshaping how value is transferred and governance is conducted. Simultaneously, advancements in AI, particularly in machine learning and autonomous agents, are enabling systems to perform complex tasks, make decisions, and interact with digital environments with increasing sophistication.
The convergence of these two technologies manifests in AI agents leveraging blockchain for various functions. These agents can execute smart contracts, manage digital assets, participate in DeFi protocols, and conduct micro-payments, creating a new layer of automated economic activity. The 138 million crypto payments made by AI agents highlight a practical, scaled application of this synergy, indicating that AI is not just observing but actively participating in the crypto economy. This development is particularly concentrated in the U.S., which leads global spending on AI models, suggesting a fertile ground for further integration.
Prediction markets, like Kalshi, represent another fascinating intersection. They allow participants to trade on the outcome of future events, aggregating dispersed information into a probabilistic forecast. While Kalshi operates within a regulated framework, decentralized prediction markets such as Augur and Polymarket utilize blockchain to offer similar services in a trustless, permissionless manner. These platforms exemplify the innovative potential but also the inherent regulatory ambiguity. The U.S. regulatory landscape, characterized by a patchwork of state and federal bodies (e.g., CFTC, SEC), often struggles to classify novel digital assets and activities, leading to concerns about innovation being "pushed out" to more permissive jurisdictions.
Underpinning these technological and regulatory discussions are critical ethical considerations regarding AI. The call from eminent figures like Geoffrey Hinton, often referred to as the "Godfather of AI," and hundreds of other scientists, to restrict AI models' access to the internet reflects a deep-seated concern about the potential for uncontrolled or misaligned advanced AI to pose existential risks. This debate directly challenges the vision of AI agents operating freely and autonomously on global, decentralized networks like blockchains, introducing a fundamental tension between innovation, autonomy, and control.
The phenomenon of AI agents executing millions of crypto payments is a testament to the robust interoperability developing between AI and blockchain infrastructure. At its core, this involves AI models being programmed to interact with blockchain networks via Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) or direct integration with wallet software. These AI agents typically manage cryptographic keys (or access them securely) to sign transactions, enabling them to initiate payments, interact with smart contracts, and participate in decentralized applications (dApps).
For instance, an AI agent might be designed to identify arbitrage opportunities across various Decentralized Exchanges (DEXs) like Uniswap or Curve. Upon detection, the AI would programmatically construct and broadcast a transaction to a blockchain network (e.g., Ethereum, Solana, Polygon), paying network fees (gas) and executing token swaps to capitalize on price discrepancies. The choice of blockchain often depends on the required transaction speed and cost; Layer 2 solutions like Arbitrum or Optimism on Ethereum, or high-throughput chains like Solana, are increasingly favored for such high-frequency, low-latency operations to manage transaction volume efficiently and reduce costs associated with 138 million payments.
The regulatory friction highlighted by Kalshi's CEO is particularly acute in the U.S. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and state regulators often view prediction markets through the lens of gambling or unregulated derivatives, applying frameworks designed for traditional financial instruments. This approach often fails to account for the unique characteristics of blockchain-based markets, which are inherently transparent and often designed to aggregate information rather than solely facilitate speculative betting. The lack of a clear, unified federal framework for digital assets means that projects like Polymarket, a decentralized prediction market, often navigate complex legal gray areas or choose to restrict U.S. participation to avoid regulatory entanglement, directly illustrating the "push them out" scenario. The "Howey Test," a long-standing Supreme Court precedent used to define an "investment contract" (and thus a security), often struggles to clearly categorize novel digital assets or the participation in decentralized protocols, leading to inconsistent enforcement and uncertainty.
Furthermore, the integration of AI agents introduces novel regulatory challenges regarding legal personhood and accountability. If an autonomous AI agent, for example, executes a transaction deemed illegal or causes financial harm, who is liable? The developer? The user who deployed it? The protocol itself? Existing Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) regulations are designed for human or corporate entities, not autonomous digital agents. This necessitates a re-evaluation of legal frameworks to define the rights, responsibilities, and auditing mechanisms for AI agents operating on public blockchains.
The call to disconnect AI models from the internet presents a profound technical and philosophical challenge. From a technical standpoint, completely isolating a highly advanced, potentially self-improving AI model from its data sources and interaction vectors is incredibly complex, especially if such models become widely distributed or open-source. For AI agents making crypto payments, internet access is fundamental for market data, transaction broadcasting, and network interaction. Cutting off this access would effectively halt their economic activity on blockchains, undermining the very premise of AI-driven decentralized economies. This proposed measure reflects a deeper tension: the decentralized, permissionless ethos of blockchain versus a desire for centralized control and containment of potentially dangerous AI. It raises questions about whether global, immutable ledgers can ever truly be "disconnected" from intelligent agents, or if the very nature of decentralization makes such control efforts futile, or at best, geographically limited.
The emergence of AI agents making crypto payments is not merely theoretical; it is actively shaping various facets of the digital economy. While specific projects responsible for the 138 million payments are not individually named in the news, we can infer common applications:
  DeFi Arbitrage and Liquidation Bots: These are perhaps the most prevalent AI-driven crypto agents. Sophisticated algorithms monitor real-time price feeds across multiple DEXs (e.g., Uniswap, SushiSwap, Balancer) and lending protocols (e.g., Aave, Compound). Upon identifying price discrepancies or undercollateralized loans, these AI bots instantly execute complex multi-step transactions, often involving flash loans, to profit from arbitrage or liquidate positions. Each step in these atomic transactions, including token swaps and fee payments, constitutes a "crypto payment" on the underlying blockchain (e.g., Ethereum, BNB Chain).
  Automated Market Making (AMM) Strategies: AI can optimize liquidity provision on DEXs by dynamically adjusting token ratios and pricing strategies. These AI agents contribute liquidity, earn trading fees, and rebalance their portfolios through on-chain transactions, effectively making continuous "payments" as they manage their positions.
  DAO Treasury Management and Proposal Execution: While still nascent, AI is being explored for assisting DAOs in managing their treasuries. An AI could, for example, execute predefined investment strategies, allocate funds for grants, or manage operational expenses by initiating crypto payments based on DAO-approved proposals. This moves towards a truly autonomous organizational structure where AI acts as an executive agent.
  Machine-to-Machine (M2M) Micro-transactions: In the Internet of Things (IoT) space, AI-enabled devices could autonomously pay for services or resources using cryptocurrencies. For instance, an autonomous vehicle could pay for charging services or road usage fees directly from its crypto wallet, orchestrated by its onboard AI. While not yet generating millions of payments, this represents a future application.
In the realm of prediction markets, the news highlights Kalshi, a U.S.-based regulated exchange that allows users to bet on real-world events. Kalshi's CEO's comments underscore the challenge of operating such a platform under a fragmented regulatory regime, where state-level oversight can create inconsistencies and burdens. In contrast, Polymarket and Augur represent prominent decentralized prediction markets built on Ethereum. These platforms operate without a central intermediary, using smart contracts to manage funds and resolve outcomes. Their decentralized nature often places them in a regulatory gray area, leading Polymarket, for instance, to face enforcement actions from the CFTC and subsequently block U.S. users, illustrating the exact "pushing out" phenomenon described by Kalshi's CEO.
The concerns about AI safety and control, leading to calls for internet disconnection, are championed by figures like Geoffrey Hinton, who left Google to speak more freely about AI's dangers, and organizations like the Center for AI Safety. Their open letters, signed by hundreds of AI researchers and public figures, emphasize the potential for "extinction-level" risks from advanced AI. This perspective directly challenges the unbridled integration of AI with global, permissionless networks, suggesting a need for robust governance mechanisms that extend beyond mere financial regulation to encompass existential risk management.
Despite the burgeoning synergy between AI and blockchain, several significant limitations and challenges must be addressed for this ecosystem to mature responsibly.
Firstly, regulatory ambiguity remains a paramount concern, particularly within the U.S. The current patchwork of state and federal regulations, often designed for traditional industries, struggles to adequately categorize and govern novel digital assets and the autonomous actions of AI agents. The "push them out" scenario for prediction markets is a microcosm of a broader issue: without clear, comprehensive, and innovation-friendly federal guidance, the U.S. risks stifling domestic development and driving talent and capital to jurisdictions with more defined (or less restrictive) frameworks. This uncertainty impedes institutional adoption and discourages long-term investment in AI-blockchain ventures.
Secondly, technical challenges of AI integration persist. While AI agents are making millions of payments, ensuring the security, auditability, and explainability of these autonomous financial actions is crucial. Malicious AI agents, or even benign ones with programming flaws, could exploit vulnerabilities in smart contracts or market inefficiencies, leading to significant financial losses. Developing robust security protocols, formal verification methods for AI-driven smart contract interactions, and mechanisms for "circuit breakers" or emergency shutdowns for autonomous agents are essential. Furthermore, reliable and tamper-proof data feeds (oracles) are critical for AI agents to interact with real-world information and execute conditional payments accurately.
Thirdly, the ethical and safety concerns surrounding AI autonomy, as highlighted by the "Godfather of AI" and other scientists, pose a fundamental limitation to unchecked integration. The debate over potentially disconnecting AI from the internet underscores a deep-seated fear of losing control over increasingly intelligent and autonomous systems. If AI models become capable of self-improvement and goal-setting beyond human comprehension, their interaction with immutable, global financial systems via blockchain could introduce unprecedented risks. This necessitates a proactive approach to AI ethics, alignment, and governance that goes beyond mere financial compliance, focusing on existential risk mitigation and ensuring human oversight where necessary.
Finally, while blockchains are becoming more scalable, network congestion and transaction costs can still be a limitation for extremely high volumes of AI-driven microtransactions. While Layer 2 solutions and alternative Layer 1 blockchains offer improvements, a truly global, real-time, AI-driven economy would demand further advancements in transaction throughput and cost efficiency without compromising decentralization and security. The current infrastructure, while capable of 138 million payments, might face bottlenecks with an order-of-magnitude increase in activity from fully autonomous, pervasive AI agents.
The intersection of AI and blockchain technology is undoubtedly one of the most transformative frontiers of the 21st century. The concrete evidence of AI agents executing 138 million cryptocurrency payments signals a profound shift towards an increasingly automated and decentralized global economy. This synergy promises to unlock unprecedented efficiencies, foster new economic models, and democratize access to financial services, with the U.S. playing a leading role in AI development.
However, this revolutionary potential is inextricably linked to a complex trilemma involving regulatory clarity and the existential questions of AI control. The concerns voiced by Kalshi's CEO about fragmented state-led oversight pushing innovation offshore are a critical bellwether, underscoring the urgent need for a cohesive, forward-looking regulatory framework in the U.S. Such a framework must balance consumer protection and market integrity with the imperative to foster innovation, providing legal certainty for both blockchain-based enterprises and AI-driven applications. Without it, the U.S. risks ceding its leadership in these pivotal technological domains.
Concurrently, the call from leading AI scientists to consider disconnecting AI models from the internet introduces a vital, albeit challenging, debate about the fundamental limits of AI autonomy and integration. While potentially hindering the seamless operation of AI agents on decentralized networks, this perspective highlights the profound ethical and safety considerations that must accompany technological advancement. A balanced approach is required: one that acknowledges the immense benefits of AI-blockchain synergy while proactively developing robust governance, safety protocols, and ethical guidelines to mitigate potential risks.
In conclusion, the future will likely see a nuanced evolution where autonomous AI agents leverage blockchain for secure and efficient operations, but within a carefully constructed framework of human oversight and clear regulation. The success of this integration hinges on the ability of policymakers, technologists, and ethicists to collaborate on creating an environment that encourages innovation, manages risk, and ensures that the power of AI and blockchain serves humanity's best interests. Ignoring these challenges or adopting overly restrictive measures would not only stifle progress but also risk the U.S. losing its competitive edge in shaping the next generation of the digital economy.

articles.title: Preventing Cross-Tenant Data Leaks in Multi-Tenant Batch Pipelines: Static AST Analysis for Missing Tenant Filters
articles.description:
Preventing Cross-Tenant Data Leaks in Multi-Tenant Batch Pipelines: Static AST Analysis for Missing Tenant Filters In multi-tenant software architectures where shared database schemes or shared tables are utilized, ensuring strict tenant isolation is paramount. One missing tenant_id predicate in a batch processing query can easily trigger a catastrophic cross-tenant data leak. While runtime middleware or Row-Level Security (RLS) can mitigate some of these hazards, batch jobs, background workers, and ad-hoc analytics queries often operate with administrative credentials that bypass RLS or ORM-level tenant scopes. To bridge this security gap before runtime execution, we designed a lightweight, zero-dependency static analysis verification script tailored for CI/CD pipelines. This article details the architectural design, an unexpected operational post-mortem during QA, robust mitigation patterns, and the theoretical limits of AST-based static verification in dynamic languages. The following diagram illustrates how the verification pipeline inspects source code, parses AST nodes, evaluates vulnerability patterns, and handles fallback logic: flowchart TD subgraph Pipeline ["CI/CD Static Analysis Pipeline"] SourceCode["Python Batch Worker Script"] ASTParser["Python ast.parse()"] Visitor["AST Call & Expression Visitor"] end subgraph Inspection ["Node Inspection Criteria"] TargetMethod{"Method matches query execution?
execute, query, filter, select"} TenantCheck{"Contains 'tenant_id' in args/kwargs?"} DynamicSQL{"Contains FormattedValue, JoinedStr, or BinOp?"} end subgraph Evaluation ["Result Evaluation & Serialization"] Pass["Pass Static Gate"] ViolationFlag["Flag Violation:
Missing Tenant ID or Dangerous Dynamic SQL"] Serializer["Serialization Engine"] OrjsonEngine["orjson (Fast C-Extension)"] StdJsonEngine["json (Standard Library Fallback)"] end SourceCode -- "Read Source AST" --> ASTParser ASTParser -- "Generate Node Tree" --> Visitor Visitor -- "Traverse ast.Call" --> TargetMethod TargetMethod -- "Yes" --> TenantCheck TargetMethod -- "No" --> Pass TenantCheck -- "Missing" --> ViolationFlag TenantCheck -- "Present" --> DynamicSQL DynamicSQL -- "Detected" --> ViolationFlag DynamicSQL -- "Clean" --> Pass ViolationFlag -- "Format Violation" --> Serializer Serializer -- "If HAS_ORJSON == True" --> OrjsonEngine Serializer -- "If ImportError" --> StdJsonEngine 💡 For immediate deployment: The complete source code suite (ZIP) for this architecture is available on Gumroad for $0+ (Pay What You Want). The primary engineering goal was to avoid the organizational friction and maintenance overhead of heavyweight static analysis frameworks (e.g., bespoke Flake8 or Pylint AST plugins). Instead, we targeted a standalone, single-file validation script that drops seamlessly into GitHub Actions or GitLab CI runners without polluting project dependencies. Using Python's built-in ast module, target scripts are transformed into Abstract Syntax Trees to inspect function and method invocation nodes (ast.Call). Targeting Query Execution Points: The visitor identifies invocation nodes where the method or function identifier matches standard persistence operations, such as execute, query, filter, or select. Validating Tenant Predicates: The visitor inspects positional arguments (node.args) and keyword arguments (node.keywords) to verify whether the token "tenant_id" is explicitly present as an argument identifier or literal parameter. Detecting Risky Dynamic SQL Construction: The parser flags nodes employing ast.FormattedValue (f-strings), ast.JoinedStr, or ast.BinOp (string concatenation with + or %). These patterns represent acute SQL injection risks and query-obfuscation patterns that circumvent static parameter inspection. To ensure violations can be consumed downstream by automated policy enforcers or pipeline annotations, violations are represented as strongly-typed data structures via Pydantic (v2), paired with orjson for high-throughput serialization: from pydantic import BaseModel, Field class ViolationModel(BaseModel): file_path: str = Field(..., description="File path where the violation was detected") line_number: int = Field(..., description="Line number of the violating node") query_snippet: str = Field(..., description="Code snippet or query expression flagged") reason: str = Field(..., description="Detection reason (e.g., Missing tenant_id, Unsafe dynamic concatenation)") While the core AST algorithm met all static analysis functional criteria during local prototyping, the script encountered a fatal runtime crash immediately upon execution inside the staging QA verification environment. When executed against the target repository batch files, the verification process aborted instantly with an uncaught exception: Traceback (most recent call last): File "/home/phenox/gemini-sandbox/TOAI_Workspace/V2_SandBox/V2_PROD_20261012_081157_test.py", line 7, in import orjson ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'orjson' In the local engineering environment, orjson had been previously compiled and cached in the virtual environment. As a result, import orjson resolved transparently, giving the illusion of a self-contained script. In the stripped-down QA testing runner, however, only the Python standard library was available. The script crashed at module initialization before a single line of AST analysis was evaluated. During the early phases of CI rollout, exit code 1 was observed. There was an initial false assumption that: "The pipeline guarded the build because our static analyzer successfully flagged 46 multi-tenant isolation violations and called sys.exit(1)." In reality, the pipeline had failed entirely due to an unhandled ModuleNotFoundError. The build broke not because of active security policy enforcement, but because the evaluation script itself failed to run. This failure illustrates an essential rule in pipeline safety: runtime crashes must never be conflated with intentional policy denials. Performance-critical libraries like orjson provide noticeable benefits when serializing large AST manifests. However, verification scripts and developer tooling must prioritize zero-dependency resilience over peak serialization speed. To safeguard against environment discrepancies, static tooling should utilize graceful degradation patterns with a transparent fallback to the standard library json module: try: import orjson HAS_ORJSON = True except ImportError: import json HAS_ORJSON = False def dump_json(data: dict) -> str: """ Serializes dictionary payloads into formatted JSON strings. Prefers orjson when compiled C-extensions are available; transparently falls back to stdlib json on minimal CI runners. """ if HAS_ORJSON: return orjson.dumps( data, option=orjson.OPT_INDENT_2 | orjson.OPT_SORT_KEYS ).decode("utf-8") else: return json.dumps( data, indent=2, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False ) By decoupling execution viability from external C-extension packages, the verification script guarantees consistent execution across local developer workstations, staging Docker containers, and minimal CI runners. Applying static analysis to dynamic, interpreted languages like Python reveals fundamental architectural boundaries that simple AST visitors cannot cross: Simple AST visitors rely heavily on syntactic matching (e.g., checking if the call attribute equals execute or filter). In mature production codebases, data access layers are typically wrapped inside custom domain repositories or abstracted utility functions (e.g., fetch_organization_records(...)). Without semantic symbol resolution, syntactically naive AST visitors cannot determine whether a custom helper executes database queries underneath. When query fragments, raw SQL strings, or predicate dictionaries are constructed in upstream functions or imported from separate configuration modules, a single-file AST visitor cannot trace the data flow. Solving this requires inter-procedural Taint Analysis, Control Flow Graphs (CFG), and static type inference (such as those provided by Pyright or mypy AST hooks), which significantly increases computational complexity. While this verification pipeline initially stumbled due to a dependency management oversight, automating multi-tenant query validation via static analysis remains an essential layer in defense-in-depth security strategies. When building developer infrastructure and security gates: Never rely on unpinned or external dependencies in scripts expected to enforce pipeline integrity across diverse deployment runners. Distinguish cleanly between script crash exits and security policy rejection exits through distinct exit codes and structured telemetry. Account for static analysis limitations by complementing lightweight AST checks with schema-level database safeguards like Row-Level Security (RLS) and schema-per-tenant isolation. If this engineering log saved your production server (and your sanity), consider supporting our architecture on GitHub Sponsors.

articles.title: 「AWS Certified AI Business Strategist (AIB-C01)」を受験してきた！新設ビジネス認定の概要と合格体験記
articles.description:
はじめに
#
これは、興味のままに新試験を受験してきた記録です。
先日、AWS認定に新設された注目のベータ試験「AWS Certified AI Business Strategist (AIB-C01、ベータ試験コード: AB1-C01)」を受験してきました。本記事では、新設された試験の概要や学習準備、受験当日のリアルな所感、そして合否結果についてまとめます。
 -->
 Information
秘密保持契約（NDA）があるため、詳細な試験問題の内容や個別設問については触れることができませんので、ご了承ください。
試験について
#
AWS Certified AI Business Strategist（以下、AI Business Strategist）は、ビジネスリーダーやDX推進担当者、企画職などを対象とした認定資格です。AIおよび生成AI技術を活用したビジネス価値の創出、戦略的な意思決定、ガバナンス推進に関する知識が総合的に評価されます。
これまでのAWS認定は「Solutions Architect」や各種Specialtyなど、主にインフラ構築や実装技術（How）に焦点を当てていました。
試験の概要

試験コード: AIB-C01（ベータ試験コード: AB1-C01）
カテゴリ: Business（※新設カテゴリー）
試験時間: 170分 + 10分（前後のアンケートなど）
出題数: 85問程度（※ベータ試験）
合格基準スコア: 700点（100〜1,000点満点）
受験料: 8,250円（税込、※半額バウチャーなどは利用不可）
※ベータ試験であるため、正式リリース後は試験時間や出題数などが一部変更される可能性があります。
出題分野（試験ガイドより）
#
試験ガイドに記載されている主な出題分野は以下の4つです。
分野 1: AIの基礎とビジネスリテラシー

機械学習や生成AIの基本概念、適用可能なビジネス課題の特定
従来の予測型AIと生成AI（基盤モデル）の特性の違いとビジネスへの影響
分野 2: AI戦略とビジネス価値の創出

AI導入に伴うビジネスケースの策定、ROI（投資対効果）の評価手法
自社開発（Build）か外部サービス・既存モデル採用（Buy）かのトレードオフ判断
定量・定性のKPI（重要業績指標）の設定
分野 3: AIガバナンスと責任あるAIリーダーシップ

責任あるAI（公平性、透明性、説明責任、プライバシー保護）の推進
ハルシネーション（幻覚）リスクへの対策やHuman-in-the-Loop（人間の介在）の設計
知的財産権、著作権、業界コンプライアンスの遵守
分野 4: 組織のAIレディネスと変革推進（トランスフォーメーション）

全社的なAI活用を支える組織体制（AI Center of Excellence: CoE）の立ち上げ
従業員のスキルアップ、チェンジマネジメント（変化への抵抗の克服）
パイロット運用から全社展開へのスケール戦略
申し込み
#
ベータ試験のアナウンスを確認後、認定ポータルサイトから申し込みました。
AWS認定の新設試験ベータ版は、8,250円（税込）という特別価格で最新トレンドの出題傾向をいち早く体験できる貴重な機会です。今回もスケジュールを調整し、テストセンターでの受験枠を確保しました。
準備したこと
#
本認定はコーディングや詳細なインフラ構成コマンドを問う試験ではないため、ビジネス視点でのAI活用戦略やガバナンスに焦点を当てて準備を進めました。
1. 試験ガイドの精読
#
まずは公式の試験ガイドを読み、出題範囲を確認しました。
2. AWS Skill Builder
#
AWS公式の学習プラットフォーム「AWS Skill Builder」にて、公式問題集や関連教材を確認・活用しました。
Official Practice Question Set: AWS Certified AI Business Strategist (AIB-C01 - 日本語)

公式の練習問題集（日本語）が提供されており、出題傾向やシナリオ問題の形式、選択肢の問われ方を事前に把握するのに最適
試験準備カテゴリ（AIB-C01 / AB1-C01）

ビジネスリーダー向けの生成AIコース（「Generative AI for Executives」等）や、責任あるAI（Responsible AI）に関する教材を活用した基礎概念のインプット
3. 公式ホワイトペーパー・ブログの確認
#
ビジネス価値やガバナンスに関するAWSの公式ドキュメントやフレームワークを復習しました。
AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) for Artificial Intelligence
責任あるAI（Responsible AI）に関する公式ガイダンス
Amazon Bedrock / AWSの生成AIサービス活用事例（金融、ヘルスケア、小売など業界ごとのユースケース）
準備しながら気づいたこと
#
学習を進める中で、従来のエンジニア向け試験とは異なるいくつかの重要な視点が見えてきました。
「技術的に可能か」ではなく「ビジネス投資として妥当か」が問われる点
Build vs Buy の明確な判断基準
責任あるAI（Responsible AI）とリスク管理のウェイトの高さ
組織・人材のチェンジマネジメントの重要性
受験当日の様子
#
いつものテストセンターで受験しました。
問題文の分量・出題内容
時間配分とコンディション
受験結果について
#
当日夜、スコアレポートが届き、無事に合格できました。
さらに、ベータ試験の合格者に対する特典であるアーリーアダプター（Early Adopter）のデジタルバッジも無事獲得できました。

手応えとしても感じていた通り、細かなAWS CLIコマンドなどを問う問題はありませんでした。ビジネスの文脈に即して「適切なAI活用判断ができるか」「責任ある推進体制を築けるか」という本質的な理解が問われる試験でした。
活かせる前提知識（他のAI認定との親和性）
#
実際に受験してみて感じたのは、他社クラウドや既存のAI認定で培った知識が大きなアドバンテージになる点です。
だいぶ楽に受験できると感じました。
AWS Certified Generative AI Developer - Professional (AIP-C01)
AWS Certified AI Practitioner (AIF-C01)
Google Cloud認定 Generative AI Leader (GAIL)
Microsoft認定: Azure AI の基礎 (AI-901)
生成AIパスポート（GUGA）
ちなみに、私自身は上記のうち「生成AIパスポート」以外はすべて合格・取得済みです。
まとめ
#
新設カテゴリ「Business」として、非エンジニアにも最適
エンジニアにとっても「視座を引き上げる」絶好の機会
早期受験でアーリーアダプターバッジも獲得可能
以上、簡単な受験記録となりますが、これから受験を検討されている方の参考になれば幸いです。
