CVE-2026-92262: Nine Characters — "#mysql50#" — Is All It Takes to Break MariaDB (CVSS 9.9)
articles.description:
Item
Detail




CVE ID
CVE-2026-92262


Affected product
MariaDB Server


Affected versions
10.6.1–10.6.27, 10.11.1–10.11.18, 11.4.1–11.4.12, 11.8.1–11.8.8, 12.3.1–12.3.2, 13.0.1


Fixed in
10.6.28, 10.11.19, 11.4.13, 11.8.9, 12.3.3, 13.0.2


CVSS
9.9 (Critical)


Type

CWE-706 (Use of Incorrectly-Resolved Name or Reference) — a different category from the classic "path traversal" label


Official sources
GHSA-65jj-h265-3m7h (MariaDB's official security advisory), MDEV-40362 (MariaDB's own JIRA bug)


Authentication required
Yes — and at a very low bar. The public PoC reproduces this with nothing more than an ordinary ALL grant on your own schema (create tables, insert, select) — no FILE, no SUPER, no plugin-load privilege


Disclosed
2026-10-16, alongside the 10.6.28 and other patched releases


Note
Disclosed the same day as two other 9.9-scored CVEs — CVE-2026-85748 (a SYS_REFCURSOR UAF) and CVE-2026-85746 (an ST_AsText OOB write) — all three bundled into a single PoC repository by the same researcher



Correction notice: An earlier version of this post described this flaw as classic path traversal (#mysql50#../../../etc/passwd-style). That characterization didn't match the official CWE classification (CWE-706, not CWE-22) or how the published PoC actually behaves. The public PoC demonstrates that a name containing ../ is explicitly rejected elsewhere with ERROR 1103 Incorrect table name. What follows has been rewritten based on the official advisory (GHSA-65jj-h265-3m7h), MariaDB's own bug tracker (MDEV-40362), and the published PoC code.
MariaDB has to run table names through a "translation step" before they become actual filesystem paths. SQL allows characters like - and @ in table names, but not every filesystem handles those characters safely. So MariaDB replaces "potentially unsafe" characters in a table name with a hex-coded form prefixed by @ (like @002d) when building the filename.
This CVE comes from a nearly 20-year-old compatibility feature that can skip that translation step entirely. A table name carrying the #mysql50# prefix is meant to reference "a table stored under MySQL 5.1-era encoding, as-is" — and to do that, it skips the encoding step altogether. An overt ../ sequence is blocked by a separate name-validity check, but a quieter problem remained underneath: a name with this prefix and the same name without it aren't properly distinguished inside the table cache.
Here's the normal flow for turning a table name into a file in MariaDB:
A user specifies a table name, as in CREATE TABLE t (...).
The server encodes it for the filename character set via something like tablename_to_filename(). Characters like - and @ become @002d, @0040, and so on.
At the same time, the server builds a table cache key to identify this table, so subsequent queries using the same name can reuse a cached handler instead of hitting disk every time.
The #mysql50# prefix was designed to affect step 2 (filename encoding). In practice, it also affects step 3 (cache key computation) — with the result that t and #mysql50#t, despite being different names, end up sharing the same cache entry and handler.
CREATE TABLE `a-b` (id INT) ENGINE=MyISAM;

This table gets stored on disk as a@002db.frm, a@002db.MYD, a@002db.MYI. Because - was replaced with @002d, you can't tell from the filename alone that the original table name contained a - — but that substitution is exactly what keeps filesystem-ambiguous characters from ever appearing literally in a path.
CREATE TABLE `#mysql50#a-b` (id INT) ENGINE=MyISAM;

According to what the public PoC actually confirms, running this command creates the following files in the data directory:
a-b.frm
a-b.MYD
a-b.MYI

a@002db.frm never gets created. The - stayed unencoded, literally, in the filename. But the PoC repository also makes an important point here — putting ../ in the table name is rejected by a separate check, before it ever gets this far, with ERROR 1103 Incorrect table name. So this isn't the classic "escape to an arbitrary path" kind of flaw — it's the narrower, but still real, problem of "a character that should have been encoded ends up in the filename unencoded."
t and #mysql50#t (CWE-706)


The real core of this flaw isn't on disk at all — it's in the in-memory table cache. The reproduction steps recorded in MDEV-40362 look like this:
CREATE TABLE t (id INT, c1 BINARY(10)) ENGINE=MEMORY;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, REPEAT(0x41, 10));
SELECT id, HEX(c1) FROM t;
-- id=1  hex=41414141414141414141   (0x41, ten bytes, exactly as inserted)

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS `#mysql50#t`;
CREATE TABLE `#mysql50#t` (id INT, c1 BINARY(1)) ENGINE=MEMORY;
INSERT INTO `#mysql50#t` VALUES (2, 0x42);
SELECT id, HEX(c1) FROM `#mysql50#t` WHERE id=2;
-- id=2  hex=42

t and #mysql50#t are two entirely distinct identifiers at the SQL level — they don't even share a column definition (BINARY(10) versus BINARY(1)). On a correctly-behaving server, these should be two completely independent tables. They aren't.
SELECT id, HEX(c1) FROM t ORDER BY id;

id=1  hex=41414141414141414141
id=2  hex=42000000000000000000

The id=2 row — inserted only into #mysql50#t — shows up when querying the original table t. The #mysql50# prefix influenced cache-key computation in a way that made the server treat the two as the same shared table (share) with the same handler. The one-byte value inserted (0x42) gets reinterpreted against t's BINARY(10) definition, padded with nine zero bytes — proof that two "separate tables" were, in fact, sharing a single storage slot the entire time.

MariaDB's official advisory describes the impact broadly, as "file access, crashes, data corruption, data exfiltration, or remote code execution." What the public PoC actually demonstrates is limited to data corruption (which succeeds silently, with no error message at all) and the fact that unencoded files accumulate in the data directory. The fact alone that tables with different names can bleed into each other at the cache level is already a serious problem for any application built on the assumption of privilege separation or data integrity. The specific chain that leads to crashes, exfiltration, or remote code execution isn't documented in detail in any public source.
Researcher SeanDishman published a PoC for this CVE bundled together with CVE-2026-85746 and CVE-2026-85748 in a single repository. Here's the full structure and what each part demonstrates.
# server/docker-compose.yml
services:
  mariadb:
    image: mariadb:13.0.1-rc
    environment:
      MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: root
      MARIADB_DATABASE: appdb
      MARIADB_USER: lowpriv
      MARIADB_PASSWORD: lowpriv
    ports:
      - "3306:3306"
    command: ["--core-file"]

One design choice here is worth flagging. The lowpriv account gets only ALL on the appdb schema — no FILE, no SUPER, no global privilege, no plugin-loading capability whatsoever. In other words, this PoC is deliberately built to demonstrate that it works with nothing more than an ordinary account that creates and writes tables within its own schema — the kind any typical application might have. The --core-file flag exists for the other two CVEs (which crash the server); this CVE on its own doesn't bring the server down.
cd server && bash start.sh
pip install -r requirements.txt
python client/exploit.py --cve 92262

client/exploit.py does nothing more exotic than send the same SQL statements found in client/sql/cve-2026-92262.sql, one at a time, over the standard MariaDB protocol. There's no exploit framework, no shellcode involved — it's just an automated version of what any ordinary SQL client would do.
CREATE TABLE t (id INT, c1 BINARY(10)) ENGINE=MEMORY;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, REPEAT(0x41, 10));
CREATE TABLE `#mysql50#t` (id INT, c1 BINARY(1)) ENGINE=MEMORY;
INSERT INTO `#mysql50#t` VALUES (2, 0x42);
SELECT id, HEX(c1) FROM t ORDER BY id;

Lines 1–2: create an ordinary table t and insert one row with the value "0x41 repeated ten times." This becomes the baseline for checking later whether t's data stayed unchanged.
Line 3: create "another table" — with a different column definition entirely — carrying the #mysql50# prefix. On a correct server, this should be a third table, entirely unrelated to t.
Line 4: insert a completely different row into that "other table."
Line 5: query the original t again. If there's no cache confusion, this should return only the one row inserted in line 1.
BEFORE   id=1  hex=41414141414141414141
MYSQL50  id=1  hex=41
MYSQL50  id=2  hex=42
AFTER_T  id=1  hex=41414141414141414141
AFTER_T  id=2  hex=42000000000000000000

In the AFTER_T section — querying the original table t again — the id=2 row, which was only ever inserted into #mysql50#t, shows up mixed in. This is the entire point the PoC proves: two syntactically distinct CREATE TABLE statements executed, yet internally the server treated them as one object sharing a single storage slot.
A second payload demonstrates the missing encoding on its own.
CREATE TABLE `#mysql50#a-b` (id INT) ENGINE=MyISAM;

Checking the data directory after this command shows unencoded files named a-b.frm, a-b.MYD, a-b.MYI — and a@002db.frm, what correct encoding should have produced, simply doesn't exist. The PoC repository states that these two payloads alone are sufficient to establish "data corruption, and writing unexpected filenames under the data directory" — and it does not publish a chain extending this further into a crash or code execution.
This PoC is focused on demonstrating a flaw that reproduces quietly. The server doesn't crash, and nothing shows up as a warning in the error log — which arguably makes it more dangerous, since an operator has no obvious way to notice an attack succeeded. What this PoC does not show is exactly how this cache confusion or unencoded-file creation gets escalated into a crash or arbitrary code execution. The "remote code execution" possibility named in the vendor advisory may require these two primitives to be combined with some additional condition — for instance, a crafted filename colliding with a different path the server later references — but that specific path can't be confirmed from publicly available material alone.
The patched versions keep the #mysql50# prefix's compatibility purpose intact (referencing a legacy-encoded name without re-encoding it), while fixing it so the prefix no longer affects table cache key computation. #mysql50#t and t are no longer treated as the same cache entry.
The lesson here is clear. When a compatibility "exception branch" doesn't precisely control the scope of what it affects, it can end up influencing far more than intended (skipping filename encoding) — reaching into things like cache identity and object-equality decisions. When two different subsystems (filename generation and cache-key computation) share the same string preprocessing logic, changing that one piece of logic can quietly change behavior in both places at once.
Update MariaDB to the patched version for your branch: 10.6.28, 10.11.19, 11.4.13, 11.8.9, 12.3.3, or 13.0.2.
Until you update, if your application has no need for CREATE TABLE/RENAME TABLE statements using a #mysql50#-prefixed name, filtering out that query pattern at the application or proxy layer can serve as a temporary mitigation.
Because this flaw requires no special privilege (an ordinary CREATE/INSERT grant on your own schema is enough), it deserves particular priority in multi-tenant environments or SaaS-style services where users can create their own tables.
If exposure is possible, check the data directory for unencoded filenames containing special characters (.frm/.MYD/.MYI files with anything beyond alphanumerics and underscores), and review query logs for table creation or manipulation attempts using the #mysql50# prefix.
Given this flaw's tendency to succeed silently, don't fully trust data integrity from before the patch was applied — for critical tables, it's worth running an integrity check against a known-good backup rather than assuming nothing happened.

articles.title: Secure Code Execution Sandbox: A Linux-Native Approach Without Docker or Containers
articles.description:
In the realm of secure software development, a code execution sandbox is a critical tool for isolating and managing untrusted code. Traditionally, Docker and similar containerization tools have been the go-to solutions for this purpose. However, their overhead—both in terms of resource consumption and execution speed—has prompted a search for lighter, more efficient alternatives. This investigation delves into a Linux-native approach that leverages kernel primitives to achieve the same isolation and security goals without the bloat of containerization tools. The core idea is to use PID, mount, network, and user namespaces, combined with cgroups v2, seccomp-BPF, and chroot, to create a sandbox that is both faster and more resource-efficient than Docker.
The challenge lies in replicating Docker’s isolation capabilities using only Linux primitives. Docker’s containerization model abstracts much of the underlying complexity, but this abstraction comes at a cost: increased resource overhead and slower execution times. By directly manipulating Linux namespaces, we can create a boundary around untrusted code that is both kernel-enforced and highly configurable. For instance, cgroups v2 allows for fine-grained control over memory and CPU limits, while seccomp-BPF restricts system calls to prevent access to sensitive kernel functionality. This approach not only reduces overhead but also provides deeper control over the execution environment, making it ideal for scenarios requiring rapid, secure code execution.
Consider the mechanism of isolation: namespaces create separate environments for processes, ensuring that untrusted code cannot interfere with the host system. For example, a PID namespace isolates process IDs, preventing the sandboxed code from seeing or interacting with other processes on the host. Similarly, a mount namespace restricts filesystem access, while a user namespace maps the sandbox’s root user to a non-privileged UID (e.g., 65534) on the host. This mapping ensures that even if the code gains root privileges inside the sandbox, it remains confined to the sandbox’s boundaries. The chroot environment, combined with a minimal per-language rootfs, further restricts the sandboxed code to a stripped-down filesystem, reducing the attack surface.
However, this approach is not without its trade-offs. While it offers performance gains and resource efficiency, it requires a deeper understanding of Linux internals and carries a higher risk of misconfiguration. For example, improperly configured cgroups limits could lead to resource exhaustion, while a misconfigured seccomp filter might expose the host to unauthorized system calls. Additionally, the solution is kernel-dependent, limiting its portability to non-Linux systems. Despite these challenges, the potential benefits—particularly in high-performance scenarios like cloud computing and online coding platforms—make this approach a compelling alternative to Docker.
To illustrate, the ContainerizationAPI project demonstrates this concept in action. It supports Python, C++17, C11, and Java, with kernel-enforced limits of 60 seconds execution time and 128MB memory. A global admission controller rejects submissions that exceed these limits before a sandbox is even created, further optimizing resource usage. While the project has undergone rigorous testing, it is hosted on a small, isolated server as a precautionary measure against potential sandbox escapes. This highlights the security trade-offs inherent in such an approach: while more lightweight, it demands meticulous configuration and a clear understanding of the underlying mechanisms.
In summary, this Linux-native sandbox represents a technical innovation in secure code execution, offering a faster and more resource-efficient alternative to Docker. By leveraging Linux primitives, it achieves fine-grained control over isolation and resource allocation, making it suitable for environments where performance and security are paramount. However, its success depends on careful implementation and a deep understanding of Linux internals, underscoring the importance of expertise in this domain.
Executing untrusted code is inherently risky. Without proper isolation, malicious or poorly written code can compromise system integrity, consume excessive resources, or even escape its intended environment. Traditional containerization tools like Docker provide a solution, but they introduce overhead—both in terms of resource consumption and execution speed. This overhead becomes a bottleneck in scenarios demanding rapid, secure code execution, such as cloud computing platforms or online coding environments.
The challenge, therefore, is to develop a secure and efficient sandbox that isolates untrusted code without relying on Docker or similar containerization tools. This sandbox must leverage Linux primitives—namespaces, cgroups, seccomp, and chroot—to achieve fine-grained control over resource allocation and process isolation. The goal is to minimize overhead while maintaining robust security, ensuring that code executes faster and with fewer resources than traditional container-based solutions.
Untrusted code poses several risks:
Resource Exhaustion: Malicious code can consume excessive CPU, memory, or disk I/O, starving other processes and potentially crashing the system. This occurs when the kernel’s scheduling and resource allocation mechanisms are not properly constrained, allowing the process to monopolize system resources.
Sandbox Escape: If isolation mechanisms are flawed, code can break out of its sandboxed environment. For example, a misconfigured namespace or seccomp filter could allow access to sensitive kernel functionality, enabling privilege escalation or system compromise.
Data Leakage: Without proper filesystem isolation, code could access or modify files outside its intended scope. This happens when mount namespaces or chroot configurations fail to restrict filesystem access to a minimal, controlled environment.
Docker and similar tools abstract away Linux primitives, providing a user-friendly interface at the cost of performance and flexibility. For instance, Docker’s use of a full-fledged container runtime introduces overhead from the container image layer, network setup, and storage drivers. In contrast, a Linux-primitive-based approach offers:
Fine-Grained Control: Direct use of namespaces (PID, mount, network, user) and cgroups v2 allows precise control over process isolation and resource limits. For example, cgroups v2 enables kernel-enforced memory and CPU constraints, preventing resource exhaustion.
Reduced Overhead: By avoiding the abstraction layer of Docker, the sandbox can achieve faster startup times and lower memory footprint. This is critical for high-concurrency scenarios where every millisecond and megabyte counts.
Deeper Security: Seccomp-BPF filters restrict system calls to a denylist, preventing access to sensitive kernel functionality. Combined with user namespaces (mapping sandbox root to host UID 65534), this ensures that even if code escapes the sandbox, it lacks elevated privileges on the host.
While a Linux-primitive-based sandbox offers performance and resource efficiency, it comes with trade-offs:
Complexity: Implementing and configuring Linux primitives requires deep understanding of kernel internals. Misconfigurations—such as incorrect cgroups limits or seccomp filters—can introduce security vulnerabilities or resource leaks.
Portability: The solution is kernel-dependent, limiting its applicability to non-Linux systems. This makes it unsuitable for cross-platform environments.
Language-Specific Nuances: Each supported language (e.g., Python, C++, Java) has unique runtime characteristics. Tailoring the sandbox for each language requires careful consideration of runtime environments and potential exploits.
The ContainerizationAPI project demonstrates the feasibility of this approach. By combining PID, mount, network, and user namespaces with cgroups v2, seccomp-BPF, and chroot, it achieves:
Faster Execution: Benchmarks show significant speed improvements over Docker and firejail, attributed to reduced overhead from container runtime initialization and image layering.
Kernel-Enforced Limits: Memory and CPU constraints are enforced by cgroups v2, preventing resource exhaustion. A global admission controller rejects submissions exceeding predefined limits (e.g., 60s execution time, 128MB memory) before sandbox creation.
Enhanced Security: Seccomp-BPF filters block unauthorized system calls, while user namespaces ensure that sandbox root privileges do not translate to host privileges. However, the risk of sandbox escape remains, necessitating isolation on a small, segregated server.
This Linux-primitive-based sandbox is optimal when:
Performance is Critical: If rapid code execution and minimal resource overhead are priorities, this approach outperforms Docker and similar tools.
Fine-Grained Control is Required: When precise resource allocation and isolation are necessary, Linux primitives offer unparalleled flexibility.
Expertise is Available: The complexity of implementation requires deep knowledge of Linux internals. Without this expertise, misconfigurations can introduce significant risks.
However, if portability, ease of use, or cross-platform compatibility are priorities, traditional containerization tools like Docker remain the better choice. The Linux-native approach is not a one-size-fits-all solution but a specialized tool for high-performance, security-critical scenarios.
The design of this Linux-native code execution sandbox hinges on a meticulous selection and orchestration of Linux primitives, eschewing Docker’s abstraction layer to achieve superior performance and resource efficiency. The core approach leverages namespaces, cgroups v2, seccomp-BPF, and chroot to construct a lightweight, kernel-enforced isolation boundary. Below is a breakdown of the methodology, grounded in the analytical model.
The sandbox employs PID, mount, network, and user namespaces to create a hermetic environment for untrusted code. PID namespaces isolate process IDs, preventing the sandboxed process from observing or interfering with host processes. Mount namespaces restrict filesystem access, while network namespaces confine network interactions. Critically, user namespaces map the sandbox’s root user to the host’s non-privileged UID (65534), ensuring that even if the sandboxed process escalates to root, it lacks host privileges. This mapping is a causal safeguard against privilege escalation exploits, as the kernel enforces UID boundaries.
A chroot into a minimal, language-specific rootfs further constrains the execution environment. For instance, Python’s rootfs contains only the runtime and essential libraries, stripping away unnecessary binaries. This mechanical reduction of the filesystem attack surface limits the potential for directory traversal or file access exploits, directly addressing the risk of sandbox escape via filesystem manipulation.
Resource allocation is governed by cgroups v2, which imposes kernel-enforced limits on CPU and memory. For example, the sandbox caps execution at 60 seconds and 128MB. These limits are physically enforced by the kernel’s resource controller, throttling or terminating processes that exceed thresholds. This mechanism prevents resource exhaustion, a common failure mode in unconstrained environments. However, improper configuration—such as setting memory limits too high relative to system capacity—can still lead to denial-of-service conditions, underscoring the need for precise tuning.
A seccomp-BPF denylist filters system calls, blocking access to sensitive kernel functions (e.g., ptrace, mount). This mechanical restriction mitigates the risk of sandbox escape by limiting the sandboxed process’s ability to interact with the kernel. For instance, disabling mount prevents the process from altering the filesystem layout, a common exploit vector. However, seccomp’s effectiveness depends on a comprehensive denylist; omissions can introduce vulnerabilities, highlighting the trade-off between security and complexity.
A global admission controller pre-screens submissions, rejecting those exceeding predefined limits before sandbox creation. This causal intervention reduces overhead by avoiding resource allocation for invalid requests. For example, a submission requiring 256MB memory is rejected outright, preventing cgroups from even initializing the sandbox. This layer is critical for high-concurrency scenarios, where unchecked submissions could overwhelm system resources.
Each supported language (Python, C++17, C11, Java) requires tailored configurations. For instance, Python’s sandbox includes a stripped-down site-packages directory, while C++’s sandbox restricts compiler flags to prevent arbitrary code generation. This mechanical tailoring ensures compatibility while maintaining security. However, language-specific exploits—such as Python’s ctypes module bypassing seccomp filters—remain a risk, necessitating runtime-specific mitigations.
While the sandbox outperforms Docker in execution speed and resource efficiency, it introduces complexity and kernel dependency. Misconfigurations in namespaces or cgroups can lead to sandbox escape or resource starvation. For example, failing to apply a seccomp filter to a critical system call creates an exploit pathway. Similarly, cgroups limits set too low can cause legitimate processes to terminate prematurely. The solution is optimal for performance-critical, Linux-exclusive environments with expertise in Linux internals. For cross-platform or less specialized use cases, Docker remains the more robust choice.
If the deployment environment prioritizes execution speed, resource efficiency, and fine-grained control over portability and ease of use, use this Linux-primitive-based sandbox. If cross-platform compatibility or simplified management is critical, use Docker or equivalent containerization tools.
The Linux-native code execution sandbox leverages a combination of kernel primitives to achieve isolation, resource control, and security. Below, we detail six specific scenarios, illustrating how these primitives are applied with code examples or pseudocode. Each scenario is grounded in the system mechanisms and environment constraints of the sandbox, highlighting the causal chain of implementation decisions and their effects.
To isolate CPU usage, the sandbox employs cgroups v2, a kernel feature that enforces resource limits. The causal chain is as follows: impact (untrusted code consumes excessive CPU) → internal process (cgroups v2 limits CPU shares) → observable effect (code execution is capped at a predefined threshold, e.g., 60s). Misconfiguration of cgroups could lead to resource exhaustion, where the host system’s CPU is starved. The optimal solution is to use cgroups v2 with precise limits, as it provides kernel-enforced control, unlike user-space solutions like Docker, which introduce overhead.
Pseudocode:
cgCreate("cpu", "sandbox_job");

cgSet("cpu.max", "60000ms"); // 60 seconds
Memory limits are enforced using cgroups v2, preventing untrusted code from consuming excessive RAM. The mechanism is: impact (code allocates more memory than allowed) → internal process (cgroups v2 triggers the OOM killer) → observable effect (process is terminated). A common failure mode is resource exhaustion, where improper limits lead to host instability. The optimal solution is to set memory limits at the kernel level (e.g., 128MB) and use an admission controller to reject submissions exceeding these limits before sandbox creation.
Pseudocode:
cgCreate("memory", "sandbox_job");

cgSet("memory.max", "128M"); // 128MB
File access is restricted using mount namespaces and chroot. The causal chain is: impact (code attempts to access sensitive files) → internal process (mount namespace isolates the filesystem, chroot confines execution to a minimal rootfs) → observable effect (code is limited to a stripped-down filesystem). A typical failure is sandbox escape via symlink attacks or misconfigured mounts. The optimal solution is to combine mount namespaces with a language-specific, minimal rootfs, reducing the attack surface.
Pseudocode:
unshare(CLONE_NEWNS);

mount("tmpfs", "/tmp", "tmpfs", 0, NULL);

chroot("/minimal_rootfs");
Network isolation is achieved via network namespaces, ensuring untrusted code cannot access the host network. The mechanism is: impact (code attempts network communication) → internal process (network namespace blocks access) → observable effect (code is confined to its own network stack). A risk is sandbox escape via kernel vulnerabilities in network stack handling. The optimal solution is to disable network access entirely for untrusted code, as it eliminates this risk.
Pseudocode:
unshare(CLONE_NEWNET);

loopbackSetup(); // Only allow localhost
Privilege escalation is mitigated using user namespaces and UID mapping. The causal chain is: impact (code gains root privileges inside the sandbox) → internal process (UID mapping to host UID 65534) → observable effect (root inside the sandbox has no privileges on the host). A common failure is kernel bugs in user namespace handling. The optimal solution is to map the sandbox root to a non-privileged UID, as it ensures containment even if the sandbox is compromised.
Pseudocode:
unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER);

write("/proc/self/uid_map", "0 65534 1");
System call restrictions are enforced using seccomp-BPF, a kernel feature that filters system calls. The mechanism is: impact (code attempts a restricted system call) → internal process (seccomp-BPF blocks the call) → observable effect (code is prevented from accessing sensitive kernel functionality). A typical failure is an incomplete denylist, allowing unintended system calls. The optimal solution is to use a comprehensive denylist tailored to each language, as it minimizes attack vectors.
Pseudocode:
seccompLoadFilter(SECCOMP_RET_KILL, ["ptrace", "mount"]);
While the sandbox offers superior performance and fine-grained control, it requires deep Linux expertise and carries a higher risk of misconfiguration. The optimal use case is high-performance, Linux-exclusive environments where execution speed and resource efficiency are critical. If cross-platform compatibility or ease of use is required, Docker remains the better choice. The rule is: if prioritizing performance and resource efficiency in a Linux-only environment with available expertise → use Linux-primitive sandbox; otherwise → use Docker.
The Linux-native code execution sandbox, as implemented in the ContainerizationAPI project, leverages a combination of Linux primitives to achieve isolation and resource management. Below is a detailed analysis of its security and performance, grounded in the system mechanisms, environment constraints, and expert observations.
Isolation Mechanisms: The sandbox employs PID, mount, network, and user namespaces to create a boundary around untrusted code. This ensures that processes, filesystems, network stacks, and user privileges are isolated from the host. For example, the user namespace maps the sandbox root to host UID 65534, preventing privilege escalation even if the code gains root access inside the sandbox. Mechanism: The kernel enforces UID boundaries, ensuring that root privileges inside the sandbox do not translate to host privileges. Risk: Kernel bugs in user namespace handling could compromise this isolation. Mitigation: Regular kernel updates and rigorous testing are essential.
Resource Management: Cgroups v2 enforces kernel-level limits on CPU and memory, preventing resource exhaustion. For instance, a 60-second CPU limit and 128MB memory cap are applied. Mechanism: Cgroups v2 triggers the OOM killer if memory limits are exceeded, terminating the process. Risk: Misconfigured limits can lead to host instability or denial-of-service. Mitigation: Use precise limits and an admission controller to pre-screen submissions.
System Call Restriction: Seccomp-BPF filters block sensitive system calls like ptrace and mount, limiting kernel interaction. Mechanism: The denylist prevents unauthorized access to kernel functions. Risk: An incomplete denylist could allow unintended system calls. Mitigation: Maintain a comprehensive, language-specific denylist and regularly update it.
File Access Restriction: Chroot confines execution to a minimal, language-specific rootfs, reducing the attack surface. Mechanism: Mount namespaces isolate the filesystem, preventing access to host directories. Risk: Symlink attacks or misconfigured mounts could lead to sandbox escape. Mitigation: Combine mount namespaces with a stripped-down rootfs and avoid unnecessary mounts.
Startup Time: The sandbox outperforms Docker and firejail in startup time due to reduced runtime overhead. Mechanism: Avoiding container initialization and using lightweight Linux primitives results in faster process creation. Benchmark: ContainerizationAPI demonstrates sub-second startup times compared to Docker’s multi-second initialization.
Resource Efficiency: The sandbox consumes significantly less memory than Docker containers. Mechanism: Minimal rootfs and absence of container runtime layers reduce memory footprint. Benchmark: A Python execution in the sandbox uses ~30MB memory vs. Docker’s ~100MB baseline.
Execution Speed: Code execution is faster due to direct kernel-level resource management. Mechanism: Cgroups v2 and seccomp-BPF operate at the kernel level, avoiding the overhead of container runtimes. Benchmark: A C++17 benchmark completes in 2.5 seconds in the sandbox vs. 4 seconds in Docker.
Complexity and Misconfiguration Risk: The sandbox requires deep Linux expertise to configure correctly. Mechanism: Misconfigurations in cgroups, seccomp filters, or namespaces can lead to vulnerabilities. Example: Improper cgroups limits may cause resource starvation. Solution: Provide configuration templates and validation tools.
Portability: The sandbox is Linux-exclusive, limiting its use in cross-platform environments. Mechanism: Reliance on Linux-specific primitives like cgroups v2 and user namespaces. Alternative: Docker remains the better choice for cross-platform compatibility.
Language-Specific Challenges: Tailoring the sandbox for languages like Python, C++, and Java requires runtime-specific configurations. Mechanism: Language-specific exploits (e.g., Python’s ctypes) must be mitigated. Solution: Maintain language-specific profiles and regularly update them for new vulnerabilities.
The Linux-native sandbox offers superior performance and resource efficiency compared to Docker, making it ideal for high-performance, Linux-exclusive environments. However, its complexity and risk of misconfiguration require expertise in Linux internals. For optimal results, use this sandbox when:
Performance is critical, and resource efficiency is a priority.
Linux expertise is available to ensure proper configuration.
Cross-platform compatibility is not required.
Otherwise, Docker remains the more accessible and portable solution. The sandbox’s success hinges on careful implementation and ongoing security audits to mitigate risks like sandbox escape and resource exhaustion.
The Linux-primitive-based code execution sandbox, as demonstrated in the ContainerizationAPI, proves to be a viable and efficient alternative to Docker for isolating and managing untrusted code execution. By leveraging namespaces, cgroups v2, seccomp-BPF, and chroot, the sandbox achieves superior performance and resource efficiency compared to traditional containerization tools. For instance, the sub-second startup time and 30MB memory footprint for Python execution starkly contrast Docker’s multi-second initialization and ~100MB overhead, as observed in benchmarks.
The sandbox’s feasibility hinges on its ability to enforce kernel-level isolation and resource limits. PID, mount, network, and user namespaces create a robust boundary, while cgroups v2 ensures CPU and memory constraints are strictly enforced. The seccomp-BPF denylist effectively mitigates kernel access risks, and UID mapping to host UID 65534 prevents privilege escalation. These mechanisms collectively enable fine-grained control over execution environments, a critical advantage over Docker’s higher-level abstractions.
However, the solution is Linux-exclusive, relying on features like cgroups v2 and user namespaces, which limits portability. Additionally, the complexity of configuration introduces risks of misconfiguration, such as improper cgroups limits leading to host instability or sandbox escape via symlink attacks due to misconfigured mounts. These trade-offs underscore the need for Linux expertise and rigorous testing.
To further enhance the sandbox, the following improvements are proposed:
Enhanced Security Features: Integrate additional seccomp-BPF rules tailored to specific languages (e.g., blocking Python’s ctypes module) to mitigate language-specific exploits. Implement kernel-level auditing to detect and log suspicious activities within the sandbox.
Resource Management Optimization: Develop dynamic cgroups tuning based on workload patterns to improve resource utilization in high-concurrency scenarios. Introduce predictive admission control to preemptively reject submissions likely to exceed resource limits.
Language Support Expansion: Extend support to additional languages (e.g., Rust, Go) by creating language-specific rootfs profiles and seccomp denylists. Address runtime-specific vulnerabilities (e.g., Go’s os/exec package) through tailored configurations.
Misconfiguration Mitigation: Provide configuration templates and validation tools to reduce the risk of errors. Implement runtime checks for critical parameters like cgroups limits and namespace setups.
The Linux-primitive sandbox is optimal when:
Performance is critical, and execution speed and resource efficiency outweigh portability needs.
Linux expertise is available to manage complexity and mitigate misconfiguration risks.
The environment is Linux-exclusive, eliminating the need for cross-platform compatibility.
Conversely, Docker remains the better choice when:
Cross-platform compatibility or simplified management is essential.
The team lacks the Linux expertise required to configure and maintain the sandbox.
In conclusion, while the Linux-primitive sandbox is not a general replacement for Docker, it represents a specialized solution for high-performance, security-critical scenarios. Its success depends on careful implementation, ongoing security audits, and a clear understanding of its trade-offs. For environments where these conditions are met, it offers a compelling alternative to traditional containerization tools.

Unpacking the Exploits: A Deep Dive into Why DeFi Protocols Remain Prime Targets for Hacking
articles.description:
TITLE: Unpacking the Exploits: A Deep Dive into Why DeFi Protocols Remain Prime Targets for Hacking
The realm of Decentralized Finance (DeFi) has emerged as one of the most transformative innovations in the financial sector over the past half-decade. Promising a future of permissionless, transparent, and censorship-resistant financial services, DeFi has attracted trillions of dollars in capital and fostered an unprecedented wave of innovation. From lending and borrowing platforms to decentralized exchanges (DEXs) and synthetic assets, the ecosystem has rapidly expanded, challenging traditional financial intermediaries and offering novel opportunities for users worldwide. However, this rapid ascent has been shadowed by a persistent and alarming vulnerability: the frequent and often devastating exploitation of DeFi protocols.
Despite the inherent security features of blockchain technology, such as cryptographic immutability and distributed consensus, DeFi protocols have repeatedly fallen victim to sophisticated attacks, resulting in billions of dollars in lost funds. These incidents not only erode user trust and deter mainstream adoption but also highlight the profound complexities and inherent risks associated with building and deploying financial applications on nascent, open-source infrastructure. This article, penned from a decade of experience in blockchain research, aims to meticulously dissect the multifaceted reasons behind these persistent security breaches. We will delve into the technical underpinnings of these vulnerabilities, examine real-world case studies, acknowledge the inherent limitations in achieving absolute security, and ultimately offer an expert perspective on the path forward for securing the future of decentralized finance.
Decentralized Finance (DeFi) represents a paradigm shift from traditional finance, leveraging blockchain technology, primarily Ethereum and its compatible networks, to create an open and interconnected financial system. At its core, DeFi operates on smart contracts—self-executing agreements whose terms are directly written into code. These contracts automate financial services like lending, borrowing, trading, and asset management without the need for intermediaries such such as banks or brokers. The allure of DeFi lies in its principles: permissionlessness (anyone can participate), transparency (all transactions are publicly verifiable), and non-custodial control (users retain ownership of their assets).
The rapid growth of DeFi can be attributed to several factors. High yield opportunities, often significantly exceeding those in traditional finance, attract capital. The promise of financial inclusion, offering services to the unbanked or underbanked, resonates deeply. Furthermore, the "money lego" nature of DeFi, where protocols can seamlessly integrate and build upon one another, fosters incredible innovation and network effects. This composability allows for complex financial products to be constructed from simpler, interoperable components.
However, this very innovation and rapid expansion also create fertile ground for exploitation. The immense value locked within DeFi protocols makes them incredibly attractive targets for malicious actors. Unlike traditional financial systems where human intervention and legal frameworks can often mitigate or reverse fraud, the immutable nature of smart contracts means that once a vulnerability is exploited and funds are transferred, recovery is often exceedingly difficult, if not impossible. The open-source nature, while promoting transparency and community vetting, also provides sophisticated attackers with ample opportunity to scrutinize code for subtle flaws. The intense pressure to launch new protocols and features quickly often leads to overlooked security considerations, insufficient auditing, and a general environment where innovation sometimes outpaces robust security practices. Understanding this backdrop is crucial before diving into the specific technical mechanisms of these attacks.
The vulnerabilities exploited in DeFi protocols are diverse, ranging from fundamental smart contract flaws to sophisticated economic manipulations. A comprehensive understanding requires dissecting these technical root causes.
The most direct form of attack often targets flaws within the smart contract code itself. These are essentially bugs that, when triggered, allow an attacker to bypass intended logic or access unauthorized funds.
  Reentrancy Attacks: This classic vulnerability, famously exploited in The DAO hack in 2016 (a precursor to modern DeFi), occurs when an external call to another contract is made before the calling contract updates its own state. An attacker can repeatedly call the vulnerable function, draining funds before the initial transaction is fully processed and the balance is updated. While defenses like the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern are now standard, variations or novel implementations can still introduce this flaw.
  Logic Errors and Bugs: These are broad categories encompassing a wide array of coding mistakes. Examples include:


  Incorrect Arithmetic: Integer overflow/underflow errors, where calculations exceed the maximum or fall below the minimum value a variable can hold, leading to incorrect balances or arbitrary value manipulation.
  Access Control Issues: Functions intended for administrative use or specific roles are left unprotected, allowing any user to call them. This can lead to unauthorized minting of tokens, disabling of critical functions, or draining of funds.
  Faulty State Transitions: Errors in how a contract's state (e.g., user balances, collateral ratios) is updated after certain operations, leading to inconsistencies that can be exploited.
  Improper Input Validation: Failing to properly validate user inputs can lead to unexpected behavior or allow attackers to craft malicious inputs that trigger vulnerabilities.
  Flash Loan Exploits: While flash loans themselves are a legitimate and innovative DeFi primitive (allowing uncollateralized loans within a single transaction block), they are frequently used as a tool to amplify other vulnerabilities. An attacker can borrow a massive amount of assets via a flash loan, use these assets to manipulate market conditions (e.g., price on a low-liquidity DEX), exploit a separate vulnerable protocol based on that manipulated price, and then repay the flash loan—all within the same atomic transaction. The key here is not the flash loan itself, but how it enables the attacker to gain sufficient capital to execute an economic exploit that would otherwise be impossible.
DeFi protocols often rely on external data feeds, known as oracles, to bring off-chain information (like asset prices) onto the blockchain. If these oracles can be manipulated, the dependent protocols become vulnerable.
  Price Oracle Manipulation: This is a common vector, often combined with flash loans. If a protocol relies on a single or easily manipulable on-chain price source (e.g., a low-liquidity DEX pair), an attacker can use a flash loan to temporarily inflate or deflate the price of an asset on that specific DEX. They then use this manipulated price to perform an exploit on a lending protocol (e.g., borrowing more assets than their collateral is truly worth, or liquidating healthy collateral at an artificially low price). Robust, decentralized oracle networks like Chainlink aim to mitigate this by aggregating data from multiple sources, making manipulation significantly harder and more expensive.
Beyond direct code bugs, some protocols suffer from fundamental economic design flaws that can be exploited, even if the code itself is technically sound.
  Undercollateralization/Liquidation Exploits: Protocols designed with specific collateralization ratios can be vulnerable if an attacker can manipulate prices or liquidation mechanisms to their advantage. For instance, front-running liquidations or exploiting a delay in oracle updates to trigger liquidations unfairly.
  Tokenomics Attacks: Flaws in how a protocol's native token is designed or integrated can lead to economic instability. This can include inflationary bugs, issues with staking/unstaking mechanisms, or vulnerabilities in governance token distribution that allow for concentrated control.
While less common than smart contract exploits, vulnerabilities outside the core smart contract logic can also lead to significant losses.
  Private Key Compromise: Centralized components, such as multi-signature wallets for bridge operations or administrative keys, can be compromised through social engineering, phishing, or direct hacking of an organization's internal systems. This isn't a smart contract bug but a failure in operational security.
  Front-end Attacks: Malicious actors can compromise the front-end user interface of a DeFi application (e.g., via DNS hijacking or injecting malicious code), redirecting user transactions to attacker-controlled addresses or tricking users into signing malicious transactions.
The interplay between these different vulnerability types often characterizes the most sophisticated attacks. An attacker might combine a flash loan to gain capital, then use that capital to manipulate an oracle, and finally exploit a logic error in a lending protocol—all within a single, atomic transaction to maximize damage and minimize detection.
Examining specific incidents provides crucial context for understanding the theoretical vulnerabilities discussed above. The history of DeFi is unfortunately replete with such examples, each offering unique insights into the attack vectors.
Poly Network (August 2021): One of the largest DeFi hacks to date, Poly Network, a cross-chain interoperability protocol, suffered an exploit resulting in over $610 million in stolen assets. The attacker exploited a vulnerability in the EthCrossChainManager smart contract, specifically in how it handled cross-chain message relaying. A flaw allowed the attacker to call a function (_executeCrossChainTx) with arbitrary data, effectively granting them the ability to sign transactions and transfer assets from the Poly Network's controlled wallets on various blockchains (Ethereum, BSC, Polygon). This was a critical smart contract logic error that allowed an unauthorized party to assume control over protocol functions, leading to massive asset drain. In a rare turn of events, the attacker, dubbed "Mr. White Hat," eventually returned most of the stolen funds.


Ronin Bridge (March 2022): The Ronin Network, an Ethereum sidechain built for the popular blockchain game Axie Infinity, experienced an exploit of approximately $625 million. This incident was distinct from a direct smart contract bug. Instead, the attacker gained control of five out of the nine validator private keys required for the Ronin Bridge's multi-signature wallet. With control over a majority of the keys, the attacker was able to forge withdrawal transactions for 173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC. The root cause was a combination of social engineering and poor operational security, where a backdoor was created through a gas-free signature for an allowlist, and later, the validator nodes were compromised. This highlights the critical vulnerability of centralized points of failure, even within ostensibly decentralized ecosystems, particularly when it comes to key management.


Cream Finance (Multiple Attacks, e.g., October 2021): Cream Finance, a prominent lending protocol, has been subjected to several significant exploits. One notable incident in October 2021 resulted in a loss of over $130 million. This attack was a sophisticated combination of a flash loan and oracle manipulation. The attacker used a flash loan to borrow a massive amount of Wrapped Ether (WETH) and other assets. They then used these borrowed assets to manipulate the price of YFI (Yearn Finance) on a low-liquidity DEX. By artificially inflating the YFI price, the attacker could then deposit the manipulated YFI as collateral into Cream Finance and borrow a disproportionately large amount of other assets (like stablecoins). After draining the protocol, the attacker repaid the flash loan, profiting from the manipulated collateral ratio. This perfectly illustrates how flash loans are often the enabler for exploiting price oracle vulnerabilities in other protocols.



These cases underscore that DeFi hacks are not monolithic. They span from intricate smart contract logic flaws (Poly Network) to failures in operational security and key management (Ronin Bridge), and sophisticated economic exploits enabled by DeFi primitives (Cream Finance). Each incident serves as a stark reminder of the continuous need for vigilance and robust security practices across the entire ecosystem.
Despite significant advancements in security auditing, formal verification, and incident response, certain inherent characteristics of the DeFi landscape present persistent limitations in preventing all forms of exploitation.
Immutability's Double Edge: The immutable nature of smart contracts, a foundational principle of blockchain, is a double-edged sword. While it guarantees censorship resistance and transparency, it also means that once a buggy contract is deployed, its flaws are permanently etched onto the blockchain. Patching or upgrading often requires deploying an entirely new contract, migrating user funds, or building in upgradeability mechanisms (e.g., proxy contracts), which themselves introduce complexity and potential centralization risks. This makes proactive bug prevention paramount, as reactive fixes are often costly, difficult, and sometimes impossible without further risk.


Complexity and Composability: The "money lego" architecture, while powerful for innovation, significantly amplifies security risks. Protocols are built on top of, and interact with, numerous other protocols, creating a vast and intricate dependency graph. A vulnerability in one foundational component can cascade through the entire ecosystem, affecting multiple dependent protocols. This interconnectedness makes comprehensive security auditing incredibly challenging, as auditors must not only assess the individual protocol's code but also its interactions with all integrated external contracts and the potential for unexpected emergent behaviors.


Rapid Innovation vs. Security Audits: The DeFi space is characterized by an exceptionally fast pace of innovation. New protocols, features, and financial primitives are launched constantly, driven by market demand and competitive pressure. This rapid development cycle often outstrips the capacity for thorough security auditing and formal verification. Comprehensive audits are expensive, time-consuming, and require highly specialized expertise. Consequently, many protocols launch with insufficient security scrutiny, making them ripe targets for exploitation.


The Human Factor: Ultimately, smart contracts are written by humans, and humans make mistakes. Developer errors, whether in logic, arithmetic, or access control, are a fundamental source of vulnerabilities. Beyond coding errors, the human element extends to operational security—private key management, social engineering resistance, and proper configuration of infrastructure. Even with the best technical safeguards, human fallibility can introduce critical weak points.


Lack of Standardized Security Practices: While the industry is maturing, there is still no universally adopted set of security standards or certifications for DeFi protocols. Best practices are evolving, but enforcement is inconsistent. This leads to a wide disparity in security postures across different projects, with some investing heavily in audits and bug bounties, while others prioritize speed to market over robust security.



These limitations underscore that achieving absolute security in DeFi is an elusive, if not impossible, goal. The challenge lies in continuously mitigating risks and building resilience in an environment characterized by complexity, rapid change, and high stakes.
The persistent challenge of hacks and exploits within the Decentralized Finance ecosystem is a critical paradox. On one hand, DeFi represents a revolutionary leap forward in financial innovation, offering unprecedented transparency, accessibility, and efficiency. On the other, the inherent complexities of smart contract development, coupled with the immense financial incentives for malicious actors, have made it a fertile ground for sophisticated attacks, leading to billions in losses and eroding public trust.
Our analysis has revealed that the reasons for these vulnerabilities are multifaceted, ranging from fundamental smart contract flaws like reentrancy and logic errors, to sophisticated economic manipulations leveraging flash loans and oracle price manipulation, and even critical failures in off-chain operational security such as private key compromises. Real-world incidents, including the Poly Network bridge hack, the Ronin Bridge private key compromise, and the repeated flash loan exploits on Cream Finance, vividly illustrate the diverse attack vectors and the profound impact on users and the broader ecosystem.
The limitations in achieving absolute security are also clear: the double-edged sword of immutability, the exponential complexity introduced by composability, the tension between rapid innovation and thorough security auditing, and the unavoidable human factor all contribute to an environment where vulnerabilities, despite best efforts, will likely continue to emerge.
However, the future of DeFi is not without hope. The industry is rapidly learning and adapting. Key mitigation strategies and improvements are continuously being developed and implemented:
  Rigor in Smart Contract Auditing and Formal Verification: There's a growing emphasis on multiple, independent security audits and the use of formal verification methods to mathematically prove the correctness of critical smart contract logic.
  Decentralized Oracle Solutions: Protocols are increasingly adopting robust, decentralized oracle networks (like Chainlink) that aggregate data from numerous sources, making price manipulation significantly more difficult and expensive.
  Bug Bounty Programs: Encouraging ethical hackers to discover and report vulnerabilities through generous bounty programs has become a standard practice, serving as a crucial layer of defense.
  Robust Incident Response and Insurance: Developing clear incident response plans and exploring decentralized insurance solutions can help mitigate the financial impact of successful attacks.
  Progressive Decentralization: Many projects are adopting a phased approach to decentralization, allowing for more centralized control and easier upgrades in early stages, gradually transitioning to full decentralization as security matures.
  Enhanced Operational Security: Improving best practices for private key management, multi-signature wallet security, and protection against social engineering attacks is paramount.
In conclusion, while DeFi offers immense promise, its journey is inextricably linked to its ability to mature its security posture. The industry must evolve from a "move fast and break things" mentality to one that prioritizes "move thoughtfully and secure everything." Perfect security remains an unattainable ideal, but through continuous research, rigorous development practices, collaborative security efforts, and a steadfast commitment to learning from past mistakes, the DeFi ecosystem can build a more resilient and trustworthy financial future.
Disclaimer: This article is for informational and educational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment, or legal advice. The cryptocurrency and blockchain space is highly volatile and complex, and readers should conduct their own research and consult with qualified professionals before making any decisions. The author is not responsible for any losses incurred as a result of relying on the information presented herein.

Kubernetes Security Is Three Problems, Not One: Admission, Identity, Runtime
articles.description:
That is the useful reframe. Kubernetes security is not one problem at the boundary. It is three problems inside it, and each one needs its own control that keeps working when the others fail:
Admission decides what is allowed to deploy, and with what configuration.
Identity decides what each running pod is allowed to reach.
Runtime watches what a pod actually does, which is often not what its manifest claimed.
None of the individual tools below are new, and none of this is a new technique. What is worth sharing is how the layers fit together, so a failure in any one of them does not open an exploitable gap. The model maps cleanly onto NIST SP 800-207 (zero trust) and NIST SP 800-190 (container security), and you can hold it to the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark as a measurable floor.
Start with what Kubernetes gives you for free. Pod Security Admission (PSA) enforces security profiles per namespace with no external tooling. The Restricted profile blocks host namespace sharing, privilege escalation, root contexts, and unsafe seccomp settings. A practical split is Restricted for externally facing namespaces and Baseline for internal platform namespaces with documented exceptions.
PSA is a floor, not a scalpel. It enforces at the namespace level, so it cannot say "this specific Deployment must run as UID 1000 with this seccomp profile." That is where Kyverno comes in. Its policies are plain YAML, they live in the same GitOps repo as your manifests, and they go through the same pull request review as any other change. Four rule types cover most needs:
validate rejects non-compliant resources (for example, require every image to come from an approved ECR registry).
mutate corrects omissions automatically, which turns "you forgot a security context" from an admission failure into a silent fix.
generate creates dependent resources on creation.
verifyImages enforces signature checks at admission time (more on that below).
For constraint logic that depends on the state of other cluster resources, or cross-namespace rules, OPA Gatekeeper and Rego express things Kyverno's YAML cannot. Running both is a reasonable choice: Kyverno for the common case, Gatekeeper where you need Rego's relational power.
One rollout lesson worth stating plainly: both tools have an audit mode, and you should use it first. Measure violations with enforcement off, remediate systematically, then switch to enforce. Flipping straight to enforcement is how a security rollout turns into a production incident.
A static AWS key in a ConfigMap or an environment variable is a persistent risk with a wide blast radius. IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) removes the category entirely. The AWS SDK in a pod annotated with an IRSA service account exchanges a short-lived, audience-scoped JWT for temporary IAM credentials through STS. Nothing static is created, stored, or rotated. The IAM trust policy validates the token's subject claim against a specific service account and namespace, so a compromised pod in one namespace cannot assume another namespace's role.
The payoff is blast-radius reduction you can describe concretely. Without IRSA, a compromised pod inherits whatever the node's instance profile can reach. With IRSA, it is limited to that one pod's scoped role.
Application secrets need a parallel mechanism, and that is the ExternalSecrets Operator. It syncs values from AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store into Kubernetes Secrets and refreshes them on the source's rotation schedule. When Secrets Manager rotates a database password, the new value propagates without a deployment. IRSA plus ExternalSecrets together removes every static credential: cloud access through IRSA, application secrets through ESO, nothing hardcoded in a Helm values file.
Scaling per-workload IAM roles across hundreds of workloads is the part teams tend to defer. Attribute-based access control with IAM permission boundaries makes it tractable: a role that expresses "this service account, in this namespace, for this environment" can be generated from workload metadata instead of hand-authored each time.
Admission decides what can deploy. Identity decides what it can reach. Neither sees what a pod does after it is running. Falco does, using eBPF probes at the kernel level to observe every syscall from every container on the node. A shell spawned in a container whose image has no shell in its approved process list raises an alert, regardless of how the compromise happened or whether the attacker edited the deployment manifest. Because eBPF sits below the container runtime, it keeps working even if the runtime is tampered with, and it needs no change to the image or the application.
Two practical notes. First, uniform rules across every workload generate false positives that erode trust in the alerts. A data-processing pod that legitimately reads many files will trip rules tuned for an application server. Per-workload rule sets, stored in Git next to the manifests, let you tighten baselines for payment or secret-handling services and loosen them for CI runners. Second, route Falco alerts into a SIEM so individual detections become correlated events. A shell-spawn alert followed within seconds by an outbound connection to an unknown IP is a pattern a correlation engine can act on, including automated network-policy quarantine of the affected pod.
Plan for a calibration period. Default Falco rules produce false-positive volume that takes iterative tuning, with both security and application knowledge, before the layer runs at production-grade sensitivity.
An image that passes admission is trusted to be what its manifest says, but only if the reference is cryptographically verified. Tags are mutable. Someone can overwrite the content behind a trusted tag and the cluster will deploy it under the same name, which bypasses every admission policy that checks the image's properties rather than its identity.
Cosign signs images at the registry, and Kyverno verifyImages rules reject anything at admission that is not signed by an approved identity. That closes the tag-mutability gap. SLSA provenance is the next step up: signing proves an image came from your build system, provenance proves what went into that build (source commit, build platform, resolved dependencies). A Software Bill of Materials attached as an attestation then lets you answer "which running images contain this newly disclosed CVE?" by querying the SBOM store instead of inspecting containers one by one.
The point of three independent layers is that no single failure is fatal. A policy gap that lets a bad pod through is still caught by scoped identity and runtime monitoring. A runtime compromise still cannot reach credentials the pod's IAM role never granted. A swapped image is rejected before it schedules.
If you are starting from scratch, a reasonable order is:
Turn on Pod Security Admission at Baseline or Restricted. Free, immediate.
Add Kyverno in audit mode, learn your violations, then enforce.
Move workloads to IRSA and ExternalSecrets to delete static credentials.
Deploy Falco, then budget real time to tune per-workload rules.
Add Cosign signing and verifyImages, then SLSA provenance and SBOMs.
The honest tradeoff is maintenance. Policy-as-code needs upkeep as Kubernetes APIs and workloads change, and Falco rule tuning is ongoing work. The reason to pay that cost is coverage no single control gives you: admission, identity, and runtime failures are different problems, and defending only one of them leaves the other two open.
NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture.
NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide.
CIS Kubernetes Benchmark.
Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, Falco, and Sigstore/Cosign project docs.
If you run this in production, I would be interested in which layer gave you the most trouble to operationalize. For me it is runtime rule tuning. Drop a comment.

Chrome’s Silent Clipboard Scan: What It Is, Why It Matters, and How to Stop It






  
  
  Introduction


Chrome’s new clipboard‑monitoring feature has turned into a privacy flashpoint after Xataka and Hipertextual revealed that the browser silently inspects copied text and ships matching snippets to Google’s servers. Within hours the story generated a 400 % spike in “Chrome clipboard privacy” searches, sparked heated debates on Reddit and Hacker News, and left thousands of users scrambling for a quick fix.  
In this guide you’ll get:  
A plain‑language breakdown of how the scanner works.

A side‑by‑side comparison with similar features in Edge, Brave, and Firefox.

Concrete, step‑by‑step instructions to disable the feature on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS.

A ready‑to‑run Python script that captures clipboard‑related network traffic for verification.

A cheat‑sheet of privacy‑first extensions and a FAQ that answers the most common concerns.







  
  
  How the Clipboard Scanner Works



Component
What Chrome Does
When It Triggers
What Gets Sent





Async Clipboard API (navigator.clipboard.readText())
Reads the current clipboard content only if the page has been granted the “clipboard‑read” permission.
After a user copies text and holds it for ≥ 500 ms.
The raw string is compared against a set of heuristics (URL, email, phone number, credit‑card pattern, address).


Heuristic Engine
Runs locally; if a match is found, the snippet is anonymised (no user‑identifying metadata).
Immediately after the match is detected.
HTTPS POST to https://clipboard.googleapis.com/v1/collect.


Policy Layer
Enterprise admins can enforce ClipboardMonitoringEnabled = false via Chrome Enterprise policies.
At browser start‑up or when policies are refreshed.
No data leaves the browser.



Key point: Chrome does not upload every clipboard entry—only those that look like “useful” data and only after a brief pause, which the developers say is meant to improve autofill and “smart copy‑paste” experiences.
Implicit data collection – Users are unaware that a copy‑paste action can become a telemetry signal.


Regulatory heat – The EU’s upcoming Digital Services Act amendments target “implicit data harvesting” in browsers.


Competitive mismatch – Edge, Brave, and Firefox explicitly require a user gesture (e.g., clicking a button) before reading the clipboard. Chrome’s background scan is the most aggressive of the major browsers.


Real‑world risk – A malicious site could trick a user into copying a credit‑card number, which Chrome would then forward to Google without the user’s knowledge.







  
  
  Quick Comparison of Major Browsers

Open Chrome → Settings.

Navigate to Privacy and security → Site Settings → Clipboard.

Toggle “Allow sites to read and write to the clipboard” to Blocked.



Alternatively, use the command line:

   # macOS / Linux (JSON policy file)
   cat <<EOF > /etc/opt/chrome/policies/managed/clipboard_policy.json
   {
     "ClipboardMonitoringEnabled": false
   }
   EOF

Restart Chrome to apply the change.

Open Chrome → Settings → Privacy → Clipboard.

For Android Enterprise: push the ClipboardMonitoringEnabled policy via an MDM solution.  
Chrome on iOS does not implement the background scanner (the feature is limited to the WebKit engine). No action required.  
Below is a minimal Python script that monitors outbound HTTPS requests to clipboard.googleapis.com. It uses mitmproxy as a local proxy; you can run it on any platform where you have Python 3.8+.
# clipboard_sniffer.py
import sys
from mitmproxy import http

TARGET_HOST = "clipboard.googleapis.com"

def request(flow: http.HTTPFlow) -> None:
    if flow.request.host == TARGET_HOST:
        print("\n=== Clipboard data detected ===")
        print(f"URL: {flow.request.url}")
        print(f"Method: {flow.request.method}")
        print(f"Headers: {flow.request.headers}")
        print(f"Body (truncated to 200 chars): {flow.request.content[:200]!r}")
        print("==============================\n")
        # Optionally block the request
        # flow.response = http.HTTPResponse.make(403, b"Blocked by user")

Run it:
pip install mitmproxy
mitmdump -s clipboard_sniffer.py

Set Chrome’s proxy to 127.0.0.1:8080.

Copy any text; if the script prints a “Clipboard data detected” block, the scanner is still active.

After you disable the feature, the script should stay silent.

  Frequently Asked Questions



Question
Answer




Does Chrome send all copied text to Google?
No. Only snippets that match predefined patterns (URL, email, phone, credit‑card, address) and only after the copy has persisted for at least 500 ms.


Can I stop Chrome from reading my clipboard completely?
Yes. Use the Settings toggle, the enterprise policy, or a blocking extension.


Will disabling the scanner break any websites?
The impact is limited to convenience features such as auto‑fill of address fields or “smart copy‑paste” suggestions. Core browsing, rendering, and JavaScript continue to work.


Is my data still sent if I’m signed into a Google account?
The scanner works independently of your sign‑in state. Disabling it stops the transmission regardless of account status.


What about Chrome on iOS?
The iOS version relies on WebKit, which does not implement this background clipboard scan. No action needed.


Can an extension re‑enable the feature?
Only an extension with the clipboardRead permission and explicit user consent could request clipboard data. It cannot toggle Chrome’s internal monitoring flag.


Will Google change this behavior after the backlash?
As of the latest Chrome 128 release (Oct 2026) the feature remains enabled by default, but Google has promised to add clearer UI disclosures in a future update.
