articles.title: Your AI Agent Has Amnesia. Mine Keeps Receipts.
articles.description:
Months of shared memory across Claude, Codex and Antigravity — versions, retractions, and why append-only notes keep failing
TL;DR. Scattered Markdown notes kept sending my agents down paths we had already rejected. I built a shared Git-backed store (KYB) with versioned records and lifecycle states — active, archived, retracted. Query current state, history, or a time slice separately; replace wrong text instead of appending; separate finished work from wrong knowledge. Pinned to KYB v0.3.3, no controlled benchmarks — mechanisms and field notes below.
Before KYB, my coding agents already had memory: Markdown files scattered across different places. The flaw showed up whenever another agent returned to a workspace, found an older note, and mistook it for the active plan. In my experience, an agent would sometimes spend hours pursuing an approach we had already investigated and rejected. The file still held a perfectly reasonable case for the old approach, while the decision to abandon it lived somewhere else.
I am Alexander Panasenko, the author of KYB (Know Your Business), so I have a stake in this story: it is my open-source project. This is an account of my engineering experience with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Google Antigravity from summer through October 2026. The text, its translation, and the diagrams were prepared with AI assistance, based on my own experience, the public source code, and saved development records.
A fresh session does not automatically inherit the conversation that just ended. A human had to step in and explain which file still mattered, why we changed course, and where the outcome was recorded. An obvious temptation is to write one more summary note, but that note needs remembering too: without updates, it goes stale like the rest.
So here is the question this piece addresses: how do you preserve operational knowledge across sessions without letting an outdated note send the next agent down a path you already abandoned? My short answer is to save a little, with versions and lifecycle state, and keep three things apart: what is true now, what was recorded then, and how an attempt ended. The rest of this piece shows where each boundary came from.
The mechanics below are pinned to the public KYB v0.3.3 release from October 27, 2026 (commit 06f63b5). The episodes below keep their dates: new features are not attributed to old versions, and the current main branch may differ. Our internal records are not public. I have not run a controlled comparison of agents with and without KYB, so the hours lost to stale notes are my personal recollection, not a measured saving after adoption.
In hindsight, the problem had three parts. First, there was no single shared entry point: notes lived in different places, and none was canonical across sessions. Second, a note had no explicit lifecycle state: a file describing a rejected plan looked just like one describing the active plan. Third, separate files do not by themselves establish which version of a decision is authoritative: even when notes are already tracked in Git, an agent reading a file in a working tree or a neighboring note cannot tell without a separate check whether that text superseded an earlier approach or was superseded later.
My first real fix was simple: a shared service for operational facts, incidents, and tasks that every session could reach. Its first interface was a CLI on top of an HTTP API; agents know how to run commands, and that was enough to start. Later, the server gained Model Context Protocol (MCP) support so agents could call its tools directly. The CLI, HTTP API, and MCP all lead to the same records: three doors into one room, not three separate memories.
What KYB did not become matters as much. It does not save hidden model reasoning or archive whole conversations. A record exists only when a human or agent explicitly saves it: knowledge under a stable key, an incident with detection and outcome, or a task with owner and status. Each record is a Markdown file in a Git repository. The search index is built on top and can be rebuilt; the repository stays canonical. I chose small, verifiable records over an automatic chat archive on purpose: an archive has everything, but finding the active conclusion in it is as hard as in a pile of files. One more distinction: the public repository holds the engine, while our working records live in a separate internal store. Installing KYB gives you your own store under your own access rules, with none of our notes.
The shared server solved place, not content. Pour the same old notes into a database and search just finds stale text faster. So the next question was: what should survive a session?
The most useful record usually answers a question source code cannot: why was it built this way? Code shows the chosen implementation, not which options were tried, where they fell short, or which constraint decided the outcome. Without that, the next agent may carefully rebuild a rejected design while sincerely believing it is an improvement—exactly my original problem.
Material therefore falls into three kinds. Knowledge is a state or rule worth returning to: a service's role, an interface agreement, a way to verify configuration. An incident is a problem that happened: symptom, impact, how to tell whether it continues, and how it ended. A task is work to be done, or the reason it was closed. The split keeps you from confusing an intention with a fact, or a finished attempt with an active recommendation.
Take an example record about choosing a message queue. "We use option B" says too little. The next agent does not need to obey an old conclusion blindly; it needs to tell whether the conditions behind it still hold. I would write such a record roughly like this (a template, not a real benchmark):
Decision: Use option B for this workload.
Reason: Option A failed requirement X under conditions Y.
Verification: Link to test, configuration, or report with revision SHA.
Revisit if: X or Y changes.
Related: Task key where the options were compared.

The "Revisit if" line turns an old decision from a prohibition into a condition: if X or Y has changed, revisiting is legitimate, and the agent does not have to guess whether the record expired.
The same logic produced habits I now treat as part of the record. A claim without a source soon becomes one more text asking to be trusted, so note how and when a fact was checked: not "the API listens on 9090," but "at revision X, checked the service-api listener, port 9090." Before creating a record, search for an existing key; the same knowledge under two names recreates the old chaos inside the new system, and Git will not clean it up. Hunches and long logs of competing hypotheses belong in an open task or incident, not standing knowledge. Secrets do not belong in the store at all; a pointer to where an authorized person or tool can fetch them suffices.
In v0.3.3, there is also a guard against silently losing tags: rewriting a task or incident keeps any tags the write omits. An explicitly empty list clears them. This is a narrow rule for metadata, not a partial update of any record: replacing the knowledge under an existing key still requires keeping the full current text.
Even a clean record serves different questions. In a toy example, Monday's entry records that service-api listens on port 8080. On Wednesday, the service moves to 9090, and the record is updated under the same key. "Where should I connect right now?" and "What was recorded on Monday?" need different answers, and both are fair questions.
Overwrite the row without history and Monday's answer is gone. Return every version without dates or states and an agent may pick the wrong one. Git offers a third path: the key stays the same while its edits form a history. Still, history alone answers nothing until you say which slice you need.
Each KYB query mode matches one question. A regular query searches current state: "where do I connect now." --history searches matching text across all saved content versions, including the current one; kyb history <key> shows a record’s complete chain of changes. --as-of builds a slice of the store at a chosen moment and searches inside it, telling you what the store knew when a release went out. --changed-between searches versions written within an interval and returns, for each key, the latest matching version from that window.

Figure 1. A toy example with synthetic ports; R1 and R2 are Git commits, not real-world events.
Figure 1 maps those answers onto one key. The current query gets R2 and port 9090; a cutoff between the commits gets R1 and port 8080; history may return both if both match; and export, discussed below, writes one latest row per key.
The old port appears in historical results by design, not by mistake. Pick the question and mode first; judge the hits second.
A note for readers checking this against the code. In --as-of, KYB first selects, for each key, the latest version recorded no later than time T—in revision order, not by the largest timestamp—and only then tests it against the query. A retraction recorded by T hides the key if the selected version is not newer than that retraction. In --as-of and at the upper bound of --changed-between, a bare date means 23:59:59 UTC; at the start of --changed-between it means 00:00:00 UTC. A SHA passed instead of a date becomes its commit timestamp rather than selecting an exact Git tree, and versions written within the same second cannot be distinguished by a time cutoff. See index.rs and main.rs in v0.3.3.
The "slice first, match second" order came from practice: we hit the same problem twice, first in notes, then in code.
A shared server did not cure the habit of appending clarifications to the end of a document. A September internal record examined a case where a correction was added below an incorrect instruction while the instruction stayed on top. A human reading the whole page might catch the contradiction; an agent taking the first matching passage still got the old advice. It was the stale-Markdown trap again, except both versions now shared one page instead of sitting in different folders.
After that, our working rule got specific: edit the active text, then search for the retired wording. Checking that "the right paragraph was added" is too weak; you must confirm the wrong one no longer reads as an instruction. Git removes the main reason to keep the old paragraph in the body, since earlier wording survives in history. And if the same instruction was once copied under another key, searching for a distinctive old phrase after the fix can help surface a duplicate within the searchable store—KYB does not deduplicate automatically or guarantee that every copy is found.
In October, we found a software version of the same mistake. Historical cutoff search first collected versions containing the query term and only then picked the latest. When a newer version no longer contained the old term, it dropped out of candidates too early, and the query returned old text even for a moment after replacement. In effect, the code did what the agent did with the page: it matched words without checking whether the passage still applied.
The fix in PR #17 of October 11 reversed the order: first select each key's state at the target moment, then test for a match. This is the order in effect in v0.3.3, the version this piece is written against. For full history search, old text is appropriate; for the state after a correction, it is the wrong answer. The patch and regression test are public; we did not measure how many real agent decisions the bug affected.
I covered both cases in more detail in a HackerNoon article. The lesson for shared memory is simple: verify the whole path from correction to the next read. A successful write says nothing on its own about which passage the next query will return.
Time slices tempt you to read the store's history as an event log. The same example shows why that is wrong. Say the service switched ports at 15:50, but the record was updated only at 16:20. An --as-of query for 16:00 returns the old port even though the cutover had already happened. The store was not wrong; it simply answers about write time, not event time.
KYB's temporal filters use Git commit time. That tells you what the store recorded and when; it does not replace deployment logs, metrics, or checking the running system. Incident fields do not prove event time on their own either. A client can supply started_at and detected_at; if detected_at is empty, the server keeps a stored value or fills in the current time. The server records the closing timestamp, resolved_at; clients do not supply that field. In an investigation, the store's history is one source, not the referee.
Another boundary appears once a record stops being current: "this record no longer applies" can mean two very different things.
First, the work is finished. An incident was resolved, or a task was done or dropped, yet the next agent still needs to know how the attempt ended, especially if it failed. KYB archives such records: they leave the active tree, while their final version stays in regular current-state search. Closing a task as done or dropped requires resolution text, including why dropped work was abandoned. The field guarantees only that text exists, not that it is true or useful; a bare "done" tells a future reader nothing.
Second, the knowledge turned out to be wrong. Then the record is retracted: it stops answering regular queries while its Git history remains. To an agent, these are distinct signals: "work is finished and its outcome is worth reading" versus "this is no longer knowledge." Collapse both into a single delete or overwrite, and a reader cannot tell whether the old record disappeared because the job was done or because it was wrong—the exact ambiguity my old Markdown files created.
States also matter for the store as a whole. Version 0.3.1 (October 15) added kyb export, which writes a commit snapshot: one row per key, with its latest content and state (active, archived, or retracted). Export answers "which keys existed at that commit, and in what state?" without including earlier versions; for those, use history.
Interface details. By default, export uses the current commit; --at pins another. The command is available in the CLI and over HTTP (GET /export), but is not an MCP tool in v0.3.3; see export.rs and mcp.rs. --changed-between returns content versions written inside the window, not retraction events. Whether a key was retracted can be checked from its history or an export snapshot.
Keeping a history of decisions still leaves another problem: open commitments. Even a correctly saved task is useless if you remember it after its deadline. The store may hold an exact date while an ordinary search for a service never shows it: the human or agent was asking about something else.
Deadlines arrived on October 27: v0.3.2 added them, and v0.3.3, released the same day, refined them and added their display in the console. A task can now carry a due date, a marker for external consequences of missing it, and a reminder window. If the date depends on a future event, it can be kept as a provisional one.
Task fields. The due date is stored in due, the marker for external consequences in hard, the reminder window in remind_days. A provisional date is set through expected together with waits_on. A deadline field omitted on rewrite keeps its previous value; moving a date remains a version in Git.
Take an example task about renewing a certificate. Writing "by December 15" in its body is not enough: to the search engine, that is just text. The due field lets a date be compared with a calendar, and hard explains why missing it matters. Successful search results, record reads, and task and incident lists can carry a deadlines block from the server: up to five overdue or soon-due open tasks. This selection is not limited to records matching the original question. Overdue items come before future ones; within each group, hard deadlines come first. The count of remaining records is shown separately. In the CLI, the reminder goes to stderr while the JSON answer stays on stdout. The block can be switched off, and if computing it fails, the main answer may arrive without it: the absence of a reminder does not prove there are no commitments.
For a "today" deadline, the reader's calendar matters. The CLI and the console send their own date; without one, the server uses its own. Historical queries work the other way: in --as-of, a bare date means the end of the day in UTC.
In the v0.3.3 web console, deadlines appear in a strip under the header, in the task queue, and in a separate by-date view. You can open a task, move its date, or close it with an outcome. But neither the strip nor the JSON does the work: KYB does not run a task on a schedule, repeat it, or send notifications. An agent still has to call the tool, read the reminder, and react — a limited way to make commitments more visible while reading, not proof that we miss deadlines less often.
Clear states still leave the last stretch: finding the right record. KYB searches current records by words and, if a model is loaded, by meaning. Historical versions in v0.3.3 are searched by words only: vectors exist only for current versions. Comparing the quality of current and historical results without accounting for that difference would mislead. The API response reports whether semantic search took part in a query.
How search works. Tantivy performs BM25 keyword search, and the multilingual-e5-small model, via ONNX Runtime, adds semantic candidates. The two lists are merged by reciprocal rank fusion. Without a model, only keyword search remains.

Figure 2. One canonical store, several interfaces, two search paths.
Figure 2 puts the pieces together: three client interfaces lead to one server, Git holds canonical versions, the index derives from them, and current and temporal queries take different paths. The web console uses the same HTTP API; its on-screen queues are not shown here. No diagram can guarantee that an agent will ask at all. A hit shows what was saved, not that it is true, and an uncalled tool never helps. How much that matters, I learned from the agents themselves.
On October 10, 2026 (PDT, UTC−7), I asked five internal coding agents how the shared store fit into their work. Four replied in writing; the replies live in an internal record committed October 11 UTC. This is a small qualitative survey, not a representative sample or usage telemetry. Still, one issue recurred: KYB works on demand, whereas some memory files load into context automatically at session start. The tool can be available while the agent forgets to call it, so part of our durable knowledge kept living in separate files instead of the shared store.
My original problem returned from the other side: before, an agent found an old file and trusted it; now it had a path to the current record but no prompt to take it. The agents asked for a short digest of workspace records at session start and an explicit verification status: who confirmed a fact, when, from what source, and at which revision. They also noted that behavioral rules for agents are awkward to model as ordinary knowledge. This is user feedback, not proof that automatic context injection improves accuracy. When that record was written, automatic kyb context was only a proposal, and the v0.3.3 server does not provide it. The deadline reminders described above arrived only after this survey, in late October. They return part of the current commitments, not the whole project context.
Separately, I tested provenance: when different agents write records, you need to know which one did. On October 11, I ran trial writes via the CLI from Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity, and via MCP from Claude Code, using the attribution mechanism from PR #16. Git history recorded labels for agent, session, workspace, and write transport, confirming those paths. In v0.3.3, the CLI refines this attribution: it walks up the process tree and picks the nearest agent with its own session. For example, Claude Code inside an Antigravity terminal should not be recorded as Antigravity; an explicit KYB_AGENT takes priority. Because clients supply the labels, they help audit changes but do not provide cryptographic identity or prove regular store usage.
An episode before the survey showed what a shared dependency costs. On October 8, an agent reported that several kyb query calls exited with no output after an external timeout expired. On October 11, repeat queries answered in under a second. Logs did not cover the first report, and nobody checked stderr or server status then, leaving the cause unknown—server, network, or client call. I treat this as an agent's report, not a reproduced defect or benchmark: when agents rely on a shared service, availability and clear timeout diagnostics become part of memory. The v0.3.3 CLI makes those diagnostics explicit: the exit code distinguishes success, a server rejection, a server error, and an unreachable server; the error goes to stderr, and stdout stays empty on failure. It still does not explain the October episode after the fact. If an agent checks only for text and ignores the exit code, even a good store history will not help.
The cases above and the agents' feedback point to Figure 3: a record must be written explicitly in one session and looked up explicitly in the next.

Figure 3. A record survives the session, but it does not enter a new context window on its own.
In Figure 3, Session A at the top learns something: the agent observes a change, checks a source, separates fact from hypothesis, and explicitly saves a version under a stable key. Git keeps the revision, and the index derives from it. Session B below is the next session. Because it does not automatically inherit the prior chat, it starts with a specific question, queries in the right mode, checks the result against a current source, and only then uses, corrects, or retracts the record. This is the intended order, not observed behavior of every agent.
Three points matter most. First, the question: "Tell me everything about the project" returns too much text, while "Why did we choose option B for this operation?" or "How did the last outage on this service end?" gives a clear target. An empty result may just need a component name, key, tag, or different wording. Second, verification: code at the right revision for an interface decision, configuration or observed responses for a running service. A record does not replace checking the primary source; it helps you locate what to check and how. Third, the update: an agent that learns a recommendation no longer applies and leaves the fix only in the current chat sets the same trap for the next session. Updating the record under its existing key, with reason and source, belongs in a task's definition of done.
Everything above rests on public code or saved internal records. Back to an earlier version of the system — v0.2.0 from August 16. One field's history shows what such records preserve. An internal task described a backlog of over fifty open tasks with no explicit priority, forcing urgency into tags. Status filtering existed; importance ranking did not. The initial request named the field severity, by analogy with incidents. Discussion refined that: severity describes damage that already happened, while priority fits future work. priority shipped in KYB v0.2.0—a concrete chain from friction to product change preserved in the store, not a measurement of agent speed.
What I lack is a reliable count of reads per agent, a link between reads and task outcomes, or a controlled comparison with and without KYB. That requires fixed tasks and models, a log of when each agent queried the store and what it got, and blind grading, knowing an available tool is not always called. Until such data exists, I describe mechanisms and observations, not causal effects.
This approach is not for everyone. A Git-backed shared store fits when several sessions or machines read and update changing knowledge and humans want history and diffs. For a single agent in one repository, a good README and a few project files are often enough. Git itself needs no server, but this design adds a shared server and an index to maintain, and the records still have to be verified and kept current. If your knowledge rarely changes, it may be one system too many.
Recall the opening scene: an agent finds a well-written note and heads down a path we abandoned long ago. What would change if that note lived in a shared store?
The agent would not get smarter. Instead, the record would have one shared entry point, an explicit lifecycle state, and a queryable version history under a single key. If the plan was abandoned, its task can be closed with the reason and wrong knowledge can be retracted from current search, separating the record's status from an active instruction. If the plan evolved, the earlier text sits in history and the body holds the current one. If the question is about the past, a slice at the right moment answers about the past without mixing it into the present. None of this guarantees that an agent will interpret a hit correctly, and it helps only when the agent asks the question and checks the answer against the source.
The practical takeaway does not require installing KYB. Next time you correct a note meant for agents, in a file, a wiki, or a store of your own, check three things. Did you replace the wrong text instead of appending a fix below it? Can a reader tell whether the plan was canceled, completed, or turned out to be wrong? Did you record why the decision was made and when it should be revisited? Three yes answers will not guarantee that the next agent never takes a wrong turn, but they give the next reader—human or session—an explicit status, the reason behind the decision, and a source to check instead of a stale note masquerading as the active plan.
To see how KYB works, start with the v0.3.3 release and the README of that version, which cover prebuilt binaries, installation, and Docker Compose. For a first check, complete that setup, save one decision with a "Revisit if" line, then query it from a fresh session. For Docker, use a separate fresh checkout: Compose keeps its data in that checkout's ./data directory.
Originally published on prod.codes.

articles.title: How Others Test Cross-Zone Locally
articles.description:
tc netem, Toxiproxy, Pumba, Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos, zone labels in kind and k3d, Jepsen and Testcontainers: what each gives, a short config form for each, and an honest comparison with what we built.
👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.
Every claim about a tool below links to its own documentation, read for this article. Our side of the comparison is what part 3 built; our failure-scenario runs are still planned.
This is part 5 of the series on testing cross-zone, cross-datacenter and cross-provider behaviour on a laptop. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.
Part 4, Placement In Every Trace, made every span say where it ran. Before going further with our own emulation, it is worth looking at what the world already uses. The tools sort into layers by where they act:



Layer
Tools
Acts on




kernel
tc netem
packets on a device


TCP proxy
Toxiproxy, Testcontainers' Toxiproxy module
one connection through a proxy


container
Pumba
a container's namespace, from outside


Kubernetes
Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos, zone labels in kind and k3d
pods selected by labels


history
Jepsen
what the system did, checked afterwards




The lower the layer, the more it can do and the less it knows about your system. The higher, the more it knows and the more it needs installed.
Everything network-shaped in this list ends at the kernel's netem sooner or later. It adds delay, jitter and loss to packets leaving a device (tc-netem(8)):
tc qdisc change dev eth0 root netem delay 100ms 20ms distribution normal
tc qdisc change dev eth0 root netem loss 0.3% 25%

The man page has one warning worth repeating: for TCP performance tests, netem should sit on the ingress of the receiver, not on the sender. On its own, netem knows nothing about which peer is which; that is up to the filters around it.
Toxiproxy is "a TCP proxy to simulate network and system conditions for chaos and resiliency testing" (Toxiproxy). The client connects to the proxy instead of the real service, and toxics are added to the proxy over an HTTP API on port 8474:
toxiproxy-cli create -l localhost:26379 -u localhost:6379 redis
toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=1000 redis

The toxics are latency, down, bandwidth, slow_close, timeout, reset_peer, slicer, limit_data and packet_loss. That is a richer vocabulary than netem has, at one price: the client must be pointed at the proxy.

Pumba does chaos and network emulation for containers on Docker, containerd and Podman (Pumba). It runs tc from a helper that joins the target's namespace, so the target image needs nothing:
pumba netem --duration 5m delay --time 3000 mydb
pumba iptables --duration 2m loss --probability 0.1 myapp

That is the same trick as our sidecar in part 3, packaged as a tool.
In Kubernetes, network chaos becomes a resource. Chaos Mesh's NetworkChaos supports netem, delay, loss, duplicate, corrupt, partition and bandwidth, selects pods by label and has a direction of to, from or both (Chaos Mesh):
apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkChaos
metadata: { name: delay-example }
spec:
  action: delay
  mode: one
  selector: { namespaces: [default], labelSelectors: { app: frontend } }
  delay: { latency: '20ms', jitter: '5ms', correlation: '0' }


LitmusChaos, a CNCF Incubating project, describes itself as "a Cloud-Native Chaos Engineering Framework with cross-cloud support" (Litmus). Its pod-network-latency experiment starts tc with netem inside the target, takes NETWORK_LATENCY, JITTER and DESTINATION_IPS or DESTINATION_HOSTS to aim at one peer, and can use Pumba as its library (pod-network-latency).
Zones on a laptop cluster are node labels. kind takes them in the cluster config (kind); k3d takes them on the command line with a node filter (k3d):
# kind
nodes:
  - role: worker
    labels: { topology.kubernetes.io/zone: a }
  - role: worker
    labels: { topology.kubernetes.io/zone: b }

# k3d
k3d cluster create --agents 3 \
  --k3s-node-label "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=a@agent:0" \
  --k3s-node-label "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=b@agent:1" \
  --k3s-node-label "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=c@agent:2"

Then topologySpreadConstraints spread the pods. DoNotSchedule tells the scheduler not to place a pod that would break the skew; ScheduleAnyway places it anyway, preferring nodes that reduce the skew (Kubernetes):
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: my-app } }



Labels and spread give zones as a scheduling fact. They give no distance: two "zones" on a laptop are as close as two processes.
Jepsen is at a different layer altogether. It "aims to improve the safety of distributed databases, queues, consensus systems" (Jepsen). While a test runs operations against a system, a nemesis process introduces faults, and a checker then analyses the recorded history for correctness (jepsen-io/jepsen). Network manipulation in its tests is typically done with iptables.

What Jepsen adds is not a better way to cut a network. It is a rigorous answer to "was the result correct", which every tool above leaves to you.
For tests in code, Testcontainers wraps Toxiproxy as a module. A ToxiproxyContainer joins the same network as the service under test, a proxy is created in front of it, and toxics are added from the test (Testcontainers):
proxy.toxics().latency("latency", ToxicDirection.DOWNSTREAM, 1_100).setJitter(100);
proxy.toxics().bandwidth("CUT_CONNECTION_DOWNSTREAM", ToxicDirection.DOWNSTREAM, 0);
proxy.toxics().bandwidth("CUT_CONNECTION_UPSTREAM", ToxicDirection.UPSTREAM, 0);

A connection cut is bandwidth zero in both directions; removing the toxics restores it.




What the world gives
What we built




latency and loss
netem directly; Pumba, Chaos Mesh, Litmus on top of it; Toxiproxy per connection
the same netem, but every rule derived from one topology file, per pair of sites


zones
node labels in kind and k3d, spread constraints
the same in k3d, plus compose with a subnet per site and zone


continents and providers
not a concept in any of these tools
levels of the declaration, with link kinds derived from them


partitions
Chaos Mesh partition, Jepsen's nemesis, Toxiproxy down
iptables DROP on both sides, each cut remembering its cause


checking the result
Jepsen's checker on the history
QA thresholds declared; the runs are planned


what we lack
bandwidth limits, a Jepsen-grade history check
—




The honest summary: we did not invent a new way to delay a packet. Under the hood it is netem and iptables, like most of the list. What is ours is the model above them - one declaration of a planet, from which every rule, every placement and every chaos action is derived. None of the tools above has a continent or a provider as a concept.
Two things, both from the top of the list. Toxiproxy's vocabulary - slow_close, reset_peer, limit_data - names failures that netem cannot express. And Jepsen's stance: a chaos run without a strict check of the result is a demonstration, not a test. Both are ideas, not plans yet.
Not a ranking of these tools. Each is good at its own layer.
Not that our emulation does what Jepsen does. It does not check histories.
Not that any of our scenarios has run. They are planned.
Not completeness. These are the tools I read for this part, not all of them.
Know the layer of a tool. Kernel, proxy, container, cluster, history - each sees a different system.
Read the documentation, not the reputation. Every claim here has a link.
A cut is not a test. The check of the result is the test.
Cross-anything on a laptop - Part 5. Next: Every Verdict Carries A Trace.
If you use Toxiproxy in tests, which toxic found the most? If you run Chaos Mesh or Litmus, do you run it locally or only on a shared cluster? If you have run Jepsen, what did the checker catch that nothing else would? Which of these would you add to a laptop first?

articles.title: Running Kali Linux on a PS4, with an installer on the TV
articles.description:
A PlayStation 4 is an x86-64 PC in disguise: an 8-core AMD Jaguar CPU, an AMD GPU and a hard drive. So in theory, Kali Linux should run on it. In practice, nothing about it is a normal PC, and stock Linux will not even get you a picture on the TV.
I built Kali Linux for PS4: Kali rolling with the XFCE desktop, installed from a graphical installer that runs on the TV. You copy five files to a jailbroken PS4 over FTP, run a payload and press X on the controller. As far as I could find, it is the first public Kali Linux release for the PS4.
Source code: github.com/blue0x1/kali-ps4

Here are the problems I had to solve along the way.
Kali's normal amd64 packages run on the Jaguar CPU without any emulation. The hard part is the kernel: mainline Linux cannot drive the PS4's southbridge (Aeolia, Belize or Baikal, depending on the model) or its GPU setup.
The community ps4-linux kernel tree solves that. My build system clones it, applies my own patches, builds it in Docker together with a Kali root filesystem, and packs everything into three files: the kernel (bzImage), my initramfs, and a 900 MB compressed Kali archive.
Linux is started by a community payload, the PS4 Linux Loader, which you run from GoldHEN. One detail cost me a lot of time: the loader extracts the console's own GPU firmware and the TV's EDID into an initramfs archive that is loaded before mine. When I shipped my own copy of the GPU firmware, it silently overwrote the correct one and the GPU failed its ring tests. The fix was to ship no GPU firmware at all and let the loader's files win.
The PS4 Slim and Pro do not output HDMI directly. The GPU sends DisplayPort to a Panasonic MN864729 bridge chip, which converts it to HDMI. With the stock kernel, the link trained, the kernel logs looked perfect, and the TV said "No signal".
To find out why, I wrote a small Python tool that talks to the bridge through the PS4's ICC interface (/dev/icc) and reads or writes its registers live, while Linux runs. That showed the actual problem: right after setup, and again after every EDID read, the bridge switched its HDMI output enables off and turned the video mute on.
The fix is a kernel patch that turns them back on after setup and after each EDID read:
/* HDMI output on, video unmuted */
mask(0x1e02, 0x70, 0x70);   /* output enables, bits 4-6 */
mask(0x1e00, 0x01, 0x01);   /* output enable, bit 0 */
write(0x705f, 0x10);        /* VMUTECNT: unmute */

The bridge still turns the output off now and then, for example when the TV renegotiates. So a small keep-alive helper checks the registers every few seconds and repairs them: a C version runs during boot, and a systemd service takes over inside Kali.
I wanted people to be able to install without a USB drive, on the PS4's internal hard drive. Two problems:
The PS4's user partition is encrypted with a key that is unique to each console. The loader hands that key to Linux, so the partition can be opened with cryptsetup (AES-XTS).
The partition uses the UFS2 file system, and Linux's UFS write support is experimental. Writing to it is a good way to corrupt the PS4's data.
My solution: Kali lives inside one big file on the PS4 drive, /user/home/kali-ps4.img, and Linux never writes the PS4's file system after creating it. At boot, the initramfs mounts UFS read-only, asks the file system where the file's blocks physically are (the FIBMAP ioctl), and turns that into a device-mapper table:
for (i = 0; i < nblocks; i++) {
    int blk = (int)i;
    ioctl(fd, FIBMAP, &blk);          /* file block -> disk block */
    /* merge contiguous runs, then print one line per extent: */
    /* "start length linear /dev/mapper/ps4hdd offset" */
}

Then it unmounts UFS and creates a dm-linear device from that table. The result is a normal block device that contains an ext4 file system, which Kali boots from. Reads and writes go straight to the file's blocks on disk, and the PS4's own file system metadata is never touched.
The only write to UFS happens once, during the first install: creating the file, filled with zeros so that every block is allocated. After that, the partition is only ever mounted read-only.
The installer runs inside the initramfs, before Kali exists: no X11, no Wayland, no GTK. So it is a small C program, fbui, that draws directly to the Linux framebuffer:
Fonts are pre-rendered: a Python script renders Noto Sans glyphs into a C header, so no font library is needed at boot.
It draws everything itself: anti-aliased rounded buttons with gradients and a glow, text, the Kali logo with a breathing aura, and a progress ring around the logo.
The controller is read straight from /dev/input/event* with evdev. The D-pad, the left stick and X work, and so does a keyboard.
Two lessons from the real hardware:
Small screen updates did not show up. Updating only the countdown digits through the amdgpu framebuffer emulation often had no visible effect until a large redraw happened later. My working theory is a write cache in the PS4's memory path. The reliable fix was to send a full frame on every update. Because the screen's pixel format matches the program's own buffer, a full 1920x1080 frame is a single write() and costs only a few milliseconds.
The animation must never slow the install. The progress screen is drawn from a separate thread. The main thread only copies the Kali archive from the drive to xz and counts bytes, which also gives an accurate progress percentage, and the drawing thread reads that counter 30 times a second.

Install to the PS4's internal drive or to a USB drive, chosen in the installer.
No PC tools, partitioning or USB stick needed.
After installing, every boot goes straight to the Kali desktop.
The whole project is GPL-2.0 and builds with make in Docker.

Most of the work was not Kali itself. It was the boot chain: payloads, initramfs, device-mapper, a misbehaving HDMI bridge, and a framebuffer that does not behave like a normal one. Reading kernel logs, poking registers live and testing on real hardware taught me more about how Linux boots than any desktop install ever has.
If you have a jailbroken PS4, try it and tell me how it works on your model:
github.com/blue0x1/kali-ps4
Built for learning and security research, on consoles you own.

articles.title: How to Setup Real-Time Voice AI on Dedicated Hardware (Step-by-Step)
articles.description:
A 500-millisecond delay destroys the illusion of human conversation.
If you are building a Real-Time Voice AI or an automated call center, you already know the latency budget is unforgiving. When a caller finishes speaking, your system has roughly half a second to hear, process, and speak the first word of its reply.
Cloud platforms struggle to hit this metric consistently. Shared hypervisors inject unpredictable scheduling delays. Network Address Translation (NAT) layers slow down audio packets. To build an AI voice agent that reacts at true human speed, you need bare-metal infrastructure.
This tutorial walks through deploying a production-ready, self-hosted voice AI pipeline directly onto dedicated GPU hardware.
Software optimization cannot fix a hardware bottleneck. Your entire stack—Voice Activity Detection (VAD), Speech-to-Text (STT), the Large Language Model (LLM), and Text-to-Speech (TTS)—must stay loaded in GPU memory (VRAM) simultaneously.
Based on production environments, here is exactly what hardware matches specific deployment scales:
  Testing & Starter Level (1x NVIDIA RTX 4090): Start here for Proof of Concept (PoC) builds. With 24GB of VRAM, an RTX 4090 easily holds a quantized model like Llama 3 8B alongside Faster-Whisper and a basic TTS engine. It reliably handles 1-2 concurrent calls.
  Production & Cost-Effective (1x NVIDIA RTX A6000, L40, or L40S): The sweet spot for SME customer service bots. 48GB of VRAM prevents the memory bottlenecks that cause latency spikes, allowing multiple concurrent streams.
  Enterprise Scale (NVIDIA H100): Built for massive concurrency and 70B+ parameter LLMs requiring instant Time-To-First-Token (TTFT). The 80GB memory bandwidth is mandatory here.
Start with a clean installation of Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. You need the proprietary NVIDIA drivers and the CUDA toolkit.
Update your system and install the baseline NVIDIA drivers:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install nvidia-driver-535 nvidia-dkms-535 -y
sudo reboot

Next, install Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit to isolate components while maintaining direct GPU access:
# Install Docker
curl -fsSL [https://get.docker.com](https://get.docker.com) -o get-docker.sh
sudo sh get-docker.sh

# Add NVIDIA Container Toolkit GPG key
curl -fsSL [https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey](https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey) | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg

# Add NVIDIA Container Toolkit repository
curl -s -L [https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list](https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list) | \
  sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list

# Update packages and install the toolkit
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y nvidia-container-toolkit

# Restart Docker to apply changes
sudo systemctl restart docker

Standard HTTP APIs cannot handle real-time audio. We use LiveKit as the media server to stream Opus-encoded audio over UDP with near-zero buffering.
Generate your LiveKit configuration:
docker run --rm -v$PWD:/output livekit/generate --local

Boot the LiveKit server:
docker run -d --network host \
  -v $PWD/livekit.yaml:/livekit.yaml \
  livekit/livekit-server \
  --config /livekit.yaml

Note: For production, secure this instance using Let’s Encrypt SSL certificates and map your domain.
The system must detect when the user stops speaking. We route incoming audio through Silero VAD, listening for a silence threshold (e.g., 300ms). The chunked audio then passes to Faster-Whisper (using CTranslate2 for accelerated inference).
from faster_whisper import WhisperModel

# Load the model directly into GPU VRAM. 
# It stays resident here to eliminate cold-start latency.
model = WhisperModel("large-v3", device="cuda", compute_type="float16")

segments, info = model.transcribe("caller_audio_chunk.wav", beam_size=5)
for segment in segments:
    print(segment.text)

You cannot wait for the AI to generate a complete paragraph before speaking. You must optimize for Time-To-First-Token (TTFT).
Deploy Llama 3 using vLLM to utilize PagedAttention and maximize memory efficiency. Launch vLLM as an OpenAI-compatible server:
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
    --model meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \
    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85

Tip: When querying this local API, always pass stream=True.
As the LLM streams tokens back, your application must parse them into complete sentences. As soon as the first sentence terminates (detecting punctuation), instantly push that string to your TTS engine.
While the TTS streams the first sentence back via LiveKit, the LLM continues generating the second sentence in the background. This overlapping asynchronous architecture is the secret to human-speed AI.
To bind these components, you need an asynchronous Python orchestrator:
Connect to the LiveKit room and subscribe to the user's audio track.
Buffer the audio until Silero VAD flags the end of speech.
Transcribe the buffer using Faster-Whisper.
Prompt the vLLM server with the transcribed text using stream=True.
Chunk the returning tokens by punctuation.
Synthesize chunks via TTS and push the audio frames back to the LiveKit room.
Orchestrating WebRTC, VAD, STT, LLM, and TTS inside a 500ms window requires eliminating network hops. By hosting this cascaded pipeline on a single dedicated GPU server, data moves between system memory and VRAM instantly.
Securing the right hardware is the first step. If you need a bare-metal server tailored for this exact architecture, browse our inventory of ready-to-deploy RTX 4090, A6000, L40S, and H100 servers to get your voice AI pipeline running today

articles.title: I'm building an open-source messenger for developers: This is what I have learned so far
articles.description:
Talking code in a regular chat app is frustrating. Snippets turn into walls of text. Pull request links get buried. And worst of all, people paste database URLs and API keys into chat, where they stay in the history forever.
So I started building Ack, an open-source messenger for developers.

What Ack does
Code blocks and diffs that look like they belong in an editor
Secret vaults: the secret is encrypted in your browser and deleted after the recipient reveals it

Where it is today
Working now: sign in with GitHub, search for people who have joined Ack, send an invite link to anyone who hasn't, and chat one on one. Messages are stored in Appwrite and sync between devices. When a friend joins through your invite link, your chat opens automatically.
Still in progress: locking each conversation so only its two participants can read it, and making the secret vault delete the secret on the server, not just in the browser. Until both are done, please don't put real passwords or keys into Ack. Treat it as a test.
Using sample data for now: the pull request cards and the Reviews inbox. Real GitHub connections through a GitHub App come next.
Not built yet: voice and video calls and pair programming. They're designed, and they're switched off behind feature flags until they work for real.
Try it: https://project-ack.vercel.app
https://github.com/kingenious0/ACK
How I'm building it
I'm not a hand-coder, and I'm upfront about that. I research the idea, write a spec, hand it to an AI coding IDE, build in small phases, test each phase, and review what the AI produced. The stack is Vite, React 19, TypeScript, Appwrite for sign-in and the database, and Vercel for hosting. I have been doing this for about 2 years now and it is really helping me.
Three things I learned
1. A display name is not a username.
2. Don't search all of GitHub.
3. Be honest about security from day one.
What's next
Real-time sync, connecting GitHub repos through a GitHub App so pull requests and CI results appear in chat, and then calls.

Thanks for reading. If you try Ack, tell me what breaks.

articles.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash Is 30% Cheaper. Your 1.1 Calls Move to It on December 3 Anyway
articles.description:
Book: Observability for LLM Applications


Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go


My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub






Google cut the price of its video model on November 5. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is generally available in the Gemini API, makes clips up to 15 seconds long, and costs about $0.07 per second of 720p video. Omni 1.1 Flash costs about $0.10 per second at the same resolution, according to Google's pricing page.
The line in the release notes that will reach your code is easier to miss. The Gemini API changelog says that starting December 3, 2026, requests to gemini-omni-1.1-flash automatically route to gemini-omni-1.2-flash and bill at 1.2 rates. You don't have to change anything for that to happen, which also means nothing in your deploy history will show the day the model changed.
Google's launch post lists what changed from 1.1:
Clips up to 15 seconds in one generation, up from 10, with the length set in one-second steps from 3 to 15.
Multi-turn editing: swap a product or a background, change lighting or aspect ratio, without regenerating the clip.
Better consistency for faces, garments, typography and brand colors across shots, with up to 6 reference images per the changelog.
Drafts at 360p or 720p, with upscaling to 1080p or 4K.
An invisible SynthID watermark on every output.
Google is specific about the weak spots. The post says development is ongoing "to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics" (Google). Google DeepMind's model page shows a side-by-side win rate of 62% to 38% for 1.2 over 1.1 on visual consistency, which The Next Web reports as testers preferring 1.2. That is a vendor's number, and it leaves room for plenty of clips where 1.1 looked as good or better.
The model ID is gemini-omni-1.2-flash, and calls go through the Interactions API. This is the basic sample from the Omni docs, with the prompt string split to fit:
import base64
from google import genai

client = genai.Client()

interaction = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-omni-1.2-flash",
    input=(
        "A marble rolling fast on a chain reaction "
        "style track, continuous smooth shot."
    ),
)
with open("marble.mp4", "wb") as f:
    f.write(base64.b64decode(interaction.output_video.data))

The same docs say: "When you don't set the duration, the model defaults to 10 seconds." Ask for more than 15 and you get an invalid argument error.

Longer clips, lower price per second. The price per call depends on how long you ask for.
Omni bills video as output tokens: $12.00 per 1M for 1.2, against $17.50 per 1M for 1.1 (pricing). The pricing page converts that into seconds:



Resolution
Tokens per second
1.2 price per second
15-second clip




360p
1,931
$0.023
about $0.35


720p
5,792
about $0.07
about $1.04


1080p (upscaled)
8,688
$0.104
about $1.56


4K (upscaled)
17,376
$0.209
about $3.13



The 720p clip total is Google's figure. The other three totals in the last column are my arithmetic from the page's token rates at $12 per 1M tokens.
A 4K clip costs three times a 720p clip of the same length, so the upscale step is where a video budget goes. The 30% cut is also per second. If your product moves from 10-second clips to 15-second ones, the bill per call goes up slightly: a 15-second 1.2 clip at 720p is about $1.04, and a 10-second 1.1 clip at the same resolution works out to about $1.01 by the same arithmetic at 1.1's rate.
There is no free tier for either model: the pricing page lists free-tier input and output as "Not available", and the rate limits page lists Free as "Not supported". A paid Tier 1 project gets 8 requests per minute and 40 per day. Tier 3 gets 40 per minute and 2,000 per day. Limits apply per project, not per API key. The changelog says paid-tier limits doubled with this release.
The deprecations page is plain about it: "Effective December 3, 2026, the endpoint is automatically routing API requests to gemini-omni-1.2-flash". The Omni docs add that this happens "with no code changes required." Omni 1.1 Flash was released on August 27, 2026, and the older gemini-omni-flash-preview was shut down on October 22, per the same deprecations page.
The switch is cheaper and needs no code change. What changes is the model answering your request, and Google's model page shows the two are not the same:
Audio. The model page lists 1.1's output as "Video" and 1.2's as "Video with native Audio, Text". The Omni docs say 1.2 "generates a video with audio based on your text description." If a step downstream assumes a silent track, check it.
Edit and extend inputs. 1.1 took input video up to 10 seconds for editing and extension. 1.2 takes up to 15 seconds for editing, uses a 10-second lookback for extension, and extends up to 30 seconds total.
The look. Google's 62% figure comes from Google DeepMind's own comparison (DeepMind). Your prompts, your brand colors and your reference images were not in that sample.

On December 3, the same model ID leads to a different model.
Google did the same thing with its December 1 reroute of gemini-2.5-pro to Gemini 3.8 Flash: the ID stayed fixed while the model and the price behind it changed.
The launch post names "audio cues" among the reference inputs (Google). The API docs say: "Uploading audio inputs or audio references is unsupported in the current version of the API." Audio inside a reference video is ignored. The blog covers several products at once, including Flow and the Gemini app, so the cue may live there. On the API, build against the docs.
Multi-turn editing chains turns with previous_interaction_id. The docs also say setting store=false "means the generated video won't be editable in subsequent turns." If your team turns storage off for data reasons, editing is off too, and every change becomes a new generation at full price.
Find every hardcoded Omni ID in your code:




grep -rn "gemini-omni-1.1-flash" .
grep -rn "gemini-omni-flash-preview" .

A hit on the preview ID points at a model the model page lists as shut down.
Move to gemini-omni-1.2-flash yourself, behind a config value, so you pick the day:




import os

OMNI_MODEL = os.environ.get(
    "OMNI_MODEL", "gemini-omni-1.2-flash"
)

Re-run a fixed set of your own prompts and reference images on 1.2, and put the results next to the 1.1 clips you shipped. Check the audio track, the duration and the file size. The docs offer a delivery setting of "uri" that returns a hosted file URI for outputs over 4MB.
Check your rate-limit tier against your peak. Tier 1 allows 8 requests a minute but only 40 a day, so a batch job running at the per-minute cap uses up the day in five minutes.
Moving early also gets you the lower price now instead of on December 3.
Does a vendor swapping the model behind an ID you pinned count as a breaking change in your book, even when it gets cheaper? Tell me in the comments.
A reroute like this is a quality change you never deployed. Catching it takes three habits: trace which model actually answered each request, keep an eval set you can re-run the week a vendor swaps the model behind an ID, and watch cost per request instead of the monthly total. Observability for LLM Applications is the book I wrote about exactly that, for LLM features running in production.
I also build Hermes IDE, so weigh this with that in mind: it's a free, source-available desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux that runs Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents side by side, each in its own worktree. Download it or read the code on GitHub.

articles.title: Moving face search off AWS Rekognition in two days: a photo marketplace's playbook
articles.description:
This article was written with AI.
Disclosure: I work on SightRadar, the API this team moved to. The figures below are the ones sellphotos.online reported. The full case study is at sightradar.com/customers/sellphotos.
sellphotos.online is a marketplace where event and sports photographers upload their shots and guests buy the ones they appear in. A guest uploads a selfie and the platform finds every photo that person is in. They process hundreds of thousands of photos a month across weddings, marathons and corporate events.
They ran this on AWS Rekognition and had two problems with it. The bill had grown to about $3,500 a month. And in crowd shots, the smaller faces in the back rows were often missed, so guests searched for themselves and came up empty. Those guests complained to the photographer, and the photographer complained to the platform.
They moved face search to SightRadar in about two days. This post is the playbook they followed, with code. Most of it applies whichever provider you move to.
A selfie-search product on Rekognition is three things:
A collection of faces indexed from every uploaded photo (IndexFaces).
A search on every guest visit (SearchFacesByImage).
A threshold that decides what counts as a match.
The first two are API calls, and they port. The third is a number tuned to one vendor's model, and it does not. Most bad migrations go wrong at the threshold, not at the API.
They set up a test collection, indexed about 5,000 photos from a recent wedding, and compared search results against what Rekognition returned for the same photos.
Pick an event with the hard cases in it: group shots, people far from the camera, bad light. Every provider handles a well-lit portrait, so clean photos tell you nothing.
Their backend is mostly Python, so they used the Rekognition shim. It keeps boto3's method names, arguments and response shapes, so the change is the import and the constructor:
from sightradar_rekognition_shim import client   # was: import boto3

rek = client(api_key="frs_...")                    # was: boto3.client("rekognition")

rek.create_collection(CollectionId="test-wedding")
rek.index_faces(
    CollectionId="test-wedding",
    Image={"URL": "https://cdn.example.com/wedding/0001.jpg"},
    ExternalImageId="0001",
)

Two things to know before you start:
The shim maps Image={"S3Object": ...} to a public S3 URL, which has to be fetchable. A private bucket needs a URL the API can fetch, such as a presigned one passed as {"URL": ...}.
The shim is Python only (PyPI). On Node or Java you map the calls to the REST API yourself, which is more work than swapping an import.
This was the biggest chunk of work: hundreds of thousands of existing photos. Indexing them one synchronous call at a time is slow at that volume. Instead they used the batch endpoint, which takes up to 1,000 photo URLs per call and delivers one webhook per photo as results land. They scripted the submissions and let it run overnight.
import os
import requests

BASE = "https://api.sightradar.com"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['SIGHTRADAR_API_KEY']}"}

def submit(collection_id, photos, webhook_id):
    """photos: up to 1,000 dicts of {"url": ..., "external_id": ...}"""
    r = requests.post(f"{BASE}/v1/batches", headers=HEADERS, timeout=30, json={
        "collection_id": collection_id,
        "op": "index",
        "webhook_endpoint_id": webhook_id,
        "photos": photos,
    })
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["batch_id"]

# all_photos: your catalogue as {"url", "external_id"} dicts; WEBHOOK_ID from POST /v1/webhooks
for i in range(0, len(all_photos), 1000):
    print(submit("events", all_photos[i:i + 1000], WEBHOOK_ID))

Each webhook carries your external_id, a status, and on failure an error.code such as image_fetch_failed. Failed photos are not charged. Keep a list of them and resubmit once you have fixed the cause. The batch guide covers registering the endpoint and verifying signatures.
Plan for this step to take longer than you expect. It did for them. While it runs you are paying both providers, because live uploads still go to the old one. That double cost is short, but put it in the budget.
For the next day, every guest search went to both providers and they compared the ranked results. The shim returns Rekognition-shaped responses, so the comparison is short:
import boto3
from sightradar_rekognition_shim import client

aws = boto3.client("rekognition", region_name="us-east-1")
sr = client()  # reads SIGHTRADAR_API_KEY

# Start loose on both sides: you are comparing what each provider finds,
# not deciding matches yet. That is step 4.
AWS_THRESHOLD = 70
SR_THRESHOLD = 50  # the shim divides by 100, so this is 0.5 cosine

def photo_ids(rek, threshold, selfie):
    res = rek.search_faces_by_image(
        CollectionId="events",
        Image={"Bytes": selfie},
        FaceMatchThreshold=threshold,
        MaxFaces=100,
    )
    return {m["Face"]["ExternalImageId"] for m in res["FaceMatches"]}

selfie = open("guest.jpg", "rb").read()
a = photo_ids(aws, AWS_THRESHOLD, selfie)
b = photo_ids(sr, SR_THRESHOLD, selfie)
print(f"both: {len(a & b)}  only AWS: {len(a - b)}  only SightRadar: {len(b - a)}")

Look at the "only" sets by eye. They tell you more than any aggregate number.
In their case, SightRadar found more faces in group shots. Its detector scans each photo at several scales, which catches smaller faces that a single-scale pass misses. The ranking order differed slightly in a few searches, but every face Rekognition found, SightRadar found too.


This is the step people skip, and then they blame the new provider when results look off.
Rekognition scores similarity from 0 to 100. SightRadar returns cosine similarity from 0 to 1. The shim converts the scale both ways, but converting the scale does not convert the decision. Two models put the same "same person" call at different scores, so a cut-off copied from Rekognition is wrong on the new model.
They spent a day on this with known match and non-match pairs from their test events. The method is short:
Collect a few hundred same-person pairs and a few hundred different-person pairs from your own photos: same cameras, same venues, same lighting.
Score every pair.
Pick your cut-offs from the scores: accept above nearly all of the different-person scores, and review the band below that where most real matches still sit.




def score(url_a, url_b):
    r = requests.post(f"{BASE}/v1/compare", headers=HEADERS, timeout=30,
                      json={"sourceUrl": url_a, "targetUrl": url_b})
    r.raise_for_status()
    body = r.json()
    return body["similarity"] if body["face_found"] else None

# same_person_pairs / different_person_pairs: lists of (url_a, url_b) you labelled by hand
same = sorted(s for a, b in same_person_pairs if (s := score(a, b)) is not None)
diff = sorted(s for a, b in different_person_pairs if (s := score(a, b)) is not None)

# Accept automatically above the score that lets through at most ~1% of
# different-person pairs. Below that, down to where 95% of real matches sit,
# ask the guest "Is this you?" instead of hiding the photo.
accept = diff[int(len(diff) * 0.99)]
review = same[int(len(same) * 0.05)]
print(f"accept >= {accept:.3f}; review band {min(review, accept):.3f} to {accept:.3f}")

Each compare is billed as two photos ($0.00186 a pair), so 600 pairs costs about $1.12. Two bands usually beat a single cut-off for photo discovery, because a wrong suggestion is cheap when the guest confirms it. The threshold guide goes further on picking bands.
By now every existing photo was indexed in both systems, so the cutover was a config change: new index calls and searches went to SightRadar. If you can afford it, keep the old collection for a while so rolling back is also just a config change.
The bill went from about $3,500 to about $1,550 a month, for the same photos and the same number of searches.
Fewer "my photos didn't show up" tickets within the first month. They didn't track it formally; the support team noticed fewer of those complaints.
Clearer visibility into costs: per-operation spend, search results and collection sizes in one console, instead of CloudWatch metrics and Cost Explorer tags.

For context on those numbers, here are the list prices. Rekognition's first US tier is $0.0010 per image. SightRadar's batch rate is $0.00062 per photo, 38% lower, and its real-time rate is $0.00093, 7% lower. Your saving depends mostly on how much of your volume can go through batch and on how many calls you make per photo. Run your own numbers with the pricing calculator before you decide anything.
You use more than faces. Labels, text detection, celebrity recognition, video and user vectors are not supported. The shim raises NotImplementedError for them instead of silently doing nothing.
You are on very high volume. Rekognition's per-image rate drops to $0.0008 after the first million images a month and lower after that. At that scale the gap narrows, and for real-time calls it can flip.
You are not on Python. There is no shim for other AWS SDKs.
You rely on final deletes. Deleting a collection is a restorable soft delete by default. Pass Immediate=True through the shim if you need Rekognition's finality.
The full case study: How sellphotos.online cut their face recognition bill

Migrating from AWS Rekognition
Rekognition shim reference
Choosing a similarity threshold
sellphotos.online
Disclosure again: I work on SightRadar. Results depend on your photo mix, your volume, and how carefully you calibrate thresholds.

articles.title: GitHub Immutable Releases を設定したリポジトリのリリース用パイプラインが静かに壊れたので直した話
articles.description:
はじめに
#
リリースの改竄を防ぎソフトウェアサプライチェーンのセキュリティを確保する Immutable releases を試すため、個人開発の Electron アプリのリポジトリに適用したのが1年前。
https://developer.mamezou-tech.com/blogs/2025/11/16/github-immutable-releases/

それから随分経ちましたが、eMudhra のインシデントで古い Electron アプリを放置しておくのはよくないということでリリース作業を行いました。
筆者の Electron アプリのリポジトリは以下です。
https://github.com/kondoumh/sbe

 -->
 eMudhra のセキュリティインシデントについて
認証局「eMudhra」の「emSign G3」階層で、中間CAの鍵8件（TLS用6件、コード署名用2件）が復元できるほど脆弱に生成されていた問題。
窓の杜の記事より
https://forest.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2152996.html

Jack さんのブログにあるように、Electron は Chromium の証明書ストアを同梱しており、Chromium や Node を更新してビルドし直さない限りストアが更新されません。つまり、古いバージョンの Electron で作られたアプリを配布し続けていると、信頼すべきでなくなったルート証明書をいつまでも信頼し続けてしまいます。
https://blog.jxck.io/entries/2026-10-25/emudhra.html

Electron アプリはビルド時点のルート証明書を内包するため、古い Electron バージョンでビルドされたままのアプリは、失効すべき証明書を信頼し続けてしまうリスクがあるということです。
リリース用ワークフローにエラーが発生
#
さて、アプリの細かい修正や Electron のバージョンアップを実施して、リリースの段階になりました。このリポジトリでは新しいバージョンのタグを作成し push するとリリース用のワークフローが起動するように設定しています。冒頭の記事で書いているように、macOS / Windows / Linux のバイナリーを strategy.matrix を使ってそれぞれのプラットフォームの Actions Runner で生成し、GitHub のリリースを作成する softprops/action-gh-release を使ってリリースしています。
今回、アプリのバージョンを v3.9.0 に bump してこのワークフローを1年ぶりに起動したところ以下のようなエラーで失敗しました。
Found release v3.9.0 (with id=432353934)
⚠️ Unexpected error fetching GitHub release for tag refs/tags/v3.9.0: HttpError: Validation Failed: {"resource":"Release","code":"custom","field":"target_commitish","message":"target_commitish cannot be changed when release is immutable"} - https://docs.github.com/rest/releases/releases#update-a-release
Error: Validation Failed: {"resource":"Release","code":"custom","field":"target_commitish","message":"target_commitish cannot be changed when release is immutable"} - https://docs.github.com/rest/releases/releases#update-a-release


  

Immutable releases にまつわるエラーのようです。
調べると、v3.9.0 のタグに2つのリリースオブジェクトが作成されているようでした。
id=432353876(draft, immutable=false): アセットに必要なファイル(sbe-Setup-3.9.0.exe, sbe-3.9.0-universal.dmg, sbe-3.9.0.AppImage)は全部揃っている。そしてまだ Imutable にはなっていない
id=432353934(published, prerelease, immutable=true): アセット0件のまま Immutable として確定されてしまい、同じタグ名を握ってしまっている
初期のワークフローの実装
#
エラーが発生した時点のワークフローファイルは以下のようになっていました。strategy.matrix で各プラットフォームの Runner のジョブでビルドとリリースを一気に行う形です。
Release.yml(エラー発生時点)
  
name: Release

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - "!*"
    tags:
      - "v*"

jobs:
  build:

    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [windows-latest, macos-latest, ubuntu-latest]

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Setup nodejs
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '20'
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm install
    - name: Package (Windows / Linux)
      if: matrix.os != 'macos-latest'
      run: npm run dist
      env:
        GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    - name: Package (macOS)
      if: matrix.os == 'macos-latest'
      run: npx electron-builder --mac --universal
      env:
        GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    - name: Publish
      uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
      with:
        files: |
          dist/**/*.exe
          dist/**/*.deb
          dist/**/*.AppImage
          dist/**/*.dmg
        prerelease: true ## Pre-release の状態で作成する


  

action-gh-release のパラメータに prerelease: true を指定しているため、それぞれの Runner でビルド成果物を Pre-release に追加するワークフローとなっています。
当時は、この設定でちゃんとドラフトのリリースが作成されていたようです。記事にも
prerelease を true にすることで、ドラフトリリースを作成してくれます。
とあり、ドラフトで添付ファイルと差分を確認してから Publish をクリックするという、人間が最後に明示的に公開する手順を踏んでいました。
失敗した Pre-release は捨てるしかない
#
今回、v3.9.0 の重複して作られたリリースのうち、空のまま immutable 化してしまった方を削除すれば、もう一方の(アセットが揃っている)ドラフトを publish できると考え、空のリリースを削除しました。ところが、ドラフトページから publish ボタンを押すと、今度は以下のエラーになりました。
There was an error creating your Release: tag name was used by an immutable release.
Pre-release とはいえ一度 immutable なリリースに使われたタグ名は、そのリリースを削除してもリポジトリ側で「使用済み」として記録され続けるようです（改竄防止のための仕様としては筋が通っています）。v3.9.0 というタグ自体がもう使えなくなってしまったので、バージョンを上げて v3.9.1 として仕切り直すことにしました。
レースコンディションの回避
#
対策として最初に考えたのは、strategy.matrix で独立した3つのプロセスで publish が実行されることによるレースの解消です。並列の matrix ジョブが実行され、各ジョブが個別に softprops/action-gh-release を呼んで同じ v3.9.0 タグのリリースを作成・更新しようとします。そこへほぼ同時にリクエストが飛んだ結果、同じタグに対してリリースオブジェクトが複数作られるような動きになったのではないか。そこで、ビルドとリリースでジョブを分けて、ビルドだけをマトリクスで実行するように修正しました。また、バイナリを作成している electron-builder のオプションに --publish never をつけることで暗黙的な公開を抑止しました。
name: Release

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - "!*"
    tags:
      - "v*"

jobs:
  build:

    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [windows-latest, macos-latest, ubuntu-latest]

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Setup nodejs
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '20'
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm install
    - name: Package (Windows / Linux)
      if: matrix.os != 'macos-latest'
      run: npm run dist -- --publish never
    - name: Package (macOS)
      if: matrix.os == 'macos-latest'
      run: npx electron-builder --mac --universal --publish never # electron-builder の暗黙リリースを抑止
    - name: Upload artifacts
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: dist-${{ matrix.os }}
        path: |
          dist/**/*.exe
          dist/**/*.exe.blockmap
          dist/**/*.deb
          dist/**/*.AppImage
          dist/**/*.dmg
          dist/**/*.dmg.blockmap
          dist/**/*.zip
          dist/**/*.zip.blockmap
          dist/latest*.yml
        if-no-files-found: ignore

  publish:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Download artifacts
      uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
      with:
        path: dist
        pattern: dist-*
        merge-multiple: true
    - name: Publish
      uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
      with:
        files: |
          dist/*.exe
          dist/*.deb
          dist/*.AppImage
          dist/*.dmg
          dist/*.zip
        prerelease: true


  

fail-fast: false にしているので、全ての Runner のジョブが終わってから後続の publish ジョブが実行されます。
Pre-release 自体が immutable になっていた
#
ジョブを分離したワークフローで v3.9.1 のタグを push し直したところ、3つの Runner のビルドジョブはすべて成功しました。ところが、最後の publish ジョブの Publish ステップそのものが、今度は以下のエラーで失敗してしまいました。
Cannot upload asset sbe-3.9.1-universal-mac.zip to an immutable release.
ジョブは1つに統合したはずなのに、4つのアセット（exe, dmg, zip, AppImage）のうち3つまではアップロードできて、最後の1つだけ弾かれる、という中途半端な失敗でした。原因は softprops/action-gh-release 自身が出力したエラーメッセージに書かれていました。
GitHub only allows asset uploads before a release is published, but draft prereleases publish with the release.published event instead of release.prereleased. If you need prereleases with assets on an immutable-release repository, keep the release as a draft with draft: true, then publish it later from that draft and subscribe downstream workflows to release.published.
つまり、Immutable releases が有効なリポジトリでは prerelease: true を指定しただけの場合、リリースの作成と同時に release.published イベントが発火して即座に公開・immutable 化されてしまうとのことでした。4つのアセットをほぼ同時にアップロードし始めたものの、その途中でリリースがロックされてしまい、間に合わなかったアセットだけ弾かれた、というわけです。
そこで、以下のように softprops/action-gh-release のオプションで draft: true を指定し、Pre-release ではなくドラフトでリリースを作成するように変更しました。
Release.yml
  
    - name: Publish
      uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
      with:
        files: |
          dist/*.exe
          dist/*.deb
          dist/*.AppImage
          dist/*.dmg
          dist/*.zip
        prerelease: true
        draft: true # ドラフトモードでリリースを作成


  

v3.9.1 のタグも、空のまま immutable 化したリリースに使われてしまっていたため、こちらも再利用できません。結局、v3.9.2 としてもう一度タグを push し直し、ようやく4つのアセットが揃ったドラフトリリースが作成されました。ドラフトのまま変更可能な状態なので、不要な .blockmap ファイルなどを削除し、内容を確認してから publish をクリックして、無事リリースが完了しました。
何が変わったのか
#
softprops/action-gh-release の現在の最新版である@v3のドキュメントにはこうあります。
GitHub only allows asset uploads before a release is published, but draft prereleases publish with the release.published event instead of release.prereleased. If you need prereleases with assets on an immutable-release repository, keep the release as a draft with draft: true, then publish it later from that draft.
つまり現時点で prerelease: true では即座に release.published イベントで公開・immutable 化されてしまうということです。
1年前は prerelease: true でも人間が「Publish」を押すまでは公開されない・ロックされない挙動だった(事実上 draft と同じように振る舞っていた)
今は prerelease: true だけだと即座に公開・ロックされ、draft: true を明示しないと同じ挙動にならない。
つまり、ジョブが並列で同じリリースに書き込みに行く構造自体は1年前から変わっていない。当時それでも壊れなかったのは、「Pre-release は人間が手動 Publish するまでロックされない」という仕様のおかげで、並列書き込みが衝突する前に猶予があったから。GitHub がこの間に「Pre-release も即ロック」という形に仕様を厳格化した(おそらく、誰も手動で publish しなければ永久にミュータブルなままで immutable release の保証が骨抜きになる抜け道を塞ぐため)。そして、今回1年ぶりに実行したことでその変更の影響を受けてしまったということのようです。
 -->
 Information
上記は推論であり、この仕様変更を明記した GitHub 公式の Changelog ブログのエントリは見つけられませんでした。確度の高い状況証拠(筆者の過去のブログの記述・softprops/action-gh-release ドキュメントの現在の注意書き)からの推測である点はご承知おきください。
さいごに
#
以上、Immutable releases の仕様変更によりリリース用ビルドパイプラインがいつの間にか壊れていた話でした。
Matrix ビルドはジョブを並列化する有効な手段ですが、Immutable Releases のようにリソースを固定化してしまう機能と併用する際は注意が必要ということがわかりました。Immutable Release 自体はよりセキュアになっていると思いますので、安心して使っていただいてよいと思います。
